\section{How to read this atlas}

The development moves from finite algebra to an infinite-dimensional operator. Each passage changes the question that must be answered. A matrix may preserve the norm of one spinor without defining an operator on every square-summable field. A finite Fourier calculation may be exact without controlling the omitted modes. A symmetric formula still needs a specified domain and an adjoint-domain argument before self-adjointness is established.

The following twelve plates isolate these transitions. They follow a single set of conventions: the unit torus $\T^3=(\R/\Z)^3$, normalized Haar measure, Fourier momentum $p(n)=2\pi n$, and four-component column spinors with coordinates $0,1,2,3$. Time evolution uses $U(t)=\exp(-itH)$ on each finite matrix. The centered symbol is
\[
q_h(n)_j=\frac{\sin(2\pi h n_j)}{h}\quad(h\ne0),
\qquad q_0(n)=2\pi n.
\]
This is a Fourier multiplier on the same torus. The integer modes have not been identified modulo a sampled grid.

\paragraph{Three kinds of visual evidence.}
The projector tree and transport square explain definitions and relationships. Their geometry is schematic. The matrix display records exact entries. Dispersion, evolution, and tail plots are recomputed numerical illustrations of explicit formulas. A smooth curve does not certify a theorem, and a finite partial sum does not decide convergence of an infinite series. The accompanying text supplies the analytic distinction in each case.

\paragraph{The current endpoint.}
Blocks 46 and 47 supply full coefficient-space and physical-space evolution. Blocks 48 and 49 supply a densely defined, self-adjoint, closed free Dirac Hamiltonian, its finite Fourier graph approximation, and its exact first-order weighted domain. The identification of the previously constructed evolution with the unbounded Hamiltonian's generated group remains outside this checkpoint. The plates keep that boundary visible.

\paragraph{Reproduction.}
All figures were regenerated using \code{tools/make_figures.py}. The script checks the Clifford relations in exact symbolic arithmetic and compares the displayed propagator with an independent matrix-exponential calculation on a stated finite set. The run contract, software versions, numerical tolerances, finite ranges, checksums and limitations are recorded in \code{evidence/figure_checks.json}. These checks validate the examples used by the atlas. They do not substitute for the Lean source or its verification receipts.

\section{Refinement preserves an exact decomposition}
\atlasfigure{01_refinement}{A four-dimensional coordinate example. Each child is an orthogonal projector and the children sum to their parent. The drawing is a schematic of refinement, not an identification with spatial dyadic boxes.}

Take $P=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0,0)$ and $Q=I-P$. The first split distinguishes two orthogonal sectors. Refining $P$ into its first two coordinate projectors preserves its range exactly. Refining $Q$ does the same for the remaining coordinates:
\[
P=P_0+P_1,\qquad Q=Q_2+Q_3,\qquad
I=P_0+P_1+Q_2+Q_3.
\]
An operator $T$ can be resolved into transfer blocks $P_aTP_b$. A block records which input sector is accepted and which output sector is retained. Summing all blocks recovers $T$ when the projectors resolve the identity. Off-diagonal blocks describe transfer between distinct sectors, while diagonal blocks describe action within one sector.

The value of the language is its bookkeeping. It distinguishes an exact decomposition from an approximation that discards some blocks. This elementary example also explains why a change of representation must preserve both the projectors and the inner product when it is used to transport norm claims.
\sourcepointer{Conceptual entry point to projector refinement and transfer blocks. The displayed coordinate example is exact elementary linear algebra. It is not a new theorem attributed to Block 49.}

\clearpage
\section{A Fourier mode lives on the three-torus}
\atlasfigure{02_torus_modes}{Three genuine three-dimensional slices of the real part of $e_{(1,1,1)}(x)$. Equal values on opposite faces reflect periodicity. Color shows a real component, not probability density.}

The scalar mode $e_n(x)=\exp(2\pi i n\cdot x)$ has absolute value one everywhere. For normalized Haar measure, its squared $L^2$ norm is also one. Distinct integer modes are orthogonal:
\[
\int_{\T^3}\overline{e_n(x)}e_k(x)\,dx=\delta_{nk}.
\]
The plate shows the mode $(1,1,1)$ at $x_3=0,1/2,1$. Its real part changes sign, while the magnitude of the full complex wave stays fixed. The upper and lower faces have the same pattern because adding one to a coordinate changes the phase by an integer multiple of $2\pi$.

A spinor amplitude $a_n\in\C^4$ multiplies this scalar mode. For a finite sum $f(x)=\sum_n e_n(x)a_n$, orthogonality removes the cross terms only after integration. It gives $\norm{f}_{L^2}^2=\sum_n\norm{a_n}^2$. Local interference can still produce a nonconstant density. This distinction is essential when reading the evolution plate.
\sourcepointer{Normalized torus Fourier realization in the finite-packet development and the full Fourier equivalence of Block 47. The plotted slice is an illustrative evaluation of one basis function.}

\clearpage
\section{The coordinate convention determines the signs}
\atlasfigure{03_clifford}{Real and imaginary parts of the four supplied $4\times4$ generators. Blank cells are zero. The lower panel records coefficients of $i$, so a displayed $-1$ denotes the entry $-i$.}

Rows and columns follow the spinor order $0,1,2,3$. In particular,
\[
\alpha_yv=(-iv_3,\;iv_2,\;-iv_1,\;iv_0)^T.
\]
The sign in this formula fixes the worked packet's fourth component. Replacing it silently with a different convention would change the explicit evolution even if another Clifford representation remained mathematically valid.

The matrices are Hermitian involutions and anticommute in distinct directions. Therefore the modal Hamiltonian
\[
H(m,p)=m\beta+p_x\alpha_x+p_y\alpha_y+p_z\alpha_z
\]
satisfies $H(m,p)^2=(m^2+|p|^2)I$. The cross terms vanish in pairs. This single identity explains the energy shell and the trigonometric formula for the matrix exponential. Hermiticity supplies exact norm preservation.

The figure generator checks all four squares and all six distinct anticommutators in exact Gaussian-integer arithmetic. That small computation is a reproducibility check of the displayed matrices, separate from the formal proofs in the project.
\sourcepointer{The traditional paper's explicit Clifford representation, consistent with the mode-action convention of the checked development.}

\clearpage
\section{Dispersion changes when momentum becomes a sine}
\atlasfigure{04_dispersion}{Continuum and centered axis energies at $m=1$, $h=1/12$. Curves interpolate real momentum. Dots mark actual integer torus modes on the positive and negative centered branches. The right panel enlarges the low momentum energy difference.}

The square of the Hamiltonian is scalar, so its two shell magnitudes are
\[
E(p)=\sqrt{m^2+|p|^2},\qquad
E_h(p)=\sqrt{m^2+\sum_j[\sin(hp_j)/h]^2}.
\]
Each nonzero shell has positive and negative spectral sectors. The centered symbol is close to $p$ when $|hp_j|$ is small. Over a larger real momentum interval it bends and returns, whereas the continuum shell continues to grow. These global curves should not be read as uniform approximation over all modes.

For the actual torus axis mode $n=(1,0,0)$, $p=(2\pi,0,0)$ and $q_{1/12}=(6,0,0)$. The corresponding positive energies are $\sqrt{1+4\pi^2}$ and $\sqrt{37}$. The torus mode labels remain integers throughout. A curve connecting those labels is a visual interpolation, not an additional family of torus eigenfunctions.
\sourcepointer{Modewise shell identities in the checked finite-dimensional development. The plotted real-momentum interpolation and numeric values are recomputed illustrations.}

\clearpage
\section{Quadratic consistency has a fixed-mode scope}
\atlasfigure{05_symbol_error}{The centered sine momentum approaches the continuum momentum. At the fixed axis mode $n=(1,0,0)$, the numerical error follows the analytic quadratic bound as $h$ decreases. The sample spacings are $2^{-2},\ldots,2^{-11}$.}

The elementary sine remainder gives
\[
\left|\frac{\sin(hp_j)}{h}-p_j\right|
\leq \frac{|h|^2|p_j|^3}{6}.
\]
For a fixed finite set of modes, the momentum factors have a finite maximum. This yields a quadratic consistency estimate with a constant depending on that set. Exact Hermitian evolution then converts a modal Hamiltonian error into an evolution error growing at most linearly with $|t|$.

The dependence on momentum matters. The factor $|p_j|^3$ grows without bound as the integer mode increases. One cannot remove a Fourier cutoff and retain the same quadratic constant for every $L^2$ field. Additional weighted regularity is needed to sum a rate estimate of this form over infinitely many coefficients.

The checked full-space convergence result instead controls a chosen finite core and its remaining tail separately. The next two plates show why exact stability makes that passage possible without assigning a universal quadratic rate to arbitrary data.
\sourcepointer{Fixed-mode and finite-packet consistency through Block 45. The infinite-space extension in Block 46 is strong compact-time convergence, without a universal rate for arbitrary $L^2$ data.}

\clearpage
\section{Local density moves while total norm is conserved}
\atlasfigure{06_packet_evolution}{The exact three-mode centered packet with $m=1$, $h=1/12$. Left: pointwise density on the line $x_2=x_3=0$. Right: integrated component weights and their conserved total. A line through the torus is a display slice, not the integration domain.}

Use modes $(0,0,0)$, $(1,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1)$, with initial spinors respectively $e_0/\sqrt2$, $e_0/2$ and $e_0/2$. Their coefficient norm squares sum to one. Each coefficient evolves by
\[
U_n(t)=\cos(E_nt)I-i\frac{\sin(E_nt)}{E_n}H_n,
\]
with the continuous zero-energy branch interpreted as $I$.

The field is a coherent sum of these evolving modes. Cross terms redistribute the local density, and individual spinor components exchange weight. Fourier orthogonality and modal unitarity nevertheless give $\norm{f_h(t)}_{L^2}^2=1$ for every real time. Component 1 remains zero in this particular example and is omitted from the right-hand legend.

The atlas checks the formula against an independent matrix exponential and verifies the total norm on 401 times in $[0,1]$. The all-time statement comes from the algebraic and Fourier arguments, not from the sampled residual.
\sourcepointer{The traditional three-mode worked example, using the exact coordinate convention. Modal unitarity and finite-packet norm conservation are within the checked frontier.}

\clearpage
\section{Removing the cutoff requires two choices}
\atlasfigure{07_two_tail}{An axis-supported example $a_n=n^{-2}/\sqrt{\zeta(4)}$ for $n\geq1$. Left: coefficient mass and a selected cutoff. Right: explicit bounds at $|t|\leq1$ for three fixed cutoffs. The horizontal floors are the two-tail term.}

Write $P_Ka$ for a finite Fourier truncation. The two exact evolutions preserve the norm, so
\[
\norm{(U_h(t)-U(t))a}
\leq\norm{(U_h(t)-U(t))P_Ka}
       +2\norm{(I-P_K)a}.
\]
The correct order is to choose $K$ so that the tail is small, then choose $h$ so that the finite-core term is small uniformly over the time interval. The plot uses the smaller of the finite-core quadratic bound and the elementary stability bound $2\norm{P_Ka}$.

Holding $K$ fixed leaves a positive tail floor even as $h\to0$. Increasing $K$ lowers that floor but increases the coefficient in the finite-core estimate. This tradeoff is not a failure of convergence. It explains why a density-and-stability proof establishes convergence without automatically providing one quadratic rate for all data.

The selected axis sequence is only an illustration. The checked density argument applies to arbitrary square-summable coefficient fields, with finite supports chosen for those fields.
\sourcepointer{The cutoff-removal strategy of Block 46. The numerical bound curves are additional illustrative calculations, not a re-run of Lean.}

\clearpage
\section{Square summability is weaker than operator membership}
\atlasfigure{08_domain_thresholds}{Finite partial sums through $N=4096$ for axis-supported coefficients $a_{(n,0,0)}=n^{-s}e_0$, $n\geq1$. The zero mode and every other mode are zero. The exact classifications below use the power-series criterion, not the apparent flattening of a curve.}

For this one-dimensional support inside $\Z^3$, ordinary square summability and first-order weighted summability have different thresholds:
\[
\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-2s}<\infty\iff s>\tfrac12,
\qquad
\sum_{n\geq1}(1+4\pi^2n^2)n^{-2s}<\infty
\iff s>\tfrac32.
\]
The choice $s=0.4$ does not define an $L^2$ coefficient field at all. The choice $s=1$ defines an $L^2$ field outside the Dirac domain. The borderline $s=1.5$ still lies outside that domain because its derivative-energy series contains a harmonic tail. The choice $s=2$ belongs to the domain.

These are thresholds for the stated axis-supported family. They must not be transferred unchanged to radially populated three-dimensional families, where the number of modes in each shell also grows. The operator domain is a condition on the complete weighted sum, not a visual smoothness judgment.
\sourcepointer{Block 49's exact first-order weighted Fourier characterization. The four power-law examples are traditional consequences illustrating the distinction.}

\clearpage
\section{A graph approximation controls the field and its image}
\atlasfigure{09_graph_truncation}{Truncation errors for the normalized positive-axis sequence $a_n=n^{-2}/\sqrt{\zeta(4)}$ at $m=1$. Both curves use infinite tail formulas, evaluated with the Hurwitz zeta function. Dotted lines show asymptotic slopes rather than fitted bounds.}

The graph norm is
\[
\norm{a}_{H_m}^2=\norm{a}^2+\norm{H_ma}^2.
\]
Convergence in ordinary $\ell^2$ controls the field. Graph convergence also controls the result of applying the unbounded operator. For the displayed sequence,
\[
\norm{a-P_Ka}^2=\frac{\zeta(4,K+1)}{\zeta(4)},\qquad
\norm{a-P_Ka}_{H_1}^2=
\frac{2\zeta(4,K+1)+4\pi^2\zeta(2,K+1)}{\zeta(4)}.
\]
The ordinary error decays like $K^{-3/2}$ while the graph error decays like $K^{-1/2}$. Both vanish, but the unbounded multiplier makes high modes more expensive in the second measurement.

Block 48 proves the structural statement behind this example: finite truncations preserve the domain, commute with the multiplier, and approximate a domain vector together with its image. This gives a finite Fourier graph core. No observed slope is needed for that existence statement.
\sourcepointer{Block 48's finite Fourier graph approximation and Block 49's exact modal energy identity. The chosen sequence and zeta evaluations are illustrative.}

\clearpage
\section{Fourier transport carries the domain as well as the formula}
\atlasfigure{10_fourier_transport}{The inverse Fourier equivalence carries coefficient fields to physical torus fields. The square commutes by the definition of the transported operator. The upper horizontal map acts on the exact domains, and the lower map acts on the ambient Hilbert spaces.}

Let $\mathcal F$ send a physical field to its Fourier coefficients. The physical Hamiltonian is defined by
\[
\mathsf H_m=\mathcal F^{-1}H_m\mathcal F,
\qquad
D(\mathsf H_m)=\mathcal F^{-1}D(H_m).
\]
The domain clause is essential. The lower horizontal equivalence is defined everywhere on the Hilbert space, but the vertical arrows need not be. They are unbounded operators with specified dense domains.

Because Fourier transport is unitary, it preserves inner products and transfers self-adjointness and closedness. It also gives the physical form of the weighted domain condition:
\[
f\in D(\mathsf H_m)
\iff \sum_{n\in\Z^3}(1+|2\pi n|^2)\norm{\widehat f(n)}^2<\infty.
\]
This is a genuine physical-space operator on torus spinor fields. The square does not by itself identify a previously constructed time-evolution group with the generator of this operator. That further relationship is an explicit next step.
\sourcepointer{Block 47's unitary Fourier equivalence and Block 49's transported physical Hamiltonian with its exact domain.}

\clearpage
\section{Changing mass changes the action, not the domain}
\atlasfigure{11_mass_domain}{Left: the graph weight relative to the first-order Fourier weight for three masses. Right: the exact graph norm square of one fixed normalized domain vector. The physical mass interpretation often takes $m\geq0$, while the mathematics permits every real $m$.}

For a square-summable coefficient field, the energy identity is
\[
\norm{H_ma}^2=m^2\norm{a}^2+
\sum_n|2\pi n|^2\norm{a_n}^2.
\]
The mass contribution is finite whenever $a\in\ell^2$. Finiteness of the unbounded part therefore depends only on the momentum-weighted sum. Consequently $D(H_{m_1})=D(H_{m_2})$ for any two real masses.

Equivalent graph norms need not have equal numerical values. For the normalized axis family $a_n=n^{-2}/\sqrt{\zeta(4)}$, the momentum contribution is exactly
\[
\frac{4\pi^2\zeta(2)}{\zeta(4)}=60.
\]
The field norm is one, hence $\norm{a}_{H_m}^2=61+m^2$. A larger mass raises this graph norm while leaving the vector inside the same domain. The graph-weight ratios in the left panel approach one at high momentum because the derivative term dominates.
\sourcepointer{Block 49's mass-independent domain and global energy identity. The zeta example is a traditional exact specialization checked symbolically for this atlas.}

\clearpage
\section{The endpoint is precise, and so is the next connection}
\atlasfigure{12_frontier}{The local progression to Block 49. The upper boxes describe results recorded as checked in the modular cumulative release. The lower boxes are subsequent targets. They are not included in the current completion claim.}

The finite-packet work controls matrices and finite sums. The next passage removes the Fourier cutoff and transports full evolution to physical fields. The final passage in this checkpoint constructs the unbounded Hamiltonian and identifies its maximal domain. These are distinct achievements with distinct proof obligations.

The immediate connecting problem is to identify the full unitary evolution already constructed with the evolution generated by this self-adjoint Hamiltonian. A proof must establish the relevant generator or spectral-exponential relationship on the correct domain. Merely displaying the same modewise matrix formula does not record that full theorem in Lean.

Operator convergence, quantitative rates under additional regularity, and coupling to background fields are further steps. Dynamical gauge fields, backreaction and gravity belong to larger research phases. Nothing in this diagram assigns them a completion percentage or treats them as consequences already obtained from the free-matter result.
\sourcepointer{The Block 49 final status and continuation boundary. The present edition reports the checked modular cumulative classification. It does not claim a new clean root build.}

\clearpage
\section{Reading the plates as one argument}

The first three plates fix the representation. Refinement resolves an operator into sectors, normalized Fourier modes identify its spatial channels, and the Clifford matrices fix how each channel acts on a four-component spinor. No convergence claim is needed at this stage. The central facts are exact algebraic identities and exact normalization choices.

The next three plates introduce evolution and approximation. The sine symbol changes the dispersion relation while retaining Hermiticity. Its small-spacing error is quadratic at fixed momentum. Exact modal unitarity then protects the total packet norm even when the local density moves. Stability and consistency serve different purposes: stability prevents growth of an error that is already present, while consistency makes the finite-core error small as the spacing decreases.

The two-tail plate explains how these finite facts reach a full Hilbert space. First approximate a given vector by finite data. Then refine the spacing on that fixed finite approximation. Unitarity controls the discarded part. The argument is powerful precisely because it does not require every square-summable vector to have finite derivative energy.

The remaining operator plates ask a different question: which fields can the continuum Hamiltonian itself act on as an $L^2$ operator? The weighted-domain criterion answers this exactly. Graph approximation strengthens ordinary approximation by controlling both a field and its image. Fourier transport carries the resulting closed, self-adjoint operator and its domain to physical torus fields. The mass identity shows that this domain reflects spatial regularity rather than a choice of mass.

\paragraph{What the companion can establish.}
The atlas makes the source architecture inspectable and supplies reproducible examples. The symbolic matrix checks are exact in their finite algebraic setting. The plotted calculations are bounded numerical evaluations with recorded conventions. Infinite-dimensional conclusions depend on the corresponding mathematical arguments and formal source statements.

\paragraph{What remains separate.}
This edition does not create Block 50, identify the full operator exponential, prove a resolvent limit, or introduce a coupled gravitational theory. Its purpose is to present the existing checkpoint as a coherent mathematical narrative and make the precise next obligations visible. That separation allows later chapters to grow without retroactively changing the meaning of the results already recorded.

\endgroup

A projector atlas divides a state into orthogonal packets and an operator into the transfers between those packets. The division can be fine or coarse, fixed or moving, and finite or countable. The useful question is always specific: which information survives the chosen representation, and what additional hypothesis makes the next operation legitimate?

These twelve plates build a common language before the specialized free Dirac construction. They begin with finite coordinates, where reconstruction is exact. They then introduce currents, changing frames, density matrices and tensor products. The final plates show what changes for positive measurement effects and for an unbounded operator on infinitely many coordinates. A finite commutative obstruction explains why ordinary pointwise differences cannot supply every desired differential identity.

States are columns. The inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument. An evolution generator $A$ obeys $\dot\psi=A\psi$. For Hamiltonian evolution, $A=-iH$ and $\hbar=1$. The first current index is the destination:
\[

=2\operatorname{Im}\inner{P_a\psi}{HP_b\psi}.

States are columns. The inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument. An evolution generator $A$ obeys $\dot\psi=A\psi$. For Hamiltonian evolution, $A=-iH$ and $\hbar=1$. The first current index is the destination:
\[
J_{a\leftarrow b}=2\operatorname{Re}\inner{P_a\psi}{AP_b\psi}
=2\operatorname{Im}\inner{P_a\psi}{HP_b\psi}.
\]
The diagonal infinite-dimensional examples use $H e_n=n e_n$ for $n\geq1$. They are transparent sequence models, rather than an identification of the full physical Hamiltonian with this particular spectrum.

\section{Packets retain amplitudes, while weights retain less}
\atlasfigure{01_packets}{An exact four-coordinate state. The left panel preserves its real and imaginary amplitudes. The right panel keeps only the two coarse packet weights. The weights add to one, but do not determine the original state.}

Take
\[
\psi=\frac1{\sqrt7}(1,i,2,-i)^T,\qquad
P_A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0,0),\qquad P_B=I-P_A.
\]
These are orthogonal projectors, so $P_AP_B=0$ and $P_A+P_B=I$. The state is reconstructed exactly as $\psi=P_A\psi+P_B\psi$. Its squared norm splits without a cross term:
\[
\norm{\psi}^2=\norm{P_A\psi}^2+\norm{P_B\psi}^2
=\frac27+\frac57=1.
\]
The packets remain vectors in the original space. Replacing each packet with its squared norm loses information. For example, changing the sign of the fourth imaginary coordinate preserves both weights, while changing the state. Relative phases can later change interference and transfer.

Refinement separates coordinates that a coarse packet groups together. Coarsening sums orthogonal projectors and their populations. Neither operation requires discarding state information when all packet vectors are retained. An approximation begins only when some data are actually omitted or replaced.



\clearpage
\section{An operator has an input packet and an output packet}
\atlasfigure{02_corners}{Left: an exact Hermitian matrix, with the coarse division after coordinate 2. Right: squared Frobenius norms of its four corners. These are descriptive matrix sizes, not transition probabilities or packet populations.}

For the same two projectors, every operator has four corners:
\[
H=P_AHP_A+P_AHP_B+P_BHP_A+P_BHP_B.
\]
The rightmost projector accepts the input packet and the leftmost projector selects the output packet. Thus $P_AHP_B$ carries the part of $H$ that sends packet $B$ into packet $A$. This convention fixes the orientation of every later transfer formula.

In the displayed example, the two within-packet blocks have squared Frobenius norm $2$, and the two between-packet blocks have squared Frobenius norm $5$. Their magnitudes alone do not determine a current. A current also depends on the evolving state and the phases in the relevant bilinear expression.

Composition introduces intermediate packets. Inserting the identity between two operators gives
\[
P_aXY P_b=\sum_c(P_aXP_c)(P_cYP_b).
\]
The sum records all two-step paths from the input packet $b$ through $c$ to the output packet $a$. This is exact matrix multiplication expressed through an atlas. Dropping an intermediate packet changes the operator unless a separate argument shows that its contribution vanishes or is acceptably small.



\clearpage
\section{A current is signed, and its direction can reverse}
\atlasfigure{03_coherent_current}{A two-level Hamiltonian with coupling $g=1$. The population curves exchange weight periodically. The lower panel uses destination-first currents, so a positive $J_{2\leftarrow1}$ increases the second population.}

Let $H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and start from $\psi(0)=(1,0)^T$. The exact solution is
\[
\psi(t)=(\cos t,-i\sin t)^T,\qquad
p_1(t)=\cos^2t,\quad p_2(t)=\sin^2t.
\]
The current and its reverse are
\[
J_{2\leftarrow1}=2\operatorname{Im}(\overline{\psi_2}\psi_1)
=\sin(2t),\qquad J_{1\leftarrow2}=-J_{2\leftarrow1}.
\]
Consequently $\dot p_2=J_{2\leftarrow1}$ and $\dot p_1=-J_{2\leftarrow1}$. Their sum is zero at every time. At a turning point of a population curve, the net current vanishes even though the coupling matrix is unchanged.

The sign distinguishes a current from a nonnegative transition rate. An antisymmetric current is a balance quantity. Its negative value means that the net transfer goes in the reverse direction. No interpretation as a classical stochastic rate follows from this identity alone.

The displayed solution is compared with an independent matrix exponential at 25 times. Its current is checked at 601 times. These checks catch sign and implementation errors. The exact formula supplies the all-time conclusion.

Adding the first two entries gives $\dot p_A=-3/2$. Adding the last two gives $\dot p_B=3/2$. The internal transfers of sizes $3$ and $1$ disappear from these coarse derivatives because each contributes once with each sign.

\[
U(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \psi(t)=e_1,\qquad \phi(t)=U(t)^*\psi(t).
\]

Differentiating the coordinate change gives
\[

\qquad \dot\phi=-\Gamma\phi.
\]
For a general laboratory generator, this becomes $\dot\phi=(U^*AU-\Gamma)\phi$. The minus sign is fixed by differentiating $U^*U=I$. Both terms are needed to describe what a moving observer records.

This example separates a physical state change from a change in the measuring atlas. They can produce similar population curves while having different causes. Omitting the connection would predict constant moving coordinates for this stationary laboratory state, contradicting the explicit rotation.

\section{Coherences and jump rates carry different information}
\atlasfigure{06_density_and_jumps}{Left: coherent Hamiltonian exchange and symmetric Lindblad jumps, both starting from population $(1,0)$. For $H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, the density equation is $\dot\rho=-i[H,\rho]$. The two pure states
\[
\rho_+=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&i\\-i&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\rho_-=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\i&1\end{pmatrix}

\[

p_1(t)=\tfrac12+(p_1(0)-\tfrac12)e^{-2t}.

The left panel therefore contrasts periodic coherent exchange with relaxation generated by these specified jumps. This does not say that all Lindblad systems reduce to a classical two-state chain. Closure holds here because of the chosen jump operators and invariant diagonal family.

\atlasfigure{09_cutoff_topology}{For $He_n=ne_n$, retain the first $N$ coordinates and set the omitted output to zero. The unitary error on one fixed state decays, while its operator norm remains exactly one. The resolvent has a decaying tail and does converge in operator norm.}

\atlasfigure{10_weighted_domains}{Partial sums through $N=4096$ for $a_n=n^{-s}$ and $He_n=ne_n$. The three panels weight the same coefficients by $1$, $n$ and $n^2$. Four exponents illustrate the distinct membership regimes. These finite plots do not decide convergence.}

\[

a\in\ell^2&\Longleftrightarrow&\sum_n n^{-2s}<\infty

a\in D(H^{1/2})&\Longleftrightarrow&\sum_n n^{1-2s}<\infty

\section{The CRT phase check and normalization}\label{a-verify-crt}

For coprime \(a,b\) and \(N=ab\), the input CRT map sends \(n\) to \((n\bmod a,n\bmod b)\). The Fourier output must instead use
\[
 k_a=kb^{-1}\pmod a,\qquad
 k_b=ka^{-1}\pmod b.
\]
Indeed the product Fourier kernel has exponent
\[
 2\pi i\left(\frac{k_an_a}{a}+\frac{k_bn_b}{b}\right).
\]
After putting over denominator \(ab\), its numerator is congruent to \(kn\) modulo \(ab\). Thus it equals the \(N\)-point kernel. The exact checker tests this congruence for all basis pairs of three selected coprime modulus pairs. It also detects that reusing the input residue map for the output fails in this family.

The test uses integer modular arithmetic, rather than floating complex exponentials. It therefore separates a phase convention mistake from a tiny numerical Fourier residual. The general congruence argument supplies the proof for arbitrary coprime moduli; enumeration supplies a bounded implementation check.

The normalization check has a similarly exact surrogate. Let \(B\) be the coarse-to-fine incidence matrix with one parent assigned to each fine address and \(p\) children per parent. Then
\[

 \qquad I=p^{-1/2}B,

\]
The rational checker verifies \(B^*B=p1\) directly and keeps the square-root normalization outside the integer matrix. Raw replication increases squared norm by \(p\); it must not be used as a counting-norm isometry.

\section{A concrete depth-compatibility failure}\label{a-verify-grover}

The product graph in the source combines a cycle with a rooted regular tree and uses the Grover coin at each vertex. At a fixed depth, the coin and arc-reversal shift are unitary. At an old leaf away from exceptional cycle sizes, the old degree is \(d=3\): two cycle arcs and one arc to its parent. After extension, \(p\) child arcs are added. The new coin is
\[
 G_{d+p}=\frac{2}{d+p}\mathbf1\mathbf1^*-1.
\]
Apply it to one old outgoing arc basis vector. Every newly added outgoing child arc receives amplitude \(2/(d+p)\). Therefore the squared norm in the new-arc sector is
\[
 \|QG_{d+p}e_j\|^2
 =\frac{4p}{(d+p)^2}>0.
\]

\[
 p=2:\quad\|QG_5e_j\|^2=\frac8{25},
 \qquad
 p=3:\quad\|QG_6e_j\|^2=\frac13.
\]
The coarse evolution followed by old-arc inclusion cannot contain these new arcs, so the intertwining defect is nonzero.

\section{Geometric transport and local work}
\label{c:core:transport}

The first gravitational question is local: how does a prescribed geometry
change transport and energy exchange? A second question is dynamical: which
equations determine that geometry? Keeping these questions distinct lets a
finite model establish an exact balance law before it is coupled to a
gravitational constraint system. Throughout this section the metric
coefficients are supplied functions. The scalar field evolves on them.

\subsection{A finite scalar action on a diagonal metric}

Take a periodic chain with $N\geq3$ sites, spacing $h>0$, and indices modulo
$N$. The continuum metric motivating its coefficients is
\[
 ds^2=-N(t,x)^2dt^2+a(t,x)^2dx^2,
 \qquad N(t,x)>0,\quad a(t,x)>0.
\]
The repeated letter $N$ in this metric is the lapse, whereas the integer
$N$ counts lattice sites. In the finite formulas below only the coefficient
names $w$, $c$, and $v$ are needed:
\[
 w_j=\frac{a_j}{N_j}>0,\qquad
 c_{j+1/2}=\frac{N_{j+1/2}}{a_{j+1/2}}>0,\qquad
 v_j=N_ja_jm^2\geq0.
\]
Thus $N/a$ is the coordinate characteristic speed of the continuum
massless equation. Assume these finite coefficient arrays are continuously
differentiable in time. For a real field $\varphi_j(t)$ set
$\Delta_j=\varphi_{j+1}-\varphi_j$ and define
\begin{equation}
 L_h=\frac h2\sum_jw_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 -\frac1{2h}\sum_jc_{j+1/2}\Delta_j^2
 -\frac h2\sum_jv_j\varphi_j^2.
 \label{c:core:scalar-action}
\end{equation}
Variations with compact time support give
\begin{equation}
 w_j\ddot\varphi_j+\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j
 =\frac{c_{j+1/2}\Delta_j-c_{j-1/2}\Delta_{j-1}}{h^2}
 -v_j\varphi_j.
 \label{c:core:scalar-evolution}
\end{equation}
The neighboring edge terms in the action produce the two terms in the
spatial numerator. The time integration by parts differentiates
$w_j\dot\varphi_j$, including the $\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j$ term.

\Needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}[Local energy, flux, and geometric work]
\label{c:core:scalar-work}
For every twice differentiable solution of
\eqref{c:core:scalar-evolution}, define
\begin{align}
 e_j&=\frac h2w_j\dot\varphi_j^2+\frac h2v_j\varphi_j^2
 +\frac{c_{j+1/2}}{4h}\Delta_j^2
 +\frac{c_{j-1/2}}{4h}\Delta_{j-1}^2,\nonumber\\
 F_{j+1/2}&=-\frac{c_{j+1/2}}{2h}\Delta_j
             (\dot\varphi_j+\dot\varphi_{j+1}),\nonumber\\
 s_j&=-\frac h2\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 +\frac h2\dot v_j\varphi_j^2
 +\frac{\dot c_{j+1/2}}{4h}\Delta_j^2
 +\frac{\dot c_{j-1/2}}{4h}\Delta_{j-1}^2.
 \label{c:core:scalar-densities}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \dot e_j+F_{j+1/2}-F_{j-1/2}=s_j.
 \label{c:core:scalar-balance}
\end{equation}
In particular, $E_h=\sum_je_j$ satisfies
$\dot E_h=\sum_js_j=-\partial_tL_h$, where the partial derivative holds
$\varphi$ and $\dot\varphi$ fixed.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}

of the kinetic and mass terms at site $j$ is
\[
 \frac{\dot\varphi_j}{h}(B_j-B_{j-1})
 -\frac h2\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 +\frac h2\dot v_j\varphi_j^2.
\]
The right edge contribution differentiates to
\[
 \frac{\dot c_{j+1/2}\Delta_j^2}{4h}
 +\frac{B_j}{2h}(\dot\varphi_{j+1}-\dot\varphi_j),
\]
and the left edge has the analogous expression. Adding these terms
leaves
$B_j(\dot\varphi_j+\dot\varphi_{j+1})/(2h)$ on the right and its
negative counterpart on the left, plus $s_j$. These are exactly the flux
terms in \eqref{c:core:scalar-balance}. Periodic summation cancels every
interface flux. Each edge coefficient derivative appears twice with
weight $1/(4h)$, giving $-\partial_tL_h$.
\end{proof}

Every $e_j$ is nonnegative under the stated coefficient assumptions. An
interval of cells $r,\ldots,s$ obeys the exact coarse balance
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\sum_{j=r}^se_j
 +F_{s+1/2}-F_{r-1/2}=\sum_{j=r}^ss_j.
\]

\subsection{Conformal curvature as an exact boost holonomy}

Consider a twice continuously differentiable real function $\phi$ on an
oriented $(t,x)$ rectangle, and the coframe
\[
 e^0=e^\phi dt,\qquad e^1=e^\phi dx,
 \qquad ds^2=e^{2\phi}(-dt^2+dx^2).
\]
Write
\[
 K=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \omega=(\phi_xdt+\phi_tdx)K.
\]
The coframe satisfies the torsion-free Cartan equations with this
connection. Since every connection value is a multiple of the same
matrix, $\omega\wedge\omega=0$. Therefore
\begin{equation}
 \Omega=d\omega=(\phi_{tt}-\phi_{xx})K\,dt\wedge dx,
 \qquad R=2e^{-2\phi}(\phi_{tt}-\phi_{xx}).
 \label{c:core:conformal-curvature}
\end{equation}
This fixes the scalar-curvature sign convention used in this monograph.

We use the archive's plus-sign edge convention: for each oriented
boundary edge define $U_e=\exp(+\int_e\omega)$. This specifies the
signed transport observable used below. Multiplying in boundary order
yields an exact identity
\begin{equation}
 W_\square
 =\exp\left(K\oint_{\partial\square}(\phi_xdt+\phi_tdx)\right)
 =\exp\left(\frac K2\int_\square e^{2\phi}R\,dt\,dx\right).
 \label{c:core:conformal-holonomy}
\end{equation}
To see the second equality directly, integrate $\phi_{tt}$ along the
two horizontal endpoints and $\phi_{xx}$ along the two vertical
endpoints, with the boundary orientation from $dt\wedge dx$. This is
the rectangular fundamental theorem of calculus. No path-order
correction survives because the edge exponents commute.

If the integrated coefficient is $\chi$, then
\[
 e^{\chi K}=\cosh\chi\,I+\sinh\chi\,K.
\]
This preserves the Lorentz form $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$ and has
positive eigenvalues $e^{\chi}$ and $e^{-\chi}$. Its real principal
matrix logarithm is $\chi K$. These are Lorentz boosts. The positive
Hilbert norm used for unitary color transport in the gauge monograph
is a different structure.

\begin{example}[Constant curvature density]
For $\phi(t,x)=b(t^2-x^2)/2$, one has
\[
 \phi_{tt}-\phi_{xx}=2b,
 \qquad R=4b\,e^{-2\phi},
 \qquad W_\square=e^{2b\,\operatorname{area}(\square)K}.
\]
The curvature density $e^{2\phi}R/2$ is constant although $R$ varies
with position. Adding oriented subrectangle integrals reconstructs
the coarse rapidity exactly.
\end{example}

The plus-sign observable is assigned the endpoint action
\[
 G(t,x)=e^{\chi(t,x)K},\qquad
 U_{a\to b}'=G(b)U_{a\to b}G(a)^{-1}.
\]
It corresponds to the signed connection rule
$\omega_+'=\omega_++d\chi\,K$. Intermediate endpoint factors cancel,
so the loop observable is conjugated at its base point. For the
Cartan convention $D=d+\omega$, a coframe transformation $e\mapsto Ge$
instead gives $\omega'=\omega-d\chi\,K$ and parallel transport

rapidity of $W_\square$ defined here. The fixed-frame curvature identity

\label{c:core:weak-field}

Weak gravity provides checks on attraction, variational signs, and

\subsection{Radial Poisson equation and a finite variational problem}

Let $G>0$, let $\rho(r)$ be a continuous spherical density, and impose
regularity $\lim_{r\downarrow0}r^2\Phi'(r)=0$. The radial Poisson
equation gives
\[
 (r^2\Phi')'=4\pi G r^2\rho,
 \qquad M_{\rm enc}(r)=4\pi\int_0^rs^2\rho(s)\,ds,
 \qquad \Phi'(r)=\frac{GM_{\rm enc}(r)}{r^2}.
\]
The acceleration is $a_r=-\Phi'$. A positive density therefore gives
an inward radial acceleration.

Putting $u(r)=r\Phi(r)$ removes the radial first derivative:
\[
 r^2\Phi'=ru'-u,\qquad
 (r^2\Phi')'=ru'',\qquad u''=4\pi G r\rho.
\]
For fixed endpoint values, this equation is the stationary condition of
\[
 S[u]=\int_0^{R_0}\left[\frac{(u')^2}{2G}+4\pi r\rho u\right]dr.
\]
On $r_i=ih$, $i=0,\ldots,M$, with $Mh=R_0$, its finite counterpart is
\begin{equation}
 S_h[u]=\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}\frac{(u_{i+1}-u_i)^2}{2Gh}
 +4\pi h\sum_{i=1}^{M-1}r_i\rho_i u_i.
 \label{c:core:poisson-action}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Unique finite radial solution]
\label{c:core:poisson-minimum}
With $u_0,u_M$ fixed, $S_h$ has a unique minimizer. Its interior values
satisfy
\[
 \frac{u_{i+1}-2u_i+u_{i-1}}{h^2}=4\pi G r_i\rho_i.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Differentiation with respect to $u_i$ gives
$(2u_i-u_{i-1}-u_{i+1})/(Gh)+4\pi h r_i\rho_i$. Setting it to zero
gives the equation. For a variation $v$ with $v_0=v_M=0$, the Hessian
quadratic form is
\[
 \frac1{Gh}\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}(v_{i+1}-v_i)^2.
\]
Its vanishing forces $v$ to be constant and hence zero. The finite
Hessian is positive definite, so the quadratic action has one
stationary point and that point is its unique minimizer.
\end{proof}

The boundary value $u_0=0$ allows a regular finite potential at the
origin. The quotient $u/r$ is used only for $r>0$, with its continuous
limit determined separately at $r=0$.

For the normalized Gaussian density
\[
 \rho(r)=\frac{M_0}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma^3}e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},
 \qquad \sigma>0,
\]
direct differentiation verifies
\begin{align*}
 M_{\rm enc}(r)&=M_0\left[
 \operatorname{erf}\left(\frac r{\sqrt2\sigma}\right)
 -\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac r\sigma e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}\right],\\
 \Phi(r)&=-\frac{GM_0}{r}
 \operatorname{erf}\left(\frac r{\sqrt2\sigma}\right).
\end{align*}
The potential tends to zero at infinity and has the finite central
value $-\sqrt{2/\pi}\,GM_0/\sigma$. This removes the point-source
singularity while preserving the attractive sign.

 \label{c:core:gowdy-action}

 \label{c:core:gowdy-euler}
\end{align}

$\partial_\tau(e^{2P}Q_\tau)-\partial_\theta(e^{2P}\gamma Q_\theta)=0$.
The stationary equations are $\mathcal E_P=\mathcal E_Q=0$.

 +e^{2P}(Q_\tau^2+\gamma Q_\theta^2),\nonumber\\

 \label{c:core:gowdy-densities}
\end{align}
The remaining reconstruction equations are
$\lambda_\tau=H_G$ and $\lambda_\theta=M_G$.

\label{c:core:gowdy-integrability}

\begin{equation}

\end{equation}
For a solution on $I\times\T$, a single-valued periodic $\lambda$ with
these two derivatives exists if and only if
$\int_0^{2\pi}M_G\,d\theta=0$ at one, and hence every, time. It is
unique up to an additive constant.
\end{proposition}

Differentiate the two densities. The terms with $P_\tau

\[
\begin{aligned}

 ={}&2P_\theta(P_{\tau\tau}-\gamma P_{\theta\theta})\\
 &+2e^{2P}\big[
 Q_\theta(Q_{\tau\tau}-\gamma Q_{\theta\theta})
 +2P_\tau Q_\tau Q_\theta
 -P_\theta Q_\tau^2-\gamma P_\theta Q_\theta^2\big].
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitute \eqref{c:core:gowdy-euler} and combine the two occurrences of
$\gamma P_\theta Q_\theta^2$. This gives
\eqref{c:core:gowdy-identity}. On a solution the identity vanishes,
so periodicity gives $d\int M_G\,d\theta/d\tau=0$.

If a periodic $\lambda$ exists, integrating $\lambda_\theta=M_G$
forces the zero-period condition. Conversely, fix $\tau_0$ and define
on the lifted strip
\[

 +\int_{\tau_0}^{\tau}H_G(s,0)\,ds
 +\int_0^{\theta}M_G(\tau,\eta)\,d\eta.
\]
Its $\theta$ derivative is $M_G$. Its $\tau$ derivative is $H_G$ by
the integrability identity and the fundamental theorem of calculus.
The zero-period condition makes it periodic. The difference of two
such functions has both derivatives zero, so is constant.
\end{proof}

This separates a local compatibility condition from a global topology

\[
 (D_hf)_j=\frac{f_{j+1}-f_{j-1}}{2h},\qquad
 (\Delta_hf)_j=\frac{f_{j+1}-2f_j+f_{j-1}}{h^2}.
\]
Here $D_h^{\mathsf T}=-D_h$. With $U=\dot P$, $V=\dot Q$, the raw
semidiscrete vector field $f_h(\tau,z)$ for $z=(P,Q,U,V)$ is
\begin{align}
 \dot P&=U,&\dot Q&=V,\nonumber\\
 \dot U&=\gamma\Delta_hP+e^{2P}[V^2-\gamma(D_hQ)^2],\nonumber\\
 \dot V&=\gamma\Delta_hQ-2[UV-\gamma(D_hP)(D_hQ)].
 \label{c:core:gowdy-raw}
\end{align}
Products and exponentials in these formulas are componentwise.
The finite global momentum is
\begin{equation}
 C_h(z)=2h\sum_j[U_j(D_hP)_j+e^{2P_j}V_j(D_hQ)_j].
 \label{c:core:gowdy-momentum}
\end{equation}
It is linear in the velocity variables when the configuration $P,Q$
is fixed.

For the ordinary Euclidean gradients, skew-adjointness of $D_h$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \nabla_PC_h&=-2hD_hU+4h e^{2P}V(D_hQ),\\
 \nabla_QC_h&=-2hD_h(e^{2P}V),\\
 g_U:=\nabla_UC_h&=2hD_hP,
 &g_V:=\nabla_VC_h&=2h e^{2P}D_hQ.
\end{align*}
Put $G_h=(0,0,g_U,g_V)$ and $d_h=\norm{g_U}_2^2+\norm{g_V}_2^2$.
On the open region $d_h>0$, define
\[
 \Lambda_h=\frac{\nabla C_h\cdot f_h}{d_h},\qquad
 \widehat f_h=f_h-\Lambda_hG_h.
\]
The chain rule proves the exact tangency identity
\[
 \nabla C_h\cdot\widehat f_h
 =\nabla C_h\cdot f_h-\Lambda_hd_h=0.
\]
Every differentiable solution that remains in this region therefore
keeps $C_h$ constant.

\begin{proposition}[Exact endpoint momentum]
\label{c:core:gowdy-endpoint}
Start from $z_n$ and let a provisional step produce
$\widetilde z=(\widetilde P,\widetilde Q,\widetilde U,\widetilde V)$.
Form $\widetilde g_U,\widetilde g_V$ at its configuration and assume
$\widetilde d_h>0$. The correction
\[
 \mu=\frac{C_h(\widetilde z)-C_h(z_n)}{\widetilde d_h},\qquad
 z_{n+1}=(\widetilde P,\widetilde Q,
 \widetilde U-\mu\widetilde g_U,
 \widetilde V-\mu\widetilde g_V)
\]
satisfies $C_h(z_{n+1})=C_h(z_n)$ exactly. It is the correction of
smallest Euclidean velocity norm at the fixed configuration.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Linearity in the velocities gives
$C_h(z_{n+1})=C_h(\widetilde z)-\mu\widetilde d_h$.
For minimality, write $g=(\widetilde g_U,\widetilde g_V)$ and
$b=C_h(z_n)-C_h(\widetilde z)$. Every admissible velocity displacement
$v$ satisfies $g\cdot v=b$. Cauchy--Schwarz implies
$\norm v\geq|b|/\norm g$, with equality only at
$v=bg/\norm g^2$. This is the displayed correction.
\end{proof}

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}[Fixed-mesh second-order time accuracy]
\label{c:core:gowdy-time-order}
Fix $h$. Suppose a smooth exact solution of
$\dot z=\widehat f_h(\tau,z)$ and its numerical steps remain in a
compact regular neighborhood where $d_h\geq d_0>0$. Assume the mixed time and state
derivatives of $\widehat f_h$ through order three and the state
derivatives of $C_h$ through order four are bounded there. Apply the endpoint correction
of Proposition~\ref{c:core:gowdy-endpoint} after explicit midpoint.
Then its local error is $O(\Delta\tau^3)$ and its global error on a
fixed time interval is $O(\Delta\tau^2)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The explicit midpoint expansion agrees with the Taylor expansion of
the exact flow through order two. Its provisional endpoint differs
from the exact endpoint by $O(\Delta\tau^3)$. Since the exact flow
keeps $C_h$ constant and $C_h$ has bounded first derivatives, the
provisional constraint defect is also $O(\Delta\tau^3)$. The lower
bound on the denominator and the upper bound on $g$ make the
correction $O(\Delta\tau^3)$. Thus the corrected local error has the
same order. Under the stated derivative bounds the corrected step
map has Lipschitz constant at most $1+L\Delta\tau$ for small steps.
If $e_n$ is its error against the exact solution, then
\[
 e_{n+1}\leq(1+L\Delta\tau)e_n+M\Delta\tau^3.
\]
Iterating this inequality for $n\Delta\tau\leq T$ bounds the error by
$MT e^{LT}\Delta\tau^2$ when $e_0=0$.
\end{proof}

These are regular-chart results. For a spatially homogeneous
configuration, $g_U=g_V=0$, and the displayed multiplier is
undefined even though $C_h=0$. Constants in the accuracy theorem
can depend on $h$. A claim about simultaneous spatial and temporal
refinement additionally needs bounds uniform in $h$.

The local compatibility diagnostic is a separate quantity. Define
$H_{G,h},M_{G,h}$ by replacing spatial derivatives in
\eqref{c:core:gowdy-densities} with $D_h$. If
$\mathcal E_{P,h}=\dot U-\dot U_{\rm raw}$ and
$\mathcal E_{Q,h}=\dot V-\dot V_{\rm raw}$, then
\[
 \mathcal I_h=\partial_\tau M_{G,h}-D_hH_{G,h}
 -2(D_hP)\mathcal E_{P,h}
 -2e^{2P}(D_hQ)\mathcal E_{Q,h}
\]
subtracts the explicit constraint-force contribution. Exact global
momentum preservation does not force $\mathcal I_h$ to vanish at each
site. Its refinement behavior tests whether the modified evolution
approaches the local continuum reconstruction identity. The archived
second-order numerical observations are experimental evidence for
that behavior, with their tested range recorded in the companion.

\section{Finite linearized ADM gravity}
\label{c:core:adm}

The symmetry-reduced model can now be compared with a finite
three-dimensional linearized constraint system. Its exact algebraic
closure rests on commuting linear derivatives. Nonlinear products
will introduce an additional requirement in the next section.

\subsection{Finite calculus and the quadratic action}

Let $V_h$ be a finite real inner-product space. Let
$\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3$ be commuting skew-adjoint operators on it:
\[
 \delta_i\delta_j=\delta_j\delta_i,
 \qquad\inner{\delta_iX}{Y}_h=-\inner{X}{\delta_iY}_h,
 \qquad\delta^2=\sum_i\delta_i^2.
\]
The periodic centered differences in three coordinate directions
provide one example. All tensor inner products below sum over both
indices, using the Frobenius inner product on symmetric tensors.

Let $h_{ij}=h_{ji}$ and $\pi_{ij}=\pi_{ji}$ take values in $V_h$.
Repeated spatial indices are summed. Put $h_{\rm tr}=h_{kk}$,
$\pi_{\rm tr}=\pi_{kk}$ and define
\begin{align}
 C&=\delta_i\delta_jh_{ij}-\delta^2h_{\rm tr},
 &C_i&=-2\delta_j\pi_{ij},\nonumber\\
 \mathcal G_{ij}(h)&=\frac12\big[
 \delta_k\delta_ih_{jk}+\delta_k\delta_jh_{ik}
 -\delta^2h_{ij}-\delta_i\delta_jh_{\rm tr}
 -\delta_{ij}C\big].
 \label{c:core:adm-operators}
\end{align}

\begin{lemma}[Linearized finite Bianchi and adjoint identities]
\label{c:core:adm-bianchi}
The spatial operator obeys $\delta_j\mathcal G_{ij}(h)=0$ and is
self-adjoint on symmetric tensors.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Twice its divergence expands as
\begin{align*}
 2\delta_j\mathcal G_{ij}
 ={}&\delta_i\delta_j\delta_kh_{jk}
 +\delta^2\delta_kh_{ik}-\delta^2\delta_jh_{ij}
 -\delta_i\delta^2h_{\rm tr}\\
 &-\delta_i\delta_k\delta_lh_{kl}
 +\delta_i\delta^2h_{\rm tr}.
\end{align*}
The terms cancel in three pairs. For self-adjointness, write
$B_i(a)=\delta_ja_{ij}$ and $A(a)=\delta_i\delta_ja_{ij}$. Two
applications of the adjoint identity give
\begin{align*}
 2\inner{a}{\mathcal G(b)}_h
 ={}&-2\inner{B(a)}{B(b)}_h
 +\sum_k\inner{\delta_ka}{\delta_kb}_h\\
 &-\inner{A(a)}{b_{\rm tr}}_h
 -\inner{a_{\rm tr}}{A(b)}_h
 -\sum_k\inner{\delta_ka_{\rm tr}}{\delta_kb_{\rm tr}}_h.
\end{align*}
This expression is symmetric in $a,b$.
\end{proof}

Set
\[
 T_h=\inner{\pi}{\pi}_h-\tfrac12\inner{\pi_{\rm tr}}{\pi_{\rm tr}}_h,
 \qquad U_h=\tfrac12\inner{h}{\mathcal G(h)}_h.
\]
With lapse perturbation $n$ and shift perturbation $n_i$, the action is
\begin{equation}
 S_h^{(2)}=\int\left[
 \inner{\pi}{\dot h}_h-T_h-U_h
 +\inner{n}{C}_h-\inner{n_i}{C_i}_h\right]dt.
 \label{c:core:adm-action}
\end{equation}
Variation of $n,n_i$ imposes $C=C_i=0$. The remaining equations are
\begin{align}
 \dot h_{ij}&=2\pi_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\pi_{\rm tr}
             +\delta_in_j+\delta_jn_i,\nonumber\\
 \dot\pi_{ij}&=-\mathcal G_{ij}(h)
              +\delta_i\delta_jn-\delta_{ij}\delta^2n.
 \label{c:core:adm-evolution}
\end{align}
The kinetic gradient is $2\pi_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\pi_{\rm tr}$.
Lemma~\ref{c:core:adm-bianchi} makes the potential gradient
$\mathcal G(h)$. The lapse gradient follows by two spatial
integrations by parts. Integrating the shift term once gives
$-\langle\delta_in_j+\delta_jn_i,\pi_{ij}\rangle_h$ in the
Lagrangian, fixing the sign in the first equation.

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}
\subsection{Constraint propagation and the canonical brackets}

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}[Exact finite linearized closure]
\label{c:core:adm-closure}
For every solution of \eqref{c:core:adm-evolution},
\[
 \dot C=-\delta_iC_i,\qquad\dot C_i=0.
\]
Thus initially vanishing constraints remain zero. With the canonical
Frobenius bracket and smearings
$C[n]=\langle n,C\rangle_h$, $D[\xi]=\langle\xi_i,C_i\rangle_h$,
all three brackets $\{C[n],C[m]\}$, $\{D[\xi],D[\eta]\}$, and
$\{C[n],D[\xi]\}$ vanish identically.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The trace of the momentum part of $\dot h$ is $-\pi_{\rm tr}$.
Its contribution to $\dot C$ is therefore
$2\delta_i\delta_j\pi_{ij}=-\delta_iC_i$. The shift contribution is
\[
 \delta_i\delta_j(\delta_in_j+\delta_jn_i)
 -\delta^2(2\delta_kn_k)=0.
\]
For $\dot C_i$, the divergence of $\mathcal G$ vanishes by
Lemma~\ref{c:core:adm-bianchi}, and
$\delta_j(\delta_i\delta_jn-\delta_{ij}\delta^2n)=0$.
This proves the propagation equations and their stated implication.

For the bracket, use
$\{F,G\}=\langle\nabla_hF,\nabla_\pi G\rangle_h
-\langle\nabla_\pi F,\nabla_hG\rangle_h$.
Two scalar constraints depend only on $h$ and two momentum
constraints depend only on $\pi$, so their brackets vanish.
The gradients for the mixed bracket are
\[
 (\nabla_hC[n])_{ij}=\delta_i\delta_jn-\delta_{ij}\delta^2n,
 \qquad(\nabla_\pi D[\xi])_{ij}=\delta_i\xi_j+\delta_j\xi_i.
\]
Their contraction vanishes after one integration by parts because
the first tensor is divergence-free.
\end{proof}

The momentum generator changes the metric perturbation by
$h_{ij}\mapsto h_{ij}+\delta_i\xi_j+\delta_j\xi_i$.
The corresponding change of the scalar constraint is
$2\delta^2\delta_k\xi_k-2\delta^2\delta_k\xi_k=0$.
No product rule is used in these cancellations.

For a partition of fine spatial sites into coarse regions $A$, the
nonnegative diagnostic
\[
 E_A^{\rm con}=\sum_{x\in A}h^3
 \left(|C_x|^2+\sum_i|C_{i,x}|^2\right)
\]
adds exactly to the full fine diagnostic. This is an exact partition
identity. It does not assert that differentiating a coarse field
reconstructs its fine constraint values.

\subsection{Tensor waves, positive reduced energy, and resolved dispersion}

Choose $n=n_i=0$ and impose the transverse and traceless conditions
\[
 \delta_jh_{ij}=0,\quad h_{\rm tr}=0,
 \qquad\delta_j\pi_{ij}=0,\quad\pi_{\rm tr}=0.
\]
They are preserved by the evolution because
\[
 \mathcal G_{ij}(h)=-\tfrac12\delta^2h_{ij},\qquad
 \dot h=2\pi,\qquad\dot\pi=\tfrac12\delta^2h,
 \qquad\ddot h=\delta^2h.
\]
On this reduced sector the energy is
\[
 H_{\rm TT}=\norm{\pi}_h^2
 +\frac14\sum_k\norm{\delta_kh}_h^2\geq0.
\]
Its derivative is zero: substituting the two first-order equations
reduces it to
$\langle\pi,\delta^2h\rangle_h
+\sum_k\langle\delta_kh,\delta_k\pi\rangle_h=0$.

For a Fourier mode on the periodic centered lattice, let
$\widetilde k_i=\sin(k_ih)/h$. If $\widetilde{\mathbf k}\neq0$,
define
\[
 \Pi_{ij}=\delta_{ij}
 -\frac{\widetilde k_i\widetilde k_j}{|\widetilde{\mathbf k}|^2},
 \qquad
 \Lambda^{\rm TT}_{ij,kl}
 =\tfrac12(\Pi_{ik}\Pi_{jl}+\Pi_{il}\Pi_{jk}-\Pi_{ij}\Pi_{kl}).
\]
For a symmetric tensor $X$, its image is
$\Pi X\Pi-\Pi\operatorname{tr}(\Pi X)/2$. It is transverse and
traceless because $\Pi^2=\Pi$ and $\operatorname{tr}\Pi=2$.
Applying the map again leaves it unchanged. On the transverse
two-plane, symmetric tensors have dimension three and the trace
condition removes one dimension. Thus the projector has rank two.

The resulting frequency obeys
\begin{equation}
 \omega_h^2=\sum_i\frac{\sin^2(k_ih)}{h^2}.
 \label{c:core:adm-dispersion}
\end{equation}
For fixed $\mathbf k\neq0$ as $h\to0$,
\[
 \omega_h^2=|\mathbf k|^2-\frac{h^2}{3}\sum_i k_i^4+O(h^4),
 \qquad
 \omega_h=|\mathbf k|
 -\frac{h^2}{6|\mathbf k|}\sum_i k_i^4+O(h^4).
\]
These follow by expanding the sine and then the positive square root.
The regime keeps $\mathbf k$ fixed. It is not uniform up to the
Nyquist boundary.

The spatial operator in \eqref{c:core:adm-dispersion} is the sum of
the squared centered first derivatives. It differs from the
nearest-neighbor second-difference operator used for the raw Gowdy
equations. For even site counts, an alternating sequence has centered
derivative zero. Such checkerboard modes, as well as constant modes,
belong to the derivative kernel. At a zero symbol the above TT
projector is undefined and the rank-two argument does not apply.
Exact constraint propagation consequently coexists with a finite
spatial kernel that a physical continuum comparison must address.

\section{The nonlinear pointwise obstruction and its algebraic alternative}
\label{c:core:nonlinear-obstruction}

The linearized cancellations use commuting derivatives but never ask
them to differentiate a product. A nonlinear diffeomorphism generator
does. The following scalar model isolates that issue without relying
on the more involved gravitational tensor constraints.

Let a periodic real lattice have canonical brackets
$\{q_a,p_b\}_h=\delta_{ab}/h$ and a skew matrix $D$. Define
\[
 \mathcal D_h[\xi]=h\sum_a\xi_ap_a(Dq)_a,
 \qquad
 \mathfrak L_D(f,g)=D(fg)-(Df)g-f(Dg).
\]
All products on this lattice are pointwise.

\begin{proposition}[Exact nonlinear defect identity]
\label{c:core:nonlinear-defect}
For arbitrary finite arrays $q,p,\xi,\eta$,
\begin{align}
 \{\mathcal D_h[\xi],\mathcal D_h[\eta]\}_h
 ={}&\mathcal D_h[\xi D\eta-\eta D\xi]\nonumber\\
 &+h\sum_ap_a\big[
 \xi_a\mathfrak L_D(\eta,Dq)_a
 -\eta_a\mathfrak L_D(\xi,Dq)_a\big].
 \label{c:core:nonlinear-defect-identity}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Coordinate differentiation gives
$\partial_p\mathcal D_h[\xi]=h\xi Dq$ and
$\partial_q\mathcal D_h[\xi]=-hD(\xi p)$.
Insert these in the canonical bracket and use $D^{\mathsf T}=-D$:
\[
 \{\mathcal D_h[\xi],\mathcal D_h[\eta]\}_h
 =h\sum_ap_a\left[\xi_aD(\eta Dq)_a
                  -\eta_aD(\xi Dq)_a\right].
\]
Expanding each derivative using the definition of $\mathfrak L_D$
cancels the two $\xi\eta D^2q$ terms. The remaining product-rule
terms give the first term of
\eqref{c:core:nonlinear-defect-identity}, and the two defect terms
give the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite pointwise derivation obstruction]
\label{c:core:pointwise-no-go}
A linear derivation on the complete pointwise algebra $\C^N$ is zero.
Thus a nonzero finite pointwise derivative cannot obey the undeformed
Leibniz rule on every pair of arrays.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $e_a$ be the coordinate idempotents. If $D$ is a derivation, then
$D(e_a)=D(e_a^2)=2e_aD(e_a)$. At coordinate $a$ this forces the
component to be twice itself, hence zero. At every other coordinate
the right side is zero. Therefore $D(e_a)=0$ for every $a$. Linearity
and the coordinate basis imply $D=0$.
\end{proof}

The theorem rules out a universal ordinary derivation on the full
finite pointwise algebra. For a particular generator, one must still
inspect the contracted defect in
\eqref{c:core:nonlinear-defect-identity}. A nonzero Leibniz defect
does not by itself imply that every contraction is nonzero.

\begin{example}[An exact bracket failure]
\label{c:core:bracket-negative-control}
Use $N=5$, $h=1$, and $(Df)_a=(f_{a+1}-f_{a-1})/2$.
Take $q=e_0$, $p=\xi=e_1$, and $\eta=e_2$. Then
$(Dq)_1=-1/2$, $(D\eta)_1=1/2$, and $\eta Dq=0$.
The direct bracket in the preceding proof is zero, while
\[
 \mathcal D_h[\xi D\eta-\eta D\xi]=-\tfrac14.
\]
The defect is therefore exactly $+1/4$. This finite witness shows
that the naive centered scalar constraint does fail to close
universally in the proposed undeformed form.
\end{example}

\subsection{Smooth resolved arrays and the matrix corner route}

For samples of sufficiently smooth periodic functions, the centered
derivative obeys
\[
 D_hf=f'+\frac{h^2}{6}f'''+O(h^4).
\]
If $f,g$ have uniformly bounded derivatives through order five, its
Leibniz defect consequently satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak L_{D_h}(f,g)
 =\frac{h^2}{2}(f''g'+f'g'')+O(h^4).
 \label{c:core:smooth-defect}
\end{equation}
For fixed smooth $p,\xi,\eta,q$, with sufficiently many additional
bounded derivatives of $q$ to control $D_hq$, the contraction in
\eqref{c:core:nonlinear-defect-identity} is $O(h^2)$ on a fixed periodic
interval. Each summand is uniformly $O(h^2)$ and $hN$ is the interval
length. The coordinate-idempotent witness above is outside this
uniformly smooth regime.

A spectral derivative has an exact product rule on trigonometric
polynomials when every product remains in the represented band without
aliasing. Repeated products require further headroom. These restricted
domains differ from the complete pointwise algebra. The later resolved
constraint theorem includes explicit domain bounds.

For the full matrix algebra, choose a Hermitian matrix $K$ and set
$\delta_KX=i[K,X]$. Direct multiplication gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta_K(XY)=(\delta_KX)Y+X(\delta_KY).
 \label{c:core:inner-derivation}
\end{equation}
It also obeys $\delta_K(X^*)=(\delta_KX)^*$,
$\operatorname{Tr}\delta_KX=0$, and is skew-adjoint for the
Hilbert--Schmidt inner product. The last identity follows by moving
$K$ through the trace. These properties supply an exact finite
product calculus on a noncommutative algebra.

\section{Geometric transport and local work}
\label{c:core:transport}

The first gravitational question is local: how does a prescribed geometry
change transport and energy exchange? A second question is dynamical: which
equations determine that geometry? Keeping these questions distinct lets a
finite model establish an exact balance law before it is coupled to a
gravitational constraint system. Throughout this section the metric
coefficients are supplied functions. The scalar field evolves on them.

\subsection{A finite scalar action on a diagonal metric}

Take a periodic chain with $N\geq3$ sites, spacing $h>0$, and indices modulo
$N$. The continuum metric motivating its coefficients is
\[
 ds^2=-N(t,x)^2dt^2+a(t,x)^2dx^2,
 \qquad N(t,x)>0,\quad a(t,x)>0.
\]
The repeated letter $N$ in this metric is the lapse, whereas the integer
$N$ counts lattice sites. In the finite formulas below only the coefficient
names $w$, $c$, and $v$ are needed:
\[
 w_j=\frac{a_j}{N_j}>0,\qquad
 c_{j+1/2}=\frac{N_{j+1/2}}{a_{j+1/2}}>0,\qquad
 v_j=N_ja_jm^2\geq0.
\]
Thus $N/a$ is the coordinate characteristic speed of the continuum
massless equation. Assume these finite coefficient arrays are continuously
differentiable in time. For a real field $\varphi_j(t)$ set
$\Delta_j=\varphi_{j+1}-\varphi_j$ and define
\begin{equation}
 L_h=\frac h2\sum_jw_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 -\frac1{2h}\sum_jc_{j+1/2}\Delta_j^2
 -\frac h2\sum_jv_j\varphi_j^2.
 \label{c:core:scalar-action}
\end{equation}
Variations with compact time support give
\begin{equation}
 w_j\ddot\varphi_j+\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j
 =\frac{c_{j+1/2}\Delta_j-c_{j-1/2}\Delta_{j-1}}{h^2}
 -v_j\varphi_j.
 \label{c:core:scalar-evolution}
\end{equation}
The neighboring edge terms in the action produce the two terms in the
spatial numerator. The time integration by parts differentiates
$w_j\dot\varphi_j$, including the $\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j$ term.

\Needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}[Local energy, flux, and geometric work]
\label{c:core:scalar-work}
For every twice differentiable solution of
\eqref{c:core:scalar-evolution}, define
\begin{align}
 e_j&=\frac h2w_j\dot\varphi_j^2+\frac h2v_j\varphi_j^2
 +\frac{c_{j+1/2}}{4h}\Delta_j^2
 +\frac{c_{j-1/2}}{4h}\Delta_{j-1}^2,\nonumber\\
 F_{j+1/2}&=-\frac{c_{j+1/2}}{2h}\Delta_j
             (\dot\varphi_j+\dot\varphi_{j+1}),\nonumber\\
 s_j&=-\frac h2\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 +\frac h2\dot v_j\varphi_j^2
 +\frac{\dot c_{j+1/2}}{4h}\Delta_j^2
 +\frac{\dot c_{j-1/2}}{4h}\Delta_{j-1}^2.
 \label{c:core:scalar-densities}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \dot e_j+F_{j+1/2}-F_{j-1/2}=s_j.
 \label{c:core:scalar-balance}
\end{equation}
In particular, $E_h=\sum_je_j$ satisfies
$\dot E_h=\sum_js_j=-\partial_tL_h$, where the partial derivative holds
$\varphi$ and $\dot\varphi$ fixed.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $B_j=c_{j+1/2}\Delta_j$. Using the equation of motion, the derivative
of the kinetic and mass terms at site $j$ is
\[
 \frac{\dot\varphi_j}{h}(B_j-B_{j-1})
 -\frac h2\dot w_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 +\frac h2\dot v_j\varphi_j^2.
\]
The right edge contribution differentiates to
\[
 \frac{\dot c_{j+1/2}\Delta_j^2}{4h}
 +\frac{B_j}{2h}(\dot\varphi_{j+1}-\dot\varphi_j),
\]
and the left edge has the analogous expression. Adding these terms
leaves
$B_j(\dot\varphi_j+\dot\varphi_{j+1})/(2h)$ on the right and its
negative counterpart on the left, plus $s_j$. These are exactly the flux
terms in \eqref{c:core:scalar-balance}. Periodic summation cancels every
interface flux. Each edge coefficient derivative appears twice with
weight $1/(4h)$, giving $-\partial_tL_h$.
\end{proof}

Every $e_j$ is nonnegative under the stated coefficient assumptions. An
interval of cells $r,\ldots,s$ obeys the exact coarse balance
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\sum_{j=r}^se_j
 +F_{s+1/2}-F_{r-1/2}=\sum_{j=r}^ss_j.
\]
Thus coarse energy is obtained by adding fine cell energies and retaining
only the exposed boundary fluxes. This is the same cancellation mechanism
as projector transfer, applied here to a classical field energy. Its
physical units and constitutive coefficients come from the action.

\begin{example}[Time dependent expansion]
Let the lapse equal one, let $a(t)>0$ be spatially uniform, and let $m=0$.
Then $w=a$, $c=1/a$, and
\[
 \dot E_h=-\frac h2\dot a\sum_j\dot\varphi_j^2
 -\frac{\dot a}{2ha^2}\sum_j\Delta_j^2.
\]
An increasing $a$ transfers energy out of this coordinate-time field
Hamiltonian. The supplied background receives no evolution equation
from this calculation. A self-consistent matter--geometry model must
also evolve its gravitational variables.
\end{example}

For a smooth field sampled at sites and a smooth coefficient sampled at
edge midpoints, the spatial expression is second-order consistent with
$\partial_x(c\partial_x\varphi)$. Indeed, expanding at $x_j$ gives
\[
 c(x_j+h/2)[\varphi(x_j+h)-\varphi(x_j)]
 -c(x_j-h/2)[\varphi(x_j)-\varphi(x_j-h)]
 =h^2(c\varphi_x)_x(x_j)+O(h^4).
\]
Uniform bounds on the requisite fourth derivatives make the remainder
uniform on a compact spatial region. The exact finite balance holds
without any Taylor approximation.
