\section{One Hilbert space behind all cylinder depths}
\label{a-limit-hilbert}

An isometric refinement map compares two finite registers. An infinite
quantum dynamics requires more: a common completed Hilbert space, a
specified operator domain, and a topology in which the cutoffs converge.
These requirements can all be met for the cylinder tower. They are separate
requirements for a walk on a growing finite tree.

Fix a prime $p$. The compact additive group $\Z_p$ has normalized Haar
measure $\mu_p$, with
\[
 B_{m,a}=a+p^m\Z_p,\qquad 0\leq a<p^m,\qquad
 \mu_p(B_{m,a})=p^{-m}.
\]
Write $\HH_p=L^2(\Z_p,\mu_p;\C)$. We use the complex inner product
$\inner{f}{g}=\int\overline f g\,d\mu_p$, linear in its second argument.
The $p$-adic coordinate belongs to the measurable space. Amplitudes and the
Born probabilities use ordinary complex Hilbert space.

\subsection{Counting amplitudes and Haar densities}

At depth $m$, the finite space $\HH_{p,m}=\ell^2(\Z/p^m\Z)$ has counting
inner product and orthonormal basis $e_a$. Define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U_{p,m}e_a=p^{m/2}\mathbf1_{B_{m,a}},
 \qquad \mathcal V_m=\operatorname{span}
 \{\mathbf1_{B_{m,a}}:0\leq a<p^m\}.
 \label{a-limit-cylinder-embedding}
\end{equation}
The cylinders are disjoint. Consequently
\[
 \inner{\mathcal U_{p,m}e_a}{\mathcal U_{p,m}e_b}
 =p^m\mu_p(B_{m,a}\cap B_{m,b})=\delta_{ab}.
\]
The same indicators span $\mathcal V_m$, so $\mathcal U_{p,m}$ is unitary
onto this subspace. For $c=\sum_a c_ae_a$, its image has constant value
$p^{m/2}c_a$ on $B_{m,a}$. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \int_{B_{m,a}}|\mathcal U_{p,m}c|^2\,d\mu_p=|c_a|^2.
 \label{a-limit-born-normalization}
\end{equation}
There is no extra probability factor after this normalization.

The finite refinement map is
\[
 V_{p,m}e_a=\frac1{\sqrt p}
 \sum_{d=0}^{p-1}e_{a+d p^m}.
\]
Since $B_{m,a}=\bigsqcup_d B_{m+1,a+d p^m}$, it satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U_{p,m+1}V_{p,m}=\mathcal U_{p,m}.
 \label{a-limit-common-embedding}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the coefficient on each child indicator is
$p^{-1/2}p^{(m+1)/2}=p^{m/2}$, precisely the coefficient on the parent.
Thus the refinement changes the address resolution of an embedded state
without changing the function in $\HH_p$.

An equivalent finite convention uses the weighted norm
\[
 \norm{f}_{m,\mathrm{Haar}}^2=p^{-m}\sum_a|f(a)|^2.
\]
Here $f(a)$ is a density amplitude rather than a counting amplitude, and
the embedding into $\HH_p$ sends $f$ to
$\sum_a f(a)\mathbf1_{B_{m,a}}$. Its refinement repeats the parent value
on all children, without $p^{-1/2}$. The coordinate change
$f(a)=p^{m/2}c_a$ identifies the two conventions. The factors
$p^{-m}$ in the measure and $p^{m/2}$ in the counting embedding are a
single normalization expressed in two places.

\subsection{Cylinder averaging as an orthogonal projection}

For $f\in\HH_p$, define
\begin{equation}
 (\mathsf E_m f)(x)
 =p^m\int_{x+p^m\Z_p} f(y)\,d\mu_p(y).
 \label{a-limit-expectation}
\end{equation}
The integral is defined since $L^2$ is contained in $L^1$ on this
probability space. It produces a function constant on each depth-$m$
cylinder.

\begin{proposition}[Nested cylinder projections]
\label{a-limit-expectation-algebra}
The operator $\mathsf E_m$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal V_m$.
For $m,n\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf E_m^*=\mathsf E_m,\qquad
 \mathsf E_m^2=\mathsf E_m,\qquad
 \mathsf E_m\mathsf E_n=\mathsf E_{\min(m,n)}.
 \label{a-limit-projection-product}
\end{equation}
Moreover $\mathsf E_m f\to f$ in $L^2$ for every $f\in\HH_p$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a cylinder-constant $g$, the integral of $f-\mathsf E_m f$ over each
depth-$m$ cylinder is zero. Multiplying by the constant value of
$\overline g$ there and summing shows
$\inner{g}{f-\mathsf E_mf}=0$. The image is in $\mathcal V_m$, and averaging
a function in $\mathcal V_m$ returns the function. These statements
characterize the orthogonal projection and establish the first two
identities. The spaces are nested, because every cylinder partitions into
its children. Orthogonal projections onto nested subspaces satisfy the
third identity: the larger projection fixes the smaller range, and the
reverse order follows by taking adjoints.

For completeness, the union of these ranges is dense. Cylinders form a
countable clopen base for the topology on $\Z_p$ and generate its Borel
sigma-algebra. If $f\in L^2$ is orthogonal to every cylinder indicator,
the finite complex measure $\nu(A)=\int_A f\,d\mu_p$ vanishes on
cylinders and their finite unions. The class of sets on which $\nu$ is
zero contains the whole space, is closed under complements, and is
closed under countable disjoint unions. The elementary monotone-class
extension from the cylinder algebra therefore gives $\nu(A)=0$ for every
Borel set. Applying this to the positive and negative level sets of the
real and imaginary parts of $f$ yields $f=0$ almost everywhere.
The orthogonal complement of $\bigcup_m\mathcal V_m$ is thus zero.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $g\in\mathcal V_M$ with
$\norm{f-g}_2<\varepsilon$. For $m\geq M$, the projection fixes $g$, so
$\norm{f-\mathsf E_m f}_2
=\norm{(I-\mathsf E_m)(f-g)}_2\leq\norm{f-g}_2<\varepsilon$.
This proves strong convergence without exchanging an infinite integral
with a limit.
\end{proof}

The completion of the isometric direct system
$(\HH_{p,m},V_{p,m})$ is therefore $\HH_p$: equation
\eqref{a-limit-common-embedding} gives a single isometric map on the
algebraic direct limit, and its image is the dense union of the
$\mathcal V_m$. For $m\leq M$, with
$V_{p,m\to M}=V_{p,M-1}\cdots V_{p,m}$, one also has
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf E_m\big|_{\mathcal V_M}
 =\mathcal U_{p,M}V_{p,m\to M}V_{p,m\to M}^*
 \mathcal U_{p,M}^*.
 \label{a-limit-finite-projection}
\end{equation}
Both sides are the orthogonal projection in $\mathcal V_M$ onto
$\mathcal V_m$. This is the exact relation between the finite matrices
and the common infinite Hilbert space.

\subsection{Orthogonal details and a complete Haar basis}

Use $\mathsf F_0=\mathsf E_0$ and
$\mathsf F_m=\mathsf E_m-\mathsf E_{m-1}$ for $m\geq1$. These are the
infinite depth details called $\mathsf D_m$ in the archived chapter.
They correspond to the finite $D_m^{(M)}$ after the embedding
$\mathcal U_{p,M}$. Equation \eqref{a-limit-projection-product} gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf F_m\mathsf F_n=\delta_{mn}\mathsf F_m,
 \qquad \sum_{m=0}^M\mathsf F_m=\mathsf E_M.
 \label{a-limit-detail-algebra}
\end{equation}
For example, if $1\leq m<n$, the four products in
$(\mathsf E_m-\mathsf E_{m-1})(\mathsf E_n-\mathsf E_{n-1})$
are $\mathsf E_m,\mathsf E_m,\mathsf E_{m-1},\mathsf E_{m-1}$ and cancel.
For $m=n$ the same expansion is
$\mathsf E_m-\mathsf E_{m-1}$. The cases involving $m=0$ use
$\mathsf E_0\mathsf E_n=\mathsf E_0$.

Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \HH_p=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{\infty}\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf F_m,
 \qquad \norm{f}_2^2=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2.
 \label{a-limit-parseval}
\end{equation}
The sum of the projections is $I$ in the strong operator topology.
The detail ranks are $d_0=1$ and $d_m=(p-1)p^{m-1}$ for $m\geq1$,
the differences of the dimensions $p^m-p^{m-1}$.

For an explicit basis, put $\omega_p=\exp(2\pi i/p)$ and define
\begin{equation}
 \psi_{m,a,q}=p^{(m-1)/2}\sum_{d=0}^{p-1}
 \omega_p^{qd}\mathbf1_{B_{m,a+d p^{m-1}}},
 \quad
 \begin{matrix}m\geq1,\quad 0\leq a<p^{m-1},\\1\leq q<p.\end{matrix}
 \label{a-limit-haar-wavelets}
\end{equation}
Each has zero average over its parent, since
$\sum_d\omega_p^{qd}=0$, and lies in $\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf F_m$.
Its norm squared is $p^{m-1}p\,p^{-m}=1$. Distinct parents have disjoint
support, while two characters at the same parent have inner product
$p^{-1}\sum_d\omega_p^{(q'-q)d}=\delta_{qq'}$. The number of these
orthonormal functions is exactly $d_m$, so they span that level.
Together with $\psi_0=1$, they form a complete orthonormal basis by
\eqref{a-limit-parseval}.

\subsection{A statewise approximation rate}

For $s>0$, define the Haar regularity norm
\[
 \norm{f}_{\mathfrak H_p^s}^2
 =\sum_{m\geq0}p^{2sm}\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2,
 \qquad
 \mathfrak H_p^s=\{f\in\HH_p:\norm{f}_{\mathfrak H_p^s}<\infty\}.
\]
No identification with another Sobolev convention is required here.
The definition itself gives the quantitative cutoff estimate.

\begin{proposition}[Exact tail and regularity bound]
\label{a-limit-tail}
For $f\in\HH_p$ and every $M\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)f}_2^2
 =\sum_{m>M}\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2.
 \label{a-limit-tail-identity}
\end{equation}
If $f\in\mathfrak H_p^s$, then
\begin{equation}
 \norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)f}_2
 \leq p^{-s(M+1)}\norm{f}_{\mathfrak H_p^s}.
 \label{a-limit-tail-bound}
\end{equation}
The convergence $\mathsf E_M\to I$ is strong and is not convergence in
operator norm.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The omitted details are orthogonal, so Parseval gives the equality.
For $m>M$, $p^{2sm}\geq p^{2s(M+1)}$. Multiplying the omitted summands
by this lower bound proves the squared estimate, and taking square roots
gives \eqref{a-limit-tail-bound}. At every finite $M$ there is a unit
vector in $\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf F_{M+1}$, on which
$I-\mathsf E_M$ acts as the identity. Thus
$\norm{I-\mathsf E_M}=1$ for every $M$.
\end{proof}

The rate is a bound on states in the displayed regularity class. For an
arbitrary $L^2$ state the tail still tends to zero, but no common geometric
rate follows. A finite array already in $\mathcal V_L$ has zero tail once
$M\geq L$, which is a different statement from testing an infinite tail.


\section{Self-adjoint dynamics and what a cutoff converges to}
\label{a-limit-dynamics}

\subsection{The maximal domain for level energies}

Let $(\epsilon_m)_{m\geq0}$ be any sequence of real numbers. Define
\begin{align}
 \Dom(H_\epsilon)
 &=\left\{f\in\HH_p:
 \sum_{m\geq0}|\epsilon_m|^2\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2<\infty\right\},
 \nonumber\\
 H_\epsilon f&=\sum_{m\geq0}\epsilon_m\mathsf F_mf.
 \label{a-limit-hamiltonian-domain}
\end{align}
The series converges in $L^2$ exactly on this domain. It is not necessary
to bound the energies uniformly, but it is necessary to state the domain.

\begin{theorem}[Real level energies define a self-adjoint operator]
\label{a-limit-selfadjoint}
The operator in \eqref{a-limit-hamiltonian-domain} is densely defined,
closed, and self-adjoint. The finite cylinder functions form an operator
core. It is bounded if and only if $\sup_m|\epsilon_m|<\infty$, and its
spectrum is
\begin{equation}
 \sigma(H_\epsilon)=\overline{\{\epsilon_m:m\geq0\}}.
 \label{a-limit-spectrum}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The orthogonal decomposition \eqref{a-limit-parseval} identifies $f$ with
the square-summable sequence $f_m=\mathsf F_mf$. Finite sequences belong
to the domain, so it is dense. The real multipliers imply symmetry.
To identify the adjoint, suppose $g\in\Dom(H_\epsilon^*)$ and write
$k=H_\epsilon^*g$. Testing the adjoint identity against an arbitrary
vector supported on level $m$ gives $k_m=\epsilon_m g_m$. Since $k$ is
square summable, $\sum_m|\epsilon_m|^2\norm{g_m}^2<\infty$.
Thus $g\in\Dom(H_\epsilon)$ and the adjoint agrees with $H_\epsilon$.
The reverse inclusion is symmetry. This proves self-adjointness and
therefore closedness.

For $f\in\Dom(H_\epsilon)$, the cylinder truncation $\mathsf E_M f$
satisfies both
$\norm{f-\mathsf E_M f}_2\to0$ and
$\norm{H_\epsilon(f-\mathsf E_M f)}_2\to0$, because the two squared norms
are the tails of convergent nonnegative series. This is precisely density
in the graph norm and proves the core assertion.
If the energies have supremum $C<\infty$, Parseval gives
$\norm{H_\epsilon f}_2\leq C\norm f_2$. Conversely, a unit vector on
level $m$ has image norm $|\epsilon_m|$, so boundedness forces a finite
supremum.

If $z$ is outside the closed energy set, the sequence
$(\epsilon_m-z)^{-1}$ is bounded and defines an inverse for
$H_\epsilon-z$. Its image lies in the domain because
$\epsilon_m/(\epsilon_m-z)=1+z/(\epsilon_m-z)$ is bounded as well.
This proves that such $z$ is in the resolvent set. An energy
$\epsilon_m$ is an eigenvalue, while a limit point $z$ has unit level
vectors $u_j$ with $\norm{(H_\epsilon-z)u_j}_2\to0$.
A bounded inverse would contradict this limit. Hence the closed energy
set is exactly the spectrum.
\end{proof}

This proof also excludes a hidden choice of boundary condition at infinite
depth. On the finite-cylinder core, the real level operator has the unique
self-adjoint closure just described.

\subsection{Explicit spectral calculus and strong continuity}

For bounded Borel $F:\R\to\C$, define
\begin{equation}
 F(H_\epsilon)f=\sum_{m\geq0}F(\epsilon_m)\mathsf F_mf.
 \label{a-limit-borel-calculus}
\end{equation}
The series converges by Parseval and
$\norm{F(H_\epsilon)f}_2\leq\sup_m|F(\epsilon_m)|\norm f_2$.
The same level decomposition verifies sums, products, and adjoints of
these multipliers directly. In particular,
\begin{align}
 U(t)&=e^{-itH_\epsilon}
 =\sum_{m\geq0}e^{-it\epsilon_m}\mathsf F_m,
 \label{a-limit-unitary}\\
 (z-H_\epsilon)^{-1}
 &=\sum_{m\geq0}(z-\epsilon_m)^{-1}\mathsf F_m,
 \quad z\notin\sigma(H_\epsilon).
 \label{a-limit-resolvent}
\end{align}
The projections in these sums converge strongly, not absolutely in
operator norm in general.

The modulus-one multipliers give $U(t)^*U(t)=I$ and
$U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$. They also give strong continuity:
\[
 \norm{(U(t)-U(t_0))f}_2^2
 =\sum_m|e^{-it\epsilon_m}-e^{-it_0\epsilon_m}|^2
 \norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
To justify this limit, first bound the omitted summands by
$4\sum_{m>M}\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2$, then use ordinary continuity in
the finite sum up to $M$. On $\Dom(H_\epsilon)$ the same argument,
using $|(e^{-it\epsilon}-1)/t|\leq|\epsilon|$, proves
\[
 \lim_{t\to0}\frac{U(t)f-f}{t}=-iH_\epsilon f.
\]
Thus the declared self-adjoint operator is the generator. A general
$L^2$ state evolves unitarily even if this derivative does not exist.

\subsection{Two distinct extensions of the finite dynamics}

Let $H_\epsilon^{(M)}$ be the finite restriction of $H_\epsilon$ to
$\mathcal V_M$. One useful approximation to $U(t)$ is its embedded
finite propagator, extended by zero on the omitted subspace:
\begin{equation}
 U_M^{\mathrm{emb}}(t)
 =\sum_{m=0}^{M}e^{-it\epsilon_m}\mathsf F_m
 =U(t)\mathsf E_M.
 \label{a-limit-embedded-propagator}
\end{equation}
It is unitary on $\mathcal V_M$ and has kernel
$\mathcal V_M^\perp$ as an operator on $\HH_p$.

\Needspace{15\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}[Exact state error for a compatible cutoff]
\label{a-limit-unitary-error}
For every $f\in\HH_p$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{U(t)f-U_M^{\mathrm{emb}}(t)f}_2
 =\norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)f}_2.
 \label{a-limit-unitary-tail}
\end{equation}
This equality is uniform for all real $t$. For
$f\in\mathfrak H_p^s$, the right side is bounded by
$p^{-s(M+1)}\norm f_{\mathfrak H_p^s}$.
For $f\in\Dom(H_\epsilon)$ there is also the exact graph-norm identity
\begin{align}
 &\norm{U(t)f-U_M^{\mathrm{emb}}(t)f}_2^2
 +\norm{H_\epsilon(U(t)f-U_M^{\mathrm{emb}}(t)f)}_2^2
 \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{2em}=
 \sum_{m>M}(1+|\epsilon_m|^2)\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2.
 \label{a-limit-graph-tail}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The difference is the omitted orthogonal sum
$\sum_{m>M}e^{-it\epsilon_m}\mathsf F_mf$. Its multipliers have modulus
one, so Parseval gives \eqref{a-limit-unitary-tail}. Applying
$H_\epsilon$ multiplies the omitted level by $\epsilon_m$ and gives the
second identity. The domain hypothesis ensures that this second series
is finite. The regularity estimate is Proposition \ref{a-limit-tail}.
\end{proof}

An alternative is to extend the finite Hamiltonian by the zero
Hamiltonian on the omitted subspace:
\[
 \widetilde H_M=H_\epsilon\mathsf E_M
 =\sum_{m\leq M}\epsilon_m\mathsf F_m.
\]
This is a bounded self-adjoint operator on all of $\HH_p$. Its
propagator is a full-space unitary, but has a different tail:
\begin{equation}
 e^{-it\widetilde H_M}
 =U_M^{\mathrm{emb}}(t)+(I-\mathsf E_M),
 \qquad
 \norm{(e^{-it\widetilde H_M}-U(t))f}_2
 \leq2\norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)f}_2.
 \label{a-limit-zero-hamiltonian-extension}
\end{equation}
Likewise, for nonreal $z$,
\begin{align}
 (z-\widetilde H_M)^{-1}
 &=\mathsf E_M(z-H_\epsilon)^{-1}
   +z^{-1}(I-\mathsf E_M),\nonumber\\
 \norm{((z-\widetilde H_M)^{-1}-(z-H_\epsilon)^{-1})f}_2
 &\leq\left(|z|^{-1}+|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-1}\right)
 \norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)f}_2.
 \label{a-limit-strong-resolvent}
\end{align}
Thus $\widetilde H_M$ converges to $H_\epsilon$ in the strong resolvent
sense. These statements specify operators on one common Hilbert space.
They do not compare matrices of changing dimensions without an embedding.

The embedded propagators converge strongly, uniformly in time on each
fixed state. Their operator norm error nevertheless satisfies
\[
 \norm{U(t)-U_M^{\mathrm{emb}}(t)}=1
 \qquad\text{for every }M,t.
\]
The fully unitary extensions also converge strongly with the bound in
\eqref{a-limit-zero-hamiltonian-extension}; norm convergence of these
extensions needs a separate condition on the omitted phases. Neither
assertion is a general norm-limit theorem for arbitrary quantum dynamics.

\subsection{A graph-domain example with exact infinite tails}

\begin{example}[Convergent states and finite energy derivatives]
\label{a-limit-geometric-example}
Choose one unit vector $u_m\in\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf F_m$ at every
level, let $0<q<1$, and set
\[
 f_q=\sum_{m\geq0}\sqrt{(1-q)q^m}\,u_m,
 \qquad \epsilon_m=2^m.
\]
Then $\norm{f_q}_2=1$ and
\begin{equation}
 \norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)f_q}_2^2=q^{M+1}.
 \label{a-limit-geometric-state-tail}
\end{equation}
However, $f_q\in\Dom(H_\epsilon)$ exactly when $4q<1$:
\[
 \norm{H_\epsilon f_q}_2^2
 =(1-q)\sum_{m\geq0}(4q)^m.
\]
For $q<1/4$, its graph tail is exactly
\begin{equation}
 q^{M+1}+\frac{(1-q)(4q)^{M+1}}{1-4q}.
 \label{a-limit-geometric-graph-tail}
\end{equation}
For $q=1/8$, the state norm tail decays faster than the graph norm tail.
For $q=1/2$, the normalized state still has a convergent $L^2$ cylinder
approximation and a well-defined unitary evolution, but is outside the
Hamiltonian domain. All these conclusions concern genuinely infinite
series, rather than a finite last level with its tail set to zero.
\end{example}

level masses of Example \ref{a-limit-geometric-example}. The operator

The parameters are declared in the plate and its reproducible Python

\subsection{Compact resolvents and thermal weights}

The omitted embedded resolvent has the exact norm
\begin{equation}
 \norm{(I-\mathsf E_M)(z-H_\epsilon)^{-1}}
 =\sup_{m>M}|z-\epsilon_m|^{-1}.
 \label{a-limit-resolvent-tail-norm}
\end{equation}
The upper bound follows by Parseval. For the lower bound, test on a unit
vector at any omitted level and take the supremum. Since every level is
nonzero and finite dimensional, this proves the following equivalence.

\begin{proposition}[Exact compactness criterion]
\label{a-limit-compact-resolvent}
The operator $H_\epsilon$ has compact resolvent if and only if
$|\epsilon_m|\to\infty$. In that case the embedded finite resolvents
converge in operator norm. This is an assertion about the embedded
resolvents, rather than the zero-Hamiltonian extensions of
\eqref{a-limit-strong-resolvent}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the absolute energies tend to infinity, the right side of
\eqref{a-limit-resolvent-tail-norm} tends to zero. The retained part of the
resolvent has finite rank, so the resolvent is a norm limit of finite-rank
operators and is compact. Conversely, if the absolute energies do not
tend to infinity, there are infinitely many distinct levels $m_j$ with
$|\epsilon_{m_j}|\leq C$ for some $C$. Unit vectors $u_j$ on these levels
are orthogonal. For a fixed nonreal $z$, their resolvent images are also
orthogonal and have norm at least $(|z|+C)^{-1}$.
They have no convergent subsequence. The resolvent is therefore not
compact.
\end{proof}

When $|\epsilon_m|\to\infty$, the omitted part of the resolvent for
$\widetilde H_M$ in \eqref{a-limit-strong-resolvent} still carries the
constant multiplier $z^{-1}$. It does not converge in norm to the omitted
resolvent of $H_\epsilon$. Strong resolvent convergence and norm
convergence of an embedded finite-rank resolvent are distinct claims.

For $\beta>0$, the multiplier $e^{-\beta H_\epsilon}$ is bounded precisely
when the energies are bounded below. If there is no lower bound, the
levelwise exponential is an unbounded operator with domain
$\{f:\sum_m e^{-2\beta\epsilon_m}\norm{\mathsf F_mf}_2^2<\infty\}$.
Thus a finite Euclidean intertwining identity does not by itself supply a
bounded infinite heat semigroup.
When bounded below, the positive operator has trace
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_\epsilon})
 =e^{-\beta\epsilon_0}
 +\sum_{m\geq1}(p-1)p^{m-1}e^{-\beta\epsilon_m},
 \label{a-limit-thermal-trace}
\end{equation}
possibly infinite. This follows by summing its nonnegative diagonal
entries in the complete Haar basis. It is trace class exactly when this
series converges. For $\epsilon_m=c m$ with $c>0$, the condition is
$\beta c>\log p$, by the geometric-series test. For
$\epsilon_m=p^{\alpha m}$ with $\alpha>0$, it converges for every
$\beta>0$, since the exponential energy term eventually dominates the
linear-in-$m$ logarithm of the multiplicity. A thermodynamic partition
function therefore needs an energy choice and a summability condition in
addition to Hilbert-space reconstruction.


\section{Compatible interactions across finitely many primes}
\label{a-limit-multiprime}

\subsection{Tensor embeddings and rectangular cutoffs}

Let $\mathcal P$ be a finite prime set and let $\KK_{\mathrm{tor}}$ be a
finite-dimensional complex space for the retained torsion and dyadic sign
registers. Set
\begin{equation}
 \HH_{\mathcal P}^{\infty}
 =\KK_{\mathrm{tor}}\otimes
 \bigotimes_{p\in\mathcal P}L^2(\Z_p,\mu_p).
 \label{a-limit-multiprime-space}
\end{equation}
The corresponding finite register embeds by
$I_{\KK_{\mathrm{tor}}}\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathcal U_{p,h_p}$.
For a multi-depth $\mathbf h=(h_p)$, define
\[
 \mathsf E_{\mathbf h}
 =I_{\KK_{\mathrm{tor}}}\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathsf E_{p,h_p}.
\]
Factorwise projection identities give
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf E_{\mathbf h}\mathsf E_{\mathbf k}
 =\mathsf E_{\min(\mathbf h,\mathbf k)},
 \qquad \mathsf E_{\mathbf h}f\to f
 \quad\text{as every }h_p\to\infty.
 \label{a-limit-rectangular-projections}
\end{equation}
To justify the second statement, first take an elementary tensor. The
difference of the tensor projections and the identity is a finite
telescoping sum, one factor of which tends strongly to zero in each term,
while all other projection factors have norm at most one. Finite sums of
elementary tensors are dense, and the projections are contractions. This
extends convergence to every $f$.

Refinement in distinct coordinates is path independent because
\[
 (V_p\otimes I)(I\otimes V_q)
 =(I\otimes V_q)(V_p\otimes I)=V_p\otimes V_q.
\]
The identity on $\KK_{\mathrm{tor}}$ leaves the separately retained sign
channel untouched by the averaging. This is a finite set of primes.
An infinite tensor product, a restricted adelic product, and a model
including the Archimedean place each require further choices.

Define the joint detail projections
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf F_{\mathbf r}
 =I_{\KK_{\mathrm{tor}}}\otimes
 \bigotimes_{p\in\mathcal P}\mathsf F_{p,r_p},
 \qquad \mathbf r\in\N^{\mathcal P}.
 \label{a-limit-joint-details}
\end{equation}
They are pairwise orthogonal and have finite-dimensional ranges.
Rectangular sums equal $\mathsf E_{\mathbf h}$, so their strong sum is
the identity. This permits interactions between primes while preserving
the exact depth filtration.

\subsection{A complete block-domain theorem}

The scalar weights are one particularly simple choice. The following
editorial extension states the exact additional input for interacting
blocks. It is useful because the torsion operators inside a joint packet
need not commute with one another.

\begin{theorem}[Self-adjoint packet blocks and compatible finite dynamics]
\label{a-limit-block-hamiltonian}
For every $\mathbf r$, let $A_{\mathbf r}$ be a self-adjoint operator on
the finite-dimensional space
$\KK_{\mathbf r}=\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf F_{\mathbf r}$.
On $\HH_{\mathcal P}^{\infty}=\bigoplus_{\mathbf r}\KK_{\mathbf r}$ define
\begin{align}
 \Dom(H_A)&=\left\{f:\sum_{\mathbf r}
 \norm{A_{\mathbf r}\mathsf F_{\mathbf r}f}^2<\infty\right\},
 \nonumber\\
 H_A f&=\sum_{\mathbf r}A_{\mathbf r}\mathsf F_{\mathbf r}f.
 \label{a-limit-block-domain}
\end{align}
Then $H_A$ is self-adjoint, and finite rectangular packet sums form a
core. Every rectangular range reduces $H_A$, and its finite restriction
$H_A^{(\mathbf h)}$ satisfies exact embedding intertwining with every
larger rectangular restriction. For bounded Borel $F$,
\begin{equation}
 F(H_A)f=\sum_{\mathbf r}F(A_{\mathbf r})\mathsf F_{\mathbf r}f,
 \qquad
 F(H_A)\mathsf E_{\mathbf h}\to F(H_A)
 \quad\text{strongly}.
 \label{a-limit-block-calculus}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{e^{-itH_A}(I-\mathsf E_{\mathbf h})f}
 =\norm{(I-\mathsf E_{\mathbf h})f}.
 \label{a-limit-block-unitary-error}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Finite rectangular sums belong to the domain and are dense. Symmetry
holds by symmetry on every block. If $g$ belongs to the adjoint domain
and $k=H_A^*g$, testing against an arbitrary vector in
$\KK_{\mathbf r}$ gives
$\mathsf F_{\mathbf r}k=A_{\mathbf r}\mathsf F_{\mathbf r}g$.
Square summability of $k$ is precisely the domain condition in
\eqref{a-limit-block-domain}. Thus $H_A^*=H_A$. Truncating the two
square-summable sequences $f_{\mathbf r}$ and
$A_{\mathbf r}f_{\mathbf r}$ proves the graph-core assertion.

The rectangular projection selects a collection of whole blocks, so it
commutes with $H_A$ on the domain and reduces the operator.
The restriction to each retained block is literally the same matrix at
every subsequent depth. This proves the finite intertwining, and
finite-dimensional spectral calculus on each block gives
\eqref{a-limit-block-calculus}. Boundedness of $F$ bounds its omitted
image by $\norm F_\infty\norm{(I-\mathsf E_{\mathbf h})f}$, proving
strong convergence. Finally, each block exponential is unitary, so
orthogonality of the omitted blocks gives
\eqref{a-limit-block-unitary-error}.
\end{proof}

For example, on a joint depth packet one may take
\[
 A_{\mathbf r}
 =\left(\sum_a\epsilon_{a,\mathbf r}T_a\right)
 \otimes I_{\mathrm{phase},\mathbf r},
 \qquad \epsilon_{a,\mathbf r}\in\R,\quad T_a=T_a^*.
\]
The matrices $T_a$ act on the sign and torsion factors. Their mutual
commutation is unnecessary because their sum is self-adjoint on the
finite block. The coefficients assigned to an existing packet are fixed
under refinement. An extension acting wholly inside a new detail
complement has no matrix element between that complement and the old
range. A cross term between them would be a different model.

There is also an exact construction for any \emph{specified}
self-adjoint compatible finite family along a cofinal nested sequence.
Suppose finite-dimensional spaces $\mathcal V_0\subset\mathcal V_1
\subset\cdots$ have dense union, and self-adjoint $K_M$ satisfy
$K_{M+1}f=K_Mf$ for $f\in\mathcal V_M$.
Self-adjointness implies that $\mathcal V_M^\perp\cap\mathcal V_{M+1}$
is invariant: for $g$ there and $f\in\mathcal V_M$,
$\inner{f}{K_{M+1}g}=\inner{K_{M+1}f}{g}=0$.
The initial space $\mathcal V_0$ and the successive difference spaces
therefore have stable self-adjoint finite blocks.
Their orthogonal direct sum with the maximal square-summability domain
is self-adjoint by the same adjoint proof above. This is an editorial
compatible-family construction, not an assertion that arbitrary finite
Hamiltonians are compatible. The identities $K_{M+1}|_{\mathcal V_M}=K_M$
are its substantive hypothesis.

\subsection{An exact cross-prime entangling generator}

Let $Z_{\mathrm{sign}}$ have eigenvalues $+1,-1$ on a dyadic sign qubit,
and let $B=B^*$ act on the remaining factors. Assume there are orthonormal
states $|b_0\rangle,|b_1\rangle$ with
$B|b_0\rangle=0$ and $B|b_1\rangle=|b_1\rangle$.
One concrete choice is an odd-prime torsion involution times a fixed
odd-prime detail projector, with the torsion state in its $+1$ eigenspace.
For real $g\neq0$, use
\[
 H_{\mathrm{int}}=gZ_{\mathrm{sign}}\otimes B,
 \qquad
 |\Psi(0)\rangle=|+_x\rangle\otimes
 \frac{|b_0\rangle+|b_1\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]
Evolution under this explicit interaction alone gives
\begin{equation}
 |\Psi(t)\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}
 \left(|+_x\rangle\otimes|b_0\rangle
 +e^{-igtZ_{\mathrm{sign}}}|+_x\rangle\otimes|b_1\rangle\right).
 \label{a-limit-entangled-state}
\end{equation}
Tracing out the orthogonal $b$ states yields the equally weighted mixture
of the two displayed sign states. Their overlap is $\cos(gt)$.
A mixture of two unit vectors with equal weights and overlap magnitude
$c$ has eigenvalues $(1+c)/2$ and $(1-c)/2$: its trace is one and its
determinant on their two-dimensional span is $(1-c^2)/4$.
Thus the sign entropy in bits is
\begin{equation}
 S_{\mathrm{sign}}(t)
 =h_2\left(\frac{1+|\cos(gt)|}{2}\right),
 \quad h_2(u)=-u\log_2u-(1-u)\log_2(1-u),
 \label{a-limit-entanglement-entropy}
\end{equation}
with $0\log_2 0=0$. At $t_* =\pi/(2|g|)$ the two sign states are
orthogonal and the entropy is one bit. A fixed level projector is
compatible under refinement, so this interaction can entangle the prime
factors while preserving the cylinder embedding.
The tensor factorization alone creates no entanglement. It is this
chosen generator and initial superposition that produce the result.


\section{Controlled leakage when compatibility is broken}
\label{a-limit-leakage}

The preceding identities are exact because the coarse range reduces the
Hamiltonian. A weighted coupling to its complement has a different,
quantifiable behavior. This section concerns finite-dimensional
self-adjoint operators; no unbounded perturbation theorem is implicit.

Let $V$ be an isometry from a coarse space to a finite fine space, set
$P=VV^*$ and $Q=I-P$, and let $H_0=H_0^*$ satisfy
$H_0V=VH_c$. Let $B=B^*$ be purely off diagonal:
\[
 PBP=0,\qquad QBQ=0.
\]
For a real $\lambda$, define $H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda B$. In the source
model $\lambda=p^{-w}$ for an assigned weight $w\geq1$.

\begin{proposition}[Defect, leakage, and a second-order self-energy]
\label{a-limit-leakage-bounds}
Under these hypotheses,
\begin{align}
 \norm{H_\lambda V-VH_c}&=|\lambda|\norm{BV},
 \label{a-limit-defect-norm}\\
 \norm{Qe^{-itH_\lambda}P}
 &\leq\min\{1,|t\lambda|\norm{QBP}\}.
 \label{a-limit-duhamel-bound}
\end{align}
For $z\notin\sigma(QH_\lambda Q|_{Q\HH})$, the coarse self-energy is
\begin{equation}
 \Sigma_P(z)=PH_\lambda Q
 (z-QH_\lambda Q|_{Q\HH})^{-1}QH_\lambda P,
 \label{a-limit-feshbach-definition}
\end{equation}
where the inverse acts only on $Q\HH$, and
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\Sigma_P(z)}
 \leq\frac{|\lambda|^2\norm{PBQ}^2}
 {\operatorname{dist}(z,\sigma(QH_\lambda Q|_{Q\HH}))}.
 \label{a-limit-feshbach-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The defect is $\lambda BV$, so the first identity is immediate.
Self-adjointness of $H_0$ makes its invariant coarse range reducing.
Hence $Qe^{-itH_0}P=0$, and Duhamel's identity gives
\[
 Qe^{-itH_\lambda}P
 =-i\lambda\int_0^t
 Qe^{-i(t-s)H_\lambda}B e^{-isH_0}P\,ds.
\]
The off-diagonal assumption and reduction by $H_0$ give
$B e^{-isH_0}P=QBP e^{-isH_0}P$. The two propagators and the exterior
projections are contractions. Integrating the norm bound over an
interval of length $|t|$ gives the second expression in
\eqref{a-limit-duhamel-bound}. The bound one follows directly from
unitarity and the norms of the projections.

The coarse/detail blocks of $H_0$ vanish, so
$PH_\lambda Q=\lambda PBQ$ and $QH_\lambda P=\lambda QBP$.
The detail compression is self-adjoint. Diagonalizing it bounds the
resolvent norm by the reciprocal spectral distance. Since
$QBP=(PBQ)^*$, submultiplicativity gives
\eqref{a-limit-feshbach-bound}.
\end{proof}

The small-time leading term is $-it\lambda QBP$. More precisely,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{Qe^{-itH_\lambda}P+it\lambda QBP}
 \leq\frac{|\lambda|t^2}{2}
 \bigl(\norm{H_\lambda}+\norm{H_0}\bigr)\norm{QBP}.
 \label{a-limit-shorttime-remainder}
\end{equation}
To verify this, subtract the constant integrand $QBP$ in Duhamel's
formula and use $\norm{e^{-iuK}-I}\leq|u|\norm K$ for a finite
self-adjoint $K$. The two deviations are bounded by
$(|t-s|\norm{H_\lambda}+|s|\norm{H_0})\norm{QBP}$ on the oriented
integration interval. Their integrals are both $t^2/2$.
For $|\lambda|\leq1$, this is a uniform $O(t^2|\lambda|)$ remainder.
A generic $O(t^2\lambda^2)$ remainder would omit the first-order
interaction with the background Hamiltonian.

For the stipulated assignment $\lambda=p^{-w}$, the operator defect and
this leakage upper bound scale linearly with $p^{-w}$. The self-energy
bound is quadratic in $p^{-w}$ away from the detail spectrum. Under the
purely off-diagonal hypothesis, $QH_\lambda Q=QH_0Q$, so the denominator
does not depend on $\lambda$. Approaching a detail resonance removes
that uniform estimate. These are exact finite quantum statements for a
chosen coupling law. An integral valuation packet does not, by itself,
force every physical interaction strength to equal $p^{-w}$.


\section{A local walk on physical position and refinement depth}
\label{a-limit-product-walk}

\subsection{The finite graph and its unitary tick}

Let $N\geq3$ and $h\geq0$. Let $C_N$ be the physical cycle and let
$T_{p,h}$ be the rooted finite $p$-ary tree of prefixes of length at most
$h$. The product graph is
\[
 \mathcal G=C_N\square T_{p,h}.
\]
A vertex is $v=(x,\mathbf d)$, with $x\in\Z/N\Z$ and $\mathbf d$ a
prefix. An edge changes either $x$ by one on the cycle or the prefix by
one parent-child step. The graph has
$N\sum_{r=0}^h p^r$ vertices. It includes all tree depths, unlike a
cylinder register which contains only the residues at its last depth.

Let $\vec E$ denote the directed arcs and let $\tau_2=2$,
$\tau_p=p-1$ for odd $p$. The finite arc Hilbert space is
\[
 \HH_{\mathrm{arc}}=\ell^2(\vec E)\otimes\C^{\tau_p}.
\]
For each vertex of degree $d_v$, define the normalized outgoing vector
$s_v=d_v^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)$ and the Grover coin
$G_v=2|s_v\rangle\langle s_v|-I$.
Its square is $I$, because $|s_v\rangle\langle s_v|$ is a projection.
Take any local unitary $R_v$ on the torsion or sign factor and put
\[
 C=\bigoplus_v(G_v\otimes R_v).
\]
The reversal shift $S$ sends the arc $v\to u$ to $u\to v$, retaining
the internal register. It is a permutation with $S^*=S$ and $S^2=I$.
The one-tick walk
\begin{equation}
 U_{p,h,N}=SC
 \label{a-limit-walk-unitary}
\end{equation}
is unitary because $U_{p,h,N}^*U_{p,h,N}=C^*S^*SC=C^*C=I$.
Here locality concerns the graph edges, with no continuum limit assumed.

\subsection{Local conservation and the product cone}

Write $\psi^n(v,u)$ for the internal amplitude on an arc leaving $v$
before the coin, and $\phi^n=C\psi^n$ for its post-coin value. Define
\[
 \rho_v^n=\sum_{u\sim v}\norm{\psi^n(v,u)}^2,
 \qquad F_{v\to u}^n=\norm{\phi^n(v,u)}^2.
\]
The local unitary coin gives
$\sum_uF_{v\to u}^n=\rho_v^n$.
The reversal shift gives
$\rho_v^{n+1}=\sum_u F_{u\to v}^n$. Subtraction proves
\begin{equation}
 \rho_v^{n+1}-\rho_v^n
 =\sum_{u\sim v}(F_{u\to v}^n-F_{v\to u}^n).
 \label{a-limit-walk-continuity}
\end{equation}
For every set of vertices $A$, summing this equation cancels every
internal directed flux once with its opposite occurrence. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{v\in A}(\rho_v^{n+1}-\rho_v^n)
 =\sum_{\substack{u\notin A,\ v\in A\\u\sim v}}F_{u\to v}^n
 -\sum_{\substack{v\in A,\ u\notin A\\u\sim v}}F_{v\to u}^n.
 \label{a-limit-walk-coarse-balance}
\end{equation}
Taking $A$ to be all vertices gives conservation of total probability.
The coarse identity uses a subset of vertices and does not presume
amplitude-level Haar refinement.

\begin{proposition}[Exact finite propagation]
\label{a-limit-walk-cone}
If the initial outgoing amplitudes are supported at $v_0$, then
\begin{equation}
 d_{C_N}(x,x_0)+d_T(\mathbf d,\mathbf d_0)>n
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho_{(x,\mathbf d)}^n=0.
 \label{a-limit-product-cone}
\end{equation}
For two prefixes, writing $\operatorname{lcp}$ for the length of their
longest common prefix,
\[
 d_T(\mathbf d,\mathbf d_0)
 =|\mathbf d|+|\mathbf d_0|-2\operatorname{lcp}(\mathbf d,\mathbf d_0).
\]
In particular, each tick allows at most one physical edge or one tree
edge, and $\bigl||\mathbf d|-|\mathbf d_0|\bigr|\leq n$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every path in a Cartesian product graph uses a number of physical edges
at least the physical distance and a number of tree edges at least the
tree distance. Their sum is a lower bound on path length. Following a
shortest physical path and then a shortest tree path attains that sum,
so it is the product graph distance. In a rooted tree the shortest path
rises to the longest common prefix and then descends, giving the
displayed formula.

The claim at $n=0$ is the support hypothesis. A coin mixes outgoing
arcs only at their common source, so it does not enlarge the vertex
support. The shift moves the source across one edge. A state supported
in the radius-$n$ ball is therefore supported in the radius-$(n+1)$
ball after a tick. Induction proves the result. Since each graph edge
changes only one factor, the individual distance and depth bounds follow.
\end{proof}

The depth difference alone is weaker than the full tree distance.
Different prefixes at the same depth can have positive distance, so a
plot aggregated over depth does not show the complete graph geometry.
The cone is an exact support property of this finite coined model.
A Lorentzian continuum dispersion law or a relativistic limiting field
equation requires a separate scaling analysis.

\section{Polyphase coordinates and folded bands}
\label{a-spectral-polyphase}

The finite Haar decomposition isolates an average and its new detail
channels. A standard polyphase decomposition instead groups the entries
of a cyclic lattice by their residue class. Both transformations preserve
the full state space. An elimination begins only when some coordinates
are solved for and removed. The spectral parameter then enters the
remaining operator, and the eliminated degrees of freedom return as
memory in time.

We use complex Hilbert spaces with inner product linear in the second
argument and set $\hbar=1$. All matrices in the finite sections act on
their stated coordinate spaces. In particular, the inverse of a low
channel block is a low channel operator, rather than a full space matrix.

\subsection{Residue coordinates and exact block reconstruction}

Fix an integer $p\geq2$ and $M\geq3$, and put $N=pM$. Primality is not
needed for the identities in this section. For $0\leq r<p$, define the
isometry $J_r:\C^M\to\C^N$ by
\[
 J_r|k\rangle=|pk+r\rangle,\qquad 0\leq k<M.
\]
Then $J_r^*J_s=\delta_{rs}I_M$ and $\sum_rJ_rJ_r^*=I_N$. The standard
analysis map $\mathcal A$ sends $|pk+r\rangle$ to
$|r\rangle\otimes|k\rangle$. This is a permutation unitary. For any
operator $X$ on $\C^N$, its residue blocks $X_{rs}=J_r^*XJ_s$ reconstruct it:
\begin{equation}
 X=\sum_{r,s=0}^{p-1}J_rX_{rs}J_s^*,\qquad
 (\mathcal A X\mathcal A^*)_{rs}=X_{rs}.
 \label{a-spectral-block-reconstruction}
\end{equation}
The first equality follows by inserting $\sum_rJ_rJ_r^*$ on both sides
of $X$. If $H=H^*$, its blocks satisfy $H_{rs}^*=H_{sr}$. If $U$ is
unitary, the same insertion gives
\begin{align}
 \sum_rU_{rs}^*U_{rt}&=J_s^*U^*UJ_t=\delta_{st}I_M,\nonumber\\
 \sum_sU_{rs}U_{ts}^*&=J_r^*UU^*J_t=\delta_{rt}I_M.
 \label{a-spectral-paraunitarity}
\end{align}
These are the block unitary identities. Every coordinate is retained.

For finite $H$, expansion of the matrix exponential proves
\[
 e^{-it\mathcal A H\mathcal A^*}
   =\mathcal A e^{-itH}\mathcal A^*.
\]
Indeed $(\mathcal A H\mathcal A^*)^n=\mathcal A H^n\mathcal A^*$,
and the series converges in matrix norm. The same transformation of
each Kraus operator gives a unitarily equivalent quantum channel:
if $\Phi(\rho)=\sum_\mu K_\mu\rho K_\mu^*$ with
$\sum_\mu K_\mu^*K_\mu=I$, then
\[
 K_\mu^{\rm poly}=\mathcal A K_\mu\mathcal A^*,\qquad
 \sum_\mu(K_\mu^{\rm poly})^*K_\mu^{\rm poly}=I.
\]
This is a change of coordinates in a given channel. It does not supply
a new dissipative dynamics.

\begin{proposition}[Probability currents between residue channels]

\[

 \mathcal J_{r\leftarrow s}
   =2\operatorname{Im}\langle\psi_r,H_{rs}\psi_s\rangle,
 \qquad
 \mathcal J_{r\leftarrow s}=-\mathcal J_{s\leftarrow r}.
\]
Consequently $\sum_rw_r$ is constant.
\end{proposition}

$\dot w_r=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\psi_r,-i\sum_sH_{rs}\psi_s\rangle$,

$\langle\psi_s,H_{sr}\psi_r\rangle
=\overline{\langle\psi_r,H_{rs}\psi_s\rangle}$.

\end{proof}

\subsection{A Bloch symbol with a fixed shift convention}

Let $S|n\rangle=|n+1\pmod N\rangle$ and
\begin{equation}
 H=\mu I+\kappa(S+S^*),\qquad \mu,\kappa\in\R.
 \label{a-spectral-free-cycle}
\end{equation}
Use the coarse Fourier matrix
$(F_M)_{jk}=M^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi ijk/M}$ and
$\theta_j=2\pi j/M$. After $\mathcal A$, Fourier transformation in $k$,
and the permutation from residue major to momentum major ordering, the
operator becomes a direct sum of $p\times p$ symbols. To see their entries,
note that $S$ sends $(r,k)$ to $(r+1,k)$ for $r<p-1$ and sends
$(p-1,k)$ to $(0,k+1)$. The coarse shift has Fourier eigenvalue
$e^{-i\theta_j}$. Thus define
\begin{equation}
 P_p(\theta)e_r=
 \begin{cases}
 e_{r+1},&r<p-1,\\
 e^{-i\theta}e_0,&r=p-1.
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \mathsf H_p(\theta)=\mu I_p+\kappa(P_p(\theta)+P_p(\theta)^*).
 \label{a-spectral-bloch-symbol}
\end{equation}
The transformed $H$ is $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{M-1}\mathsf H_p(\theta_j)$.
In particular, $P_p(\theta)^p=e^{-i\theta}I_p$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact folded cyclic spectrum]
\label{a-spectral-folded-bands}

$\mathsf H_p(\theta)$ are
\begin{equation}

     \cos\!\left(\frac{\theta+2\pi q}{p}\right).
 \label{a-spectral-band-formula}
\end{equation}
At $\theta=\theta_j$, the union of these $pM$ eigenvalues, counting
multiplicity, is exactly the spectrum of \eqref{a-spectral-free-cycle}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}

$v_q$ be $p^{-1/2}e^{i\alpha_qr}$. On the interior components,
$P_p(\theta)v_q=e^{-i\alpha_q}v_q$. The wrapped component has the
same value because $e^{ip\alpha_q}=e^{i\theta}$. The $v_q$ are
orthonormal by the finite character sum. Applying
$\mu I+\kappa(P_p+P_p^*)$ gives \eqref{a-spectral-band-formula}.
Every fine Fourier index is uniquely $k=j+qM$. Its angle satisfies
$2\pi k/(pM)=(\theta_j+2\pi q)/p$. Substitution into the fine cyclic
eigenvalue $\mu+2\kappa\cos(2\pi k/N)$ proves the multiplicity statement.
\end{proof}

\section{Regular Schur reduction and causal memory}
\label{a-spectral-feshbach}

Let a finite Hilbert space be the orthogonal sum
$\HH_L\oplus\HH_D$, and write a self-adjoint Hamiltonian as
\begin{equation}
 H=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^*&D\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=A^*,\quad D=D^*.
 \label{a-spectral-block-hamiltonian}
\end{equation}
Here $B:\HH_D\to\HH_L$. Let $\iota_L$ embed $\HH_L$ into the full
space. This notation fixes the coordinate type of every compression.

\subsection{The resolvent chart and its exceptional energies}

\begin{theorem}[Finite Feshbach identity]
\label{a-spectral-schur-theorem}
If $z\notin\sigma(D)$, define
\begin{equation}
 \Sigma(z)=B(z-D)^{-1}B^*,\qquad
 \mathcal S(z)=z-A-\Sigma(z).
 \label{a-spectral-schur-definition}
\end{equation}
Then $z-H$ is invertible exactly when $\mathcal S(z)$ is invertible.
On this common regular set,
\begin{align}
 \iota_L^*(z-H)^{-1}\iota_L&=\mathcal S(z)^{-1},\nonumber\\
 \det(z-H)&=\det(z-D)\det\mathcal S(z).
 \label{a-spectral-schur-identities}
\end{align}
For $E\in\R\setminus\sigma(D)$, an eigenvector of $H$ is equivalent to
a nonzero solution of $\mathcal S(E)u=0$, with hidden component
$v=(E-D)^{-1}B^*u$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $C=z-D$. Direct block multiplication gives
\[
 z-H=
 \begin{pmatrix}I&-BC^{-1}\\0&I\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}\mathcal S(z)&0\\0&C\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-C^{-1}B^*&I\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both outer factors are invertible and have determinant one. This proves
the invertibility equivalence and determinant formula. Inverting the
factors gives the stated upper left block. Alternatively, in
$(z-H)(u,v)^{\mathsf T}=(f,0)^{\mathsf T}$, the lower equation gives
$v=C^{-1}B^*u$ and the upper equation becomes $\mathcal S(z)u=f$.
The same elimination with $f=0$ proves the eigenvector statement.
If $u=0$ at such an $E$, invertibility of $E-D$ forces $v=0$, so a
nonzero full eigenvector indeed has $u\ne0$.
\end{proof}

If $P_L=\iota_L\iota_L^*$, the full space compression is
$P_L(z-H)^{-1}P_L=\iota_L\mathcal S(z)^{-1}\iota_L^*$.
When a Haar transform $\mathcal W$ first exposes low and detail channels,
the embedding in the original coordinates is
$\iota_L=\mathcal W^*(|0\rangle\otimes I)$.
The inverse on $\HH_L$ must be embedded in this way before it is compared
with a full space matrix.

The determinant equality is initially a rational identity on the regular
set. Multiplication by $\det(z-D)$ cancels its denominators and yields the
full characteristic polynomial, which extends across $\sigma(D)$.
This extension does not make the displayed inverse of $z-D$ exist at
a pole. At a resonant energy the uneliminated equations determine which
hidden modes couple, survive, or cancel. A resonant subspace can be kept

 \label{a-spectral-self-energy-residues}
\end{equation}
Every residue $B E_\lambda B^*$ is positive semidefinite. Its rank records
which directions of the hidden eigenspace reach the visible space.
A vanishing residue removes the corresponding pole of $\Sigma$, even
though $z-D$ is still singular there.

\begin{proposition}[Upper half-plane sign and the exact visible norm]

Applying this identity to the spectral sum gives the first formula and
then the bound on $\operatorname{Im}\mathcal S$.
For any $u$, Cauchy--Schwarz implies
$y\norm{u}^2\leq|\langle u,\mathcal S(z)u\rangle|
\leq\norm{u}\norm{\mathcal S(z)u}$.
Thus $\mathcal S(z)$ has trivial kernel and an inverse of the stated
norm in finite dimension. Differentiating the resolvent gives the minus
sign in $\Sigma'$. The reconstructed hidden norm is
$\norm{v}^2=\langle u,B(E-D)^{-2}B^*u\rangle$.
Adding $\norm{u}^2$ proves \eqref{a-spectral-visible-norm}.
\end{proof}

For a one-dimensional visible block this says that an eigenstate's
visible probability is $[1-\Sigma'(E)]^{-1}$. It is at most one, as
required. Eliminating a normalized eigenvector therefore changes its
normalization metric as well as its spectral equation. Solving only a
nonlinear energy equation does not provide that probability weight.

\subsection{Exact elimination in the time domain}

\begin{theorem}[Causal memory with the initial hidden forcing]
\label{a-spectral-memory-theorem}
The finite system
$i\dot u=Au+Bv$, $i\dot v=Dv+B^*u$, with initial data $(u_0,v_0)$,
is equivalent to
\begin{align}
 i\dot u(t)&=Au(t)+B e^{-itD}v_0
              -i\int_0^tK(t-s)u(s)\,ds,\nonumber\\
 K(\tau)&=B e^{-i\tau D}B^*,\qquad \tau\geq0,
 \label{a-spectral-memory-equation}
\end{align}
together with reconstruction
\begin{equation}
 v(t)=e^{-itD}v_0-i\int_0^te^{-i(t-s)D}B^*u(s)\,ds.
 \label{a-spectral-hidden-reconstruction}
\end{equation}
For $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, the self-energy is its exact one-sided transform:
\begin{equation}
 \Sigma(z)=-i\int_0^\infty e^{iz\tau}K(\tau)\,d\tau.
 \label{a-spectral-memory-transform}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Differentiate $e^{itD}v(t)$ and integrate the hidden equation. This gives
\eqref{a-spectral-hidden-reconstruction}, whose substitution in the
visible equation gives \eqref{a-spectral-memory-equation}. Conversely
the reconstruction differentiates to the hidden equation and supplies
the prescribed initial value, so it recovers the full evolution.
Since $D$ is self-adjoint, $\norm{K(\tau)}\leq\norm{B}^2$.
The factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}z\,\tau}$ makes the transform absolutely
convergent. On a spectral eigenvalue of $D$,
$\int_0^\infty e^{i(z-\lambda)\tau}\,d\tau=i/(z-\lambda)$.
The finite spectral sum then proves \eqref{a-spectral-memory-transform}.
\end{proof}

The memory is causal because it uses only $s\leq t$. An initially empty
hidden sector removes the forcing $B e^{-itD}v_0$, not the convolution.
In finite dimension $K$ is a finite sum of oscillatory terms. Its decay,
a Markov approximation, or irreversible damping requires additional
limits or assumptions. The closed full dynamics preserves
$\norm{u(t)}^2+\norm{v(t)}^2$, while the visible norm alone can decrease
and later return. Energy-dependent Schur reduction is consequently
different from replacing $H$ by a fixed smaller self-adjoint matrix.

\section{Rooted trees and radial Jacobi response}
\label{a-spectral-radial}

Let $T_{p,h}$ be a rooted $p$-ary tree of depth $h\geq1$. Vertices at
depth $r$ have onsite energy $\epsilon_r\in\R$. Every parent-to-child
edge from level $r$ to $r+1$ has real coupling $\gamma_r/\sqrt p$,
where $\gamma_r\in\R$. The Hamiltonian is the corresponding real
symmetric adjacency matrix with onsite diagonal. The level symmetry
and this branch normalization are structural assumptions of the model.

\subsection{The radial reducing subspace}

Define normalized level states
\[
 |r\rangle=p^{-r/2}\sum_{|v|=r}|v\rangle,
 \qquad r=0,\ldots,h.
\]
They are orthonormal because different levels are disjoint and level
$r$ contains $p^r$ vertices. A direct action calculation gives
\begin{equation}
 H|r\rangle=\gamma_{r-1}|r-1\rangle
              +\epsilon_r|r\rangle+\gamma_r|r+1\rangle,
 \label{a-spectral-radial-action}
\end{equation}
with omitted terms at the endpoints. For example, the coefficient at
each child at level $r+1$ is
$p^{-r/2}\gamma_r/\sqrt p=\gamma_r p^{-(r+1)/2}$.
At each parent at level $r-1$, the $p$ child contributions instead give
$p\,p^{-r/2}\gamma_{r-1}/\sqrt p
=\gamma_{r-1}p^{-(r-1)/2}$.

Let $R:\C^{h+1}\to\ell^2(T_{p,h})$ send $e_r$ to $|r\rangle$.
Equation \eqref{a-spectral-radial-action} proves $HR=RJ_h$, where
\begin{equation}
 J_h=\begin{pmatrix}
 \epsilon_0&\gamma_0&&&\\
 \gamma_0&\epsilon_1&\gamma_1&&\\
 &\gamma_1&\epsilon_2&\ddots&\\
 &&\ddots&\ddots&\gamma_{h-1}\\
 &&&\gamma_{h-1}&\epsilon_h
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \label{a-spectral-jacobi-matrix}
\end{equation}
Because $H$ is self-adjoint, the orthogonal complement of $\Ran R$ is
also invariant: for $w\perp\Ran R$,
$\langle Re_r,Hw\rangle=\langle HRe_r,w\rangle=0$.
Hence this is a reducing decomposition, rather than only a compressed
approximation. The root belongs to the radial block.

\subsection{Angular chains and their multiplicities}

There is a more precise form of the complementary decomposition. For
each vertex $u$ at depth $a<h$, choose an orthonormal basis of vectors
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{p-1})\in\C^p$ with $\sum_dc_d=0$. For
$s=0,\ldots,h-a-1$, set
\begin{equation}
 |u,c;s\rangle
 =p^{-s/2}\sum_{d=0}^{p-1}c_d
       \sum_{w\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}^{s}}|u d w\rangle.
 \label{a-spectral-angular-chain}
\end{equation}
For fixed $u,c$, these are unit vectors on successive levels. They obey
the Jacobi recurrence with onsite energies
$\epsilon_{a+1},\ldots,\epsilon_h$ and couplings
$\gamma_{a+1},\ldots,\gamma_{h-1}$. At $s=0$ the upward amplitude into
$u$ is proportional to $\sum_dc_d$, so it vanishes. At $s>0$ the same
branch-counting calculation as in \eqref{a-spectral-radial-action}
produces the neighboring chain vectors.

\begin{proposition}[Complete angular-chain decomposition]
\label{a-spectral-angular-completeness}
The radial chain and all the chains \eqref{a-spectral-angular-chain}
form an orthogonal decomposition of $\ell^2(T_{p,h})$. A chain starting
at depth $r$ has length $h-r+1$ and appears with multiplicity
$(p-1)p^{r-1}$, for $1\leq r\leq h$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Within one chain, different $s$ have disjoint level supports. Chains
based at the same $u$ and different contrast vectors have inner product
$\langle c,c'\rangle=0$ at a common level. If two vertices are in disjoint
subtrees, their chains have disjoint support. If one vertex lies below
another, the higher chain is constant, up to its fixed ancestral
coefficient, on all children below the lower vertex at a common level.
The lower chain has zero sum over its own child contrasts, so their
inner product is zero. The same zero-sum calculation makes every
angular vector orthogonal to the uniform radial level vector.
At a fixed depth $b$, the radial vector contributes one dimension.
The angular vectors present there contribute
$\sum_{r=1}^b(p-1)p^{r-1}=p^b-1$ dimensions. They are orthogonal and
therefore form a basis of that $p^b$-dimensional level space. Taking
all levels proves completeness. There are $p^{r-1}$ choices of the
vertex $u$ at depth $r-1$ and $p-1$ contrasts at each, giving the
stated multiplicity.
\end{proof}

The rank $(p-1)p^{r-1}$ thus counts chains born at level $r$ or
new Haar directions on a level. A single level's detail space is
usually transported to the next level; it is the entire angular
chain that is invariant under the tree Hamiltonian. The full dark
dimension is
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^h(p-1)p^{r-1}(h-r+1)
 =\sum_{b=0}^hp^b-(h+1).
\]
Every one of these states is invisible to a root-localized symmetric
source because it is orthogonal to the radial reducing block.

\subsection{Continued fractions and their meromorphic reading}

For a tail $J_{r:h}$, put
$g_r(z)=\langle r,(z-J_{r:h})^{-1}r\rangle$. On a common regular
domain, scalar Schur elimination gives
\begin{align}
 g_h(z)&=(z-\epsilon_h)^{-1},\nonumber\\
 g_r(z)&=\frac1{z-\epsilon_r-\gamma_r^2g_{r+1}(z)},
          \qquad r<h.
 \label{a-spectral-continued-fraction}
\end{align}
Defining $\Sigma_h=0$ and
$\Sigma_r=\gamma_r^2/(z-\epsilon_{r+1}-\Sigma_{r+1})$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \langle\mathrm{root},(z-H)^{-1}\mathrm{root}\rangle
   =g_0(z)=\frac1{z-\epsilon_0-\Sigma_0(z)}.
 \label{a-spectral-root-green}
\end{equation}
The equality to the tree resolvent follows from the exact reducing
decomposition. Equations \eqref{a-spectral-continued-fraction} are
rational identities. Nested denominators can become singular at a
real energy where a canceled final rational expression is finite.
One should use the resolvent or the canceled rational function at
such a point, rather than perform division by zero in the nested chart.

The Jacobi coefficients in \eqref{a-spectral-jacobi-matrix} do not
depend on $p$. Thus the root Green function and radial propagator
are prime independent when the same $\epsilon_r,\gamma_r$ are used.
The complete tree spectrum retains the $p$-dependent angular
multiplicities. If the per-edge coupling is instead a fixed $g_r$,
the radial coupling is $\sqrt p\,g_r$ and its response depends on $p$.
Prime independence is therefore a consequence of the declared
normalization, not a universality statement about arbitrary trees.

\subsection{A visible two-component block}

As a conditional finite model, take
$A=H_D(k)=k\sigma_z+m_0\sigma_x$ with $k,m_0\in\R$ and
$D=J_{1:h}\otimes I_2$. Couple the visible spinor identically to the
first site of the tail by $B=\gamma_0(\langle1|\otimes I_2)$.
Its self-energy is scalar in spin space:
\[
 \Sigma_D(z)=\sigma(z)I_2,\qquad
 \sigma(z)=\gamma_0^2\langle1,(z-J_{1:h})^{-1}1\rangle.
\]
The determinant formula from Theorem~\ref{a-spectral-schur-theorem} is
\begin{equation}
 \det(z-H_{\rm full})
 =\det(z-D)\bigl((z-\sigma(z))^2-k^2-m_0^2\bigr).
 \label{a-spectral-visible-determinant}
\end{equation}
Consequently any eigenvalue in the regular chart obeys
\begin{equation}
 (E-\sigma(E))^2=k^2+m_0^2.
 \label{a-spectral-visible-branch}
\end{equation}
The formula is a dressed dispersion relation of this specific model.
Its mass, couplings, and hidden sector have been supplied. No physical
interaction or measured dispersion follows solely from the tree split.

For a nondegenerate visible spin direction with normalized low-space
direction $u_*$, the visible weight of its normalized full eigenstate is
$[1-\sigma'(E)]^{-1}$. If $k=m_0=0$, the spin eigenspace is degenerate,
but the same normalization relation holds for each chosen unit vector
in that eigenspace.

If every internal tail hopping is nonzero, the first tail site is cyclic.
One can see this without an abstract cyclicity theorem: a tail eigenvector
with zero first component has zero second component by the first row,
and successive rows force all later components to vanish. Therefore
every tail eigenvector has nonzero first component. At an eigenvalue
$\lambda$ of that tail, solvability of
$(\lambda-D)v=B^*u$ requires its right side to be orthogonal to the tail
eigenspace. With $\gamma_0\ne0$ and identical spin coupling this forces
$u=0$. The visible equation would then require $Bv=0$, which forces
$v=0$ on the tail eigenspace. Thus in this irreducible case the full
coupled spectrum avoids the tail eigenvalues. With a vanishing hopping,
coincident visible and hidden energies can occur and the regular-chart
qualification in \eqref{a-spectral-visible-branch} is essential.

The scalar causal kernel is
$K(\tau)=\gamma_0^2\langle1,e^{-i\tau J_{1:h}}1\rangle$, multiplying
$I_2$. It uses the same radial coefficients as the rational self-energy.
Its exact causal relation is \eqref{a-spectral-memory-transform}.

\section{Chebyshev decimation and resonant channels}
\label{a-spectral-chebyshev}

We now eliminate intermediate residue sites in
\eqref{a-spectral-free-cycle}, assuming $\kappa\ne0$. The retained
sites are $C=\{0,p,\ldots,(M-1)p\}$ and the eliminated sites comprise
the $p-1$ interior sites between adjacent retained sites. Identify
$\ell^2(C)$ with $\C^M$ and let $T|j\rangle=|j+1\pmod M\rangle$.
Set
\begin{equation}
 x=\frac{z-\mu}{\kappa},\qquad
 R_n(x)=2T_n(x/2),
 \label{a-spectral-normalized-energy}
\end{equation}
where $T_n$ is the first-kind Chebyshev polynomial. The second-kind
polynomials $U_n$ satisfy $U_{-1}=0$, $U_0=1$ and
$U_{n+1}(t)=2tU_n(t)-U_{n-1}(t)$.

\subsection{The eliminated path fixes the Schur prefactor}

The stationary equation on an interior site is
$\psi_{n+1}=x\psi_n-\psi_{n-1}$. The eliminated block of $z-H$ in
one cell is $\kappa K_{p-1}(x)$, where $K_n(x)$ has diagonal $x$
and neighboring off-diagonal entries $-1$.

\begin{lemma}[Dirichlet path determinant and endpoint entries]
\label{a-spectral-path-inverse}
For $n\geq1$, $\det K_n(x)=U_n(x/2)$. If this determinant is nonzero,
\[
 (K_n(x)^{-1})_{11}=(K_n(x)^{-1})_{nn}
       =\frac{U_{n-1}(x/2)}{U_n(x/2)},\qquad
 (K_n(x)^{-1})_{1n}=\frac1{U_n(x/2)}.
\]
For $n=1$ these entries all denote the same value $1/x$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expansion along the last row gives the determinant recurrence
$d_n=xd_{n-1}-d_{n-2}$, with $d_0=1$ and $d_1=x$.
This is exactly the recurrence and initial data for $U_n(x/2)$.
Deleting the first or last row and column leaves $K_{n-1}$, proving
the diagonal inverse entries by cofactors. For the endpoint entry,
the cofactor consists of the product of $n-1$ entries $-1$ along the
unique path from the first endpoint to the last. Its cofactor sign is
$(-1)^{n+1}$, so the product has total sign
$(-1)^{n+1}(-1)^{n-1}=1$. Division by $d_n$ gives the stated value.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact free-cycle decimation]
\label{a-spectral-chebyshev-schur}
For $U_{p-1}(x/2)\ne0$, the Schur operator on the retained sublattice is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal S_p(z)=\frac{\kappa}{U_{p-1}(x/2)}
          \bigl[R_p(x)I_M-(T+T^*)\bigr].
 \label{a-spectral-decimation-formula}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $\mathcal S_p(z)=zI-H_{\rm eff}^{(p)}(z)$, where
\begin{align}
 H_{\rm eff}^{(p)}(z)&=\mu_p(z)I+\kappa_p(z)(T+T^*),\nonumber\\
 \kappa_p(z)&=\frac{\kappa}{U_{p-1}(x/2)},\qquad
 \mu_p(z)=z-\frac{\kappa R_p(x)}{U_{p-1}(x/2)}.
 \label{a-spectral-effective-coefficients}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The eliminated sites split into $M$ disjoint Dirichlet paths of length
$p-1$. Hence their resolvent exists exactly when
$U_{p-1}(x/2)\ne0$. A retained site touches one endpoint on each of
its two neighboring paths. Each path contributes the onsite
self-energy $\kappa U_{p-2}/U_{p-1}$ by
Lemma~\ref{a-spectral-path-inverse}; the two contributions add.
The path joining two adjacent retained sites contributes off-diagonal
self-energy $\kappa/U_{p-1}$. Thus
\[
 \mathcal S_p(z)
 =\kappa\left(x-\frac{2U_{p-2}(x/2)}{U_{p-1}(x/2)}\right)I
       -\frac{\kappa}{U_{p-1}(x/2)}(T+T^*).
\]
The identity
$xU_{p-1}(x/2)-2U_{p-2}(x/2)=2T_p(x/2)$ follows from the
three-term recurrence and $U_p-U_{p-2}=2T_p$.
For the latter identity, substituting $x/2=\cos\theta$ gives
$[\sin((p+1)\theta)-\sin((p-1)\theta)]/\sin\theta
=2\cos(p\theta)$, and polynomial equality extends it to all $x$.
This proves \eqref{a-spectral-decimation-formula} including its
prefactor. Rearranging its diagonal gives
\eqref{a-spectral-effective-coefficients}.
\end{proof}

The normalized effective energy is
$(z-\mu_p(z))/\kappa_p(z)=R_p(x)$. The parameter $z$ remains fixed
through the elimination. Since $\mu_p$ and $\kappa_p$ depend on it,
this is an energy-dependent spectral closure, not an energy-independent
Hamiltonian flow. For $p=2$, $R_2(x)=x^2-2$ and $U_1(x/2)=x$, giving
\begin{equation}
 H_{\rm eff}^{(2)}(z)
 =\mu I+\frac{\kappa^2}{z-\mu}(2I+T+T^*),\qquad z\ne\mu.
 \label{a-spectral-dyadic-effective}
\end{equation}
This decimation retains every other site. It does not retain the
average of each neighboring pair.

\subsection{The poles have an exact Dirichlet interpretation}

The sine formula $U_{p-1}(\cos\theta)=\sin(p\theta)/\sin\theta$
shows that the excluded normalized energies are
\begin{equation}
 x_j=2\cos(j\pi/p),\qquad
 z_j=\mu+2\kappa\cos(j\pi/p),\quad 1\leq j<p.
 \label{a-spectral-dirichlet-resonances}
\end{equation}
These are the energies of one eliminated path. Indeed its $j$th
eigenvector has interior components $\sin(j\pi r/p)$,
$r=1,\ldots,p-1$, and the nearest-neighbor recurrence gives precisely
$z_j$. Both boundary values at $r=0,p$ vanish. The eigenvectors are
orthogonal and there are $p-1$ of them, so these exhaust the path spectrum.

The polynomial map $R_p$ is defined at every $x_j$, while the Schur
coefficients in \eqref{a-spectral-effective-coefficients} are not.
Cancelling denominators in a determinant can cross this chart boundary;
dividing by them in an eigenvector reconstruction cannot. A correct
description there keeps the resonant cell modes or solves the full
finite system. The fixed poles of the eliminated path are not all
automatically eigenvalues of the full cyclic Hamiltonian.

Let $Q$ project onto the eliminated sites. On the regular chart,
\[
 \det(z-H)=\det(z-QHQ)\det\mathcal S_p(z),\qquad
 \det(z-QHQ)=\bigl[\kappa^{p-1}U_{p-1}(x/2)\bigr]^M.
\]
Their product is a polynomial identity after cancellation. It records
both the hidden path factor and the coarse Schur factor, including
their cancellations at the resonant energies.

\subsection{Transfer coordinates and many-to-one branch maps}

Define $A(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant
is one and induction gives
\begin{equation}
 A(x)^n=\begin{pmatrix}
 U_n(x/2)&-U_{n-1}(x/2)\\
 U_{n-1}(x/2)&-U_{n-2}(x/2)
 \end{pmatrix},\quad n\geq1.
 \label{a-spectral-transfer-power}
\end{equation}
For $n=1$ this uses $U_{-1}=0$. Multiplication by $A(x)$ advances
the first column through the Chebyshev recurrence and places the
negative previous first column in the second. The trace is $R_n(x)$.
Sampling the fine recurrence every $p$ steps therefore uses the
unimodular transfer matrix $A(x)^p$. Cayley--Hamilton gives the coarse
recurrence $\chi_{j+1}-R_p(x)\chi_j+\chi_{j-1}=0$ for
$\chi_j=\psi_{pj}$. It explains the normalized spectral polynomial.
The path-inverse proof above additionally supplies the prefactor needed
for the resolvent.

The folded branches from Proposition~\ref{a-spectral-folded-bands},
in normalized coordinates, satisfy
\begin{equation}
 x_{p,q}(\theta)=2\cos\!\left(\frac{\theta+2\pi q}{p}\right),
 \qquad R_p(x_{p,q}(\theta))=2\cos\theta.
 \label{a-spectral-branch-relation}
\end{equation}
The second equality is just $T_p(\cos\alpha)=\cos(p\alpha)$.
For a coarse normalized energy in the open interval $(-2,2)$,
choose its angle in $(0,\pi)$. These formulas supply the $p$ distinct
real roots of $R_p(x)=2\cos\theta$. At the endpoints, some roots
coincide and algebraic multiplicities must be retained. Globally the
branches exchange labels when the angle crosses a cell boundary.
There is no single-valued inverse of $R_p$ on $[-2,2]$.

For the fine cycle, $x_k=2\cos(2\pi k/(pM))$ maps to
$2\cos(2\pi k/M)$. Each coarse Fourier label has exactly $p$ fine
preimages. If two labels already have the same numerical energy,
their multiplicities add as usual. Band folding retains the branch
label and its vector, whereas normalized decimation identifies all
of these labels at the same coarse energy. Their spectral relation
does not make elimination an invertible operator change of basis.

\section{Composition, transfer traces, and the free spectral measure}
\label{a-spectral-semigroup}

The spectral maps compose more simply than the energy-dependent
operators that produce them. Keeping the normalized polynomial map,
the rational Schur chart, and the transfer matrix distinct prevents an
exact free-chain identity from being used outside its model.

\subsection{Polynomial composition and iterated regular elimination}

\begin{theorem}[Chebyshev composition and Schur composition]
\label{a-spectral-semigroup-theorem}
For all positive integers $m,n$, the polynomial identities
\begin{align}
 R_n(R_m(x))&=R_{mn}(x)=R_m(R_n(x)),\nonumber\\
 U_{mn-1}(t)&=U_{n-1}(T_m(t))\,U_{m-1}(t)
 \label{a-spectral-polynomial-semigroup}
\end{align}
hold over $\C$. In a free cycle with $N=mnL$, $L\geq3$, successive
$m$- then $n$-site decimation at a fixed $z$ agrees with direct
$mn$-site decimation whenever its intermediate Schur inverses exist.
Its final coefficients are
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_{mn}(z)=\frac{\kappa}{U_{mn-1}(x/2)},\qquad
 \mu_{mn}(z)=z-\frac{\kappa R_{mn}(x)}{U_{mn-1}(x/2)}.
 \label{a-spectral-iterated-coefficients}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $x=2\cos\theta$, first-kind composition gives
$R_n(R_m(x))=2\cos(mn\theta)=R_{mn}(x)$.
It holds on an interval and is therefore an identity of polynomials,
including complex $x$. For $t=\cos\theta$ away from zeros of the sine
denominators,
\[
 U_{n-1}(T_m(t))U_{m-1}(t)
 =\frac{\sin(mn\theta)}{\sin(m\theta)}
       \frac{\sin(m\theta)}{\sin\theta}
 =U_{mn-1}(t).
\]
Polynomial equality extends it through those zeros and to all $t$.
After the first regular elimination, the normalized variable is
$x_m=(z-\mu_m)/\kappa_m=R_m(x)$. A second one gives
\[
 \kappa_{m,n}
 =\frac{\kappa_m}{U_{n-1}(x_m/2)}
 =\frac{\kappa}
   {U_{m-1}(x/2)U_{n-1}(T_m(x/2))}
 =\frac{\kappa}{U_{mn-1}(x/2)}.
\]
Similarly
$\mu_{m,n}=z-\kappa_{m,n}R_n(R_m(x))$, which gives
\eqref{a-spectral-iterated-coefficients}.
At each stage the matrices remain scalar nearest-neighbor circulants
with the displayed complex coefficients, so their algebraic Schur
formula continues to apply. These are rational identities on a common
regular chart. They need not be interpreted as self-adjoint matrices at
complex $z$.
\end{proof}

The product identity in \eqref{a-spectral-polynomial-semigroup} makes
the exceptional denominators explicit. A nonzero final denominator
implies both denominators along that two-stage chart are nonzero.
At a zero of the final denominator the polynomial trace composition
is still valid, but the divided Schur formulas require a new chart or
retained resonant modes. Iterating one prime $p$ through depth $h$,
where the cycle has the required divisibility, replaces $p$ by $p^h$
in \eqref{a-spectral-iterated-coefficients}. Different prime orders
give the same regular free-chain result. A nontranslation-invariant
onsite potential, an interacting Hamiltonian, or a field-dependent
constraint elimination needs its own closure analysis.

\subsection{What remains true for a general unimodular transfer matrix}

Let $M_0\in SL_2(\C)$ and $x=\operatorname{tr}M_0$. No
diagonalizability assumption is needed. Cayley--Hamilton gives
$M_0^2-xM_0+I=0$, hence
\begin{equation}
 M_0^n=U_{n-1}(x/2)M_0-U_{n-2}(x/2)I,\qquad n\geq1,
 \label{a-spectral-sl2-power}
\end{equation}
with $U_{-1}=0$. For $n=1$ it is the identity $M_0=M_0$, and for
$n=2$ it is Cayley--Hamilton. Multiplying by $M_0$ and replacing
$M_0^2$ by $xM_0-I$ proves the induction step. Taking traces yields
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{tr}(M_0^n)=R_n(\operatorname{tr}M_0).
 \label{a-spectral-sl2-trace}
\end{equation}
The coefficient identity is the same
$xU_{n-1}-2U_{n-2}=2T_n$ used above.

If $w_{k+1}=M_0w_k$, each residue subsequence satisfies
\[
 w_{nq+j}=M_0^j(M_0^n)^q w_0,\qquad 0\leq j<n.
\]
Thus ordinary matrix powering produces the normalized trace semigroup,
including matrices with repeated eigenvalues at trace $\pm2$.
The trace alone does not determine $M_0$, its eigenvectors, or a
local Hamiltonian realization. In the free chain, $M_0=A(x)$ has
the required nearest-neighbor realization. For a general transfer
problem only the matrix power and trace statements have been proved.

\subsection{The arcsine measure and the Koopman operator}

On $[-2,2]$ define the probability measure
\begin{equation}
 d\nu(x)=\frac{dx}{\pi\sqrt{4-x^2}}.
 \label{a-spectral-arcsine-measure}
\end{equation}
It is the distribution of $2\cos\theta$ for a uniform angle on the
circle, or on $[0,\pi]$. It is also the limiting normalized spectral
measure of the free cycles: for a continuous test function $f$,
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}f(2\cos(2\pi k/N))
 \longrightarrow\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(2\cos\theta)\,d\theta.
\]
This is the Riemann-sum limit of a continuous periodic function.

\Needspace{17\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}[Invariant free measure and exact mode routing]
\label{a-spectral-arcsine-invariance}
For every integer $p\geq2$, $(R_p)_*\nu=\nu$. The map
$\mathcal K_pf=f\circ R_p$ is an isometry on $L^2(\nu)$. With
\[
 \phi_0=1,\qquad \phi_n(x)=\sqrt2\,T_n(x/2),\quad n\geq1,
\]
its action and adjoint on an orthonormal basis are
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K_p\phi_n=\phi_{pn},\qquad
 \mathcal K_p^*\phi_m=
 \begin{cases}\phi_{m/p},&p\mid m,\\0,&p\nmid m.\end{cases}
 \label{a-spectral-koopman-routing}
\end{equation}
In the first case $m=0$ is included, so $\mathcal K_p^*\phi_0=\phi_0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a bounded measurable $f$, use the full circle parameterization:
\begin{align*}
 \int f(R_p(x))\,d\nu(x)
 &=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(2\cos(p\theta))\,d\theta\\
 &=\frac1{2\pi p}\int_0^{2\pi p}f(2\cos u)\,du
 =\int f(x)\,d\nu(x).
\end{align*}
The last equality uses periodicity. Applying this equality to $|f|^2$
proves the isometry, first on bounded functions and then by truncation
on all of $L^2(\nu)$. Pulling back to $[0,\pi]$ makes the $\phi_n$
the normalized cosine functions, and elementary cosine orthogonality
proves their orthonormality. Their span is dense: Chebyshev polynomials
span ordinary polynomials; those approximate continuous functions
uniformly, for example by Bernstein polynomials after rescaling to
$[0,1]$. The approximation follows from uniform continuity and the
binomial variance bound, by separating $|k/n-t|\leq\delta$ from its
complement and then letting $n\to\infty$, $\delta\to0$.
Continuous functions are dense for this finite measure, as one sees by
approximating interval steps in the angle coordinate by continuous
ramps. This supplies completeness.
Finally, Chebyshev composition gives $\mathcal K_p\phi_n=\phi_{pn}$.
For every $n,m\geq0$,
$\langle\phi_n,\mathcal K_p^*\phi_m\rangle
=\langle\phi_{pn},\phi_m\rangle=\delta_{pn,m}$.
Completeness yields the adjoint formula.
\end{proof}

$\mathcal K_p$ is an isometry with proper range, rather than a unitary:
for example $\phi_1$ is orthogonal to its range. Its adjoint discards
nondivisible modes. Invariance of $\nu$ is a statement about the
normalized free spectral distribution under $R_p$. It is not a proof
that a sequence of growing Hilbert spaces has converged to an interacting
Hamiltonian or that its quantum state converges. The direct-limit
operator construction has separate hypotheses in the final part.

The mean logarithmic expansion of this map is also exact:
\begin{equation}
 \int_{-2}^2\log|R_p'(x)|\,d\nu(x)=\log p.
 \label{a-spectral-log-expansion}
\end{equation}
Indeed for $x=2\cos\theta$,
$R_p'(x)=p\sin(p\theta)/\sin\theta$. Logarithms at its finitely
many zeros are integrable, since they have the local form
$\log|\theta-\theta_0|$ plus a bounded term. Hence the integral is
$\log p$ plus the difference of the integrals of
$\log|\sin(p\theta)|$ and $\log\sin\theta$ over $[0,\pi]$.
The substitution $u=p\theta$ and $\pi$-periodicity of
$\log|\sin u|$ make these two integrals equal. This calculation
does not assert the entropy of a different physical dynamics.
