\section{Constructing evolution and controlling truncation}
\label{sec:foundation-spectral-evolution}

A continuity theorem that assumes a differentiable solution does not construct one. For the real diagonal model, the construction is explicit and the precise differentiability domain can be proved. This supplies a complete small model in which the preceding distinctions can be inspected directly.

For real $(\lambda_n)$ define
\begin{equation}
 (U(t)c)_n=e^{-it\lambda_n}c_n,\qquad c\in\ell^2.
 \label{eq:foundation-spectral-flow}
\end{equation}
The modulus of every multiplier is one. Hence $U(t)$ is a unitary operator, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, and $U(-t)=U(t)^*$. For each fixed state it is strongly continuous. To prove the latter claim, split $c$ into a finite head and a small $\ell^2$ tail. The finite head is continuous coordinatewise, while the norm of the difference on the tail is at most twice its initial norm.

\begin{proposition}[The exact differentiability domain]
The orbit $t\mapsto U(t)c$ is differentiable in $\ell^2$ at one, equivalently every, time precisely when $c\in D(H_\lambda)$. On that domain,
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}U(t)c=-iH_\lambda U(t)c,
 \qquad H_\lambda U(t)c=U(t)H_\lambda c.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $c\in D(H_\lambda)$, each coordinate difference quotient tends to $-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n$. The elementary bound $|e^{-iu}-1|\leq|u|$ bounds the quotient magnitude by $|\lambda_nc_n|$. The squared difference from its limit is bounded by $4\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2$, a summable sequence. Dominated convergence therefore gives convergence in $\ell^2$.

Conversely, if an $\ell^2$ derivative $d$ exists, bounded coordinate evaluation gives
\[
 d_n=-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n.
\]
Since $d\in\ell^2$, one has $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Commutation and domain preservation follow from the same coordinate formula.
\end{proof}

The constructed orbit is the unique global domain-valued solution with a given domain initial state. If two supplied solutions have the same initial value, their difference $w$ satisfies $\dot w=-iH_\lambda w$. Symmetry gives
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\norm w^2
 =2\operatorname{Re}\inner{w}{-iH_\lambda w}=0.
\]
The initial zero norm remains zero. This uniqueness proof extends to supplied solutions of a symmetric operator, but the proof of existence above uses the explicit real diagonal construction.

For domain states, the orbit also satisfies the quantitative bound
\[
 \norm{U(t)c-U(s)c}\leq|t-s|\norm{H_\lambda c}.
\]
The constant belongs to the state. It is not an operator-norm bound for the unbounded generator. Spectral coordinate populations remain constant and their interpacket currents vanish. A different domain-preserving atlas can mix spectral coordinates and carry nonzero currents under the same evolution.

\foundationfigure[H]{11_graph_tails}{For the normalized state proportional to $n^{-2}$ and $He_n=ne_n$, the state tail and generator tail decay at different rates. Graph control retains both contributions.}

\subsection{Uniformity in time for a fixed state}

Coordinate cutoffs commute with $U(t)$. Thus for every $c\in\ell^2$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{U(t)c-S_NU(t)c}=\norm{c-S_Nc}.
 \label{eq:foundation-time-tail}
\end{equation}
The right side tends to zero independently of $t\in\R$. This gives uniform convergence over all times for each fixed initial state. For $c\in D(H_\lambda)$, differentiating the finite cutoff orbit and the full orbit gives a second exact identity:
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\frac{d}{dt}U(t)c-
       \frac{d}{dt}S_NU(t)c}
 =\norm{H_\lambda c-S_NH_\lambda c}.
 \label{eq:foundation-velocity-tail}
\end{equation}
This tail also tends to zero uniformly in time. State convergence alone does not imply this velocity convergence.

\begin{example}[Strong convergence with no differentiable limiting orbit]
For $\lambda_n=n$, take $c_n=C/n$ with $C=(\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-2})^{-1/2}$. This is a normalized $\ell^2$ state outside $D(H_\lambda)$. Every finite cutoff orbit is differentiable, and \eqref{eq:foundation-time-tail} gives uniform convergence to the full orbit. Yet the full orbit is nowhere differentiable in $\ell^2$, by the preceding proposition. In fact the norm of the cutoff velocity is $C\sqrt N$, which diverges.
\end{example}

For the faster normalized tail $c_n=C/n^2$, both errors are controlled:
\[
 \norm{c-S_Nc}^2=C^2\sum_{n>N}n^{-4},\qquad
 \norm{H_\lambda c-S_NH_\lambda c}^2=C^2\sum_{n>N}n^{-2}.
\]
The state tail is $O(N^{-3/2})$ in norm, while the velocity tail is $O(N^{-1/2})$. A small state error can therefore coexist with a much larger derivative error even inside the true domain.

\section{Which topology does reconstruction use?}
\label{sec:foundation-reconstruction-topologies}

Let $S_N$ be orthogonal projections tending strongly to $I$. Their ranks need not be finite. For a bounded operator $X$, the reconstructed corner sum is $S_NXS_N$. Its natural convergence can be stronger when $X$ belongs to a smaller operator class.

\begin{theorem}[Three reconstruction statements]
Under these hypotheses:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $X$ is bounded, $S_NXS_N\to X$ strongly.
\item If $X$ is compact, $\norm{S_NXS_N-X}\to0$ in operator norm.
\item If $X$ is Hilbert--Schmidt, $\norm{S_NXS_N-X}_2\to0$ in Hilbert--Schmidt norm.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the identity
\[
 S_NXS_N-X=S_NX(S_N-I)+(S_N-I)X.
\]
Since $\norm{S_N}\leq1$, application to a fixed $x$ bounds the error by
\[
 \norm X\norm{(S_N-I)x}+\norm{(S_N-I)Xx},
\]
which tends to zero.

For compact $X$, choose finite-rank $Y$ with $\norm{X-Y}<\varepsilon$. Strong convergence is uniform on each fixed finite-dimensional subspace, and self-adjointness of $S_N$ controls the right error by the corresponding left error for $Y^*$. Thus $\norm{S_NYS_N-Y}\to0$. The difference between the two reconstruction errors is at most $2\varepsilon$, proving the claim.

For the last assertion, fix an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ and define
\[
 \norm X_2^2=\sum_j\norm{Xe_j}^2<\infty.
\]
Each column $(S_N-I)Xe_j$ tends to zero, and its squared norm is bounded by $4\norm{Xe_j}^2$. Dominated convergence gives $\norm{(S_N-I)X}_2\to0$. The right error follows by taking adjoints, using $S_N^*=S_N$ and $\norm{X^*}_2=\norm X_2$. The ideal inequality $\norm{AY}_2\leq\norm A\norm Y_2$ and the displayed decomposition finish the proof.
\end{proof}

The Hilbert--Schmidt norm is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, and it bounds the operator norm. It measures the total square size of all matrix columns. In a coordinate packet basis, it also measures the square sum of all matrix entries. Retaining a larger square of entries removes a correspondingly smaller summable tail. Operator norm instead measures the largest action on a unit vector, allowing the testing vector to depend on the cutoff.

\begin{example}[The identity never has a small omitted tail in operator norm]
On an infinite-dimensional coordinate space, let $S_N$ retain the first $N$ coordinates. For $X=I$,
\[
 \norm{S_NIS_N-I}=\norm{S_N-I}=1.
\]
A unit vector $e_{N+1}$ witnesses the lower bound. Nevertheless, $S_Nx\to x$ for every fixed $x\in\ell^2$. This is the difference between pointwise control over states and uniform control over the full unit ball.
\end{example}

\subsection{Zero padding and the correct asymptotic tail}

For a diagonal bounded multiplier $f(H_\lambda)$, zero padding gives the exact formula
\[
 \norm{f(H_\lambda)-S_Nf(H_\lambda)S_N}
 =\sup_{n>N}|f(\lambda_n)|.
\]
For the unitary multiplier $f(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}$, this norm is one at every finite cutoff. Equation \eqref{eq:foundation-time-tail} remains valid. Uniformity in time for a fixed state and failure of operator-norm convergence are therefore compatible.

For $\lambda_n=n$, a resolvent at $i\eta$, $\eta\ne0$, has zero-padded error
\[
 \sup_{n>N}\frac1{\sqrt{n^2+\eta^2}}
 =\frac1{\sqrt{(N+1)^2+\eta^2}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The heat multiplier $e^{-tn}$ has error $e^{-t(N+1)}$ for fixed $t>0$. These tails decay because the operators are compact. At $t=0$ the heat operator is the identity, so the same norm-convergence assertion is false.

Two other bounded multipliers approach one along this positive spectrum:
\[
 b(n)=\frac{n}{\sqrt{1+n^2}},\qquad
 q(n)=\frac{n-i}{n+i}.
\]
Their correct anchored cutoff is
\[
 A_N(f)=S_Nf(H_\lambda)S_N+(I-S_N).
\]
The errors are then
\[
 \norm{b(H_\lambda)-A_N(b)}
 =\sup_{n>N}\left|\frac{n}{\sqrt{1+n^2}}-1\right|\longrightarrow0,
\]
and
\[
 \norm{q(H_\lambda)-A_N(q)}
 =\sup_{n>N}\frac2{\sqrt{n^2+1}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The identity tail is an analytic choice justified by these asymptotic multipliers. It is not a universal prescription for every two-sided or non-diagonal spectrum.

On a graph-compatible atlas, an unbounded generator has another reconstruction statement:
\[
 S_NHS_N\psi-H\psi
 =S_N(HS_N\psi-H\psi)+(S_N-I)H\psi\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad\psi\in D(H).
\]
This is convergence of the displayed output vectors in the ambient Hilbert norm. It neither takes an operator norm of $H$ nor asserts graph-norm convergence of those output vectors, which would require additional domain and second-action information.

\foundationfigure[H]{09_cutoff_topology}{Zero-padded unitary cutoffs converge on a fixed state but retain operator-norm error one. For the same spectrum $n\geq1$, the resolvent multiplier has a tail that decays in operator norm.}

\subsection{A bounded certificate for a nonreducing packet}

A packet need not commute with an unbounded Hamiltonian. Suppose now that $H$ is self-adjoint, $P$ is a bounded orthogonal projection preserving $D(H)$, and $[H,P]$ on $D(H)$ extends to a bounded operator $B$. For nonreal $z$, let $R_z=(H-z)^{-1}$. It maps $\HH$ into $D(H)$, so all products used below have their stated meaning. Multiplying the commutator identity on the domain by the resolvents gives
\[
 [R_z,P]=-R_zBR_z.
\]
Indeed, for $x\in\HH$, apply $H-z$ to $PR_zx$ to obtain $Px+BR_zx$, then apply $R_z$. Hence
\[
 \norm{[R_z,P]}\leq\norm{R_z}^2\norm B,
 \qquad
 \norm{[R_{i\eta},P]}\leq\frac{\norm B}{\eta^2}
 \quad(\eta\ne0).
\]
The estimate converts a domain-sensitive commutator into a bounded one. In the generic formal certificate, the inverse and its domain properties are supplied explicitly. The diagonal modules also construct concrete inverses. Neither statement licenses a formal inverse for an unspecified operator.

\section{The finite differential obstruction and matrix corners}
\label{sec:foundation-corner-derivations}

Finite arrays support many useful difference operators. What they cannot support is a nonzero linear derivation of the full pointwise algebra $\C^N$ with its ordinary product. This obstruction explains why a finite operator calculus must declare which algebra carries its differentiation rule.

\begin{theorem}[No nonzero derivation of the finite pointwise algebra]
Let $D:\C^N\to\C^N$ be complex linear and satisfy
\[
 D(fg)=D(f)g+fD(g)
\]
for every pair of vectors, where multiplication is coordinatewise. Then $D=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the coordinate idempotent $e_a$, the identity $e_a^2=e_a$ gives $D(e_a)=2e_aD(e_a)$. At a coordinate $b\ne a$, the right side is zero. At $b=a$, the equality reads $(D(e_a))_a=2(D(e_a))_a$, again forcing zero. Thus $D(e_a)=0$ for every basis vector, and linearity gives $D=0$.
\end{proof}

The theorem concerns the semisimple pointwise algebra $\C^N$. It does not assert that every finite-dimensional commutative complex algebra has only the zero derivation. For example, on $\C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, the map $D(a+b\varepsilon)=b\varepsilon$ is a nonzero derivation. The nilpotent element changes the algebraic hypothesis.

\begin{example}[The precise defect of a forward difference]
On a cyclic grid, let $D_hf_j=(f_{j+1}-f_j)/h$, with $h\ne0$. Expanding the product gives
\[
 D_h(fg)_j-(D_hf)_jg_j-f_j(D_hg)_j
 =h(D_hf)_j(D_hg)_j.
\]
Thus the ordinary Leibniz identity fails unless the displayed product vanishes. A small defect on sufficiently regular sampled functions is compatible with the no-go theorem, because that theorem concerns an exact identity for every vector at fixed finite resolution.
\end{example}

\subsection{Exact differentiation in the full matrix algebra}

Move now to $M_N(\C)$. To avoid confusing a Hermitian observable with the skew-adjoint state generator $K$, denote a Hermitian matrix by $B=B^*$ and define
\[
 \delta_BX=i[B,X]=i(BX-XB).
\]
Then direct multiplication proves
\begin{align}
 \delta_B(XY)&=(\delta_BX)Y+X\delta_BY,\label{eq:foundation-matrix-leibniz}\\
 (\delta_BX)^*&=\delta_B(X^*),\label{eq:foundation-matrix-star}\\
 \operatorname{Tr}((\delta_BX)Y)&=-\operatorname{Tr}(X\delta_BY).
 \label{eq:foundation-matrix-ibp}
\end{align}
For the first identity, the middle terms $-iXBY$ and $iXBY$ cancel. For the second, taking the adjoint reverses the product order and conjugates $i$, with $B^*=B$ restoring the stated sign. For the third, cyclicity moves the leading $B$ in $\operatorname{Tr}(BXY)$ to the end. The trace pairing is bilinear here. Combining \eqref{eq:foundation-matrix-star} and \eqref{eq:foundation-matrix-ibp} also gives the Hilbert--Schmidt identity
\[
 \inner{\delta_BX}{Y}_{\rm HS}=-\inner{X}{\delta_BY}_{\rm HS},
 \qquad\inner{X}{Y}_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(X^*Y).
\]

These identities preserve multiplication order. They do not turn $\delta_B$ into a derivation from diagonal matrices to diagonal matrices. Usually it leaves that commutative subalgebra.

\begin{example}[A nonzero derivative leaves the pointwise subalgebra]
For
\[
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 X=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
one obtains
\[
 \delta_BX=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}\ne0.
\]
The output is off diagonal. This is exactly how the matrix algebra permits a nonzero derivation without violating the pointwise theorem.
\end{example}

For Hermitian generators $B_i,B_j$, put $\mathcal F_{ij}=i[B_i,B_j]$. This curvature matrix is Hermitian, and the Jacobi identity gives
\begin{equation}
 [\delta_{B_i},\delta_{B_j}]X
 =-[[B_i,B_j],X]
 =i[\mathcal F_{ij},X]=\delta_{\mathcal F_{ij}}X.
 \label{eq:foundation-corner-curvature}
\end{equation}
Commuting generators produce commuting derivations. A nonzero curvature matrix need not act nontrivially on every observable: its action on a particular $X$ vanishes precisely when that $X$ commutes with it. This matrix identity provides an algebraic curvature mechanism. A physical geometric interpretation requires the additional structures developed in the gauge and gravity papers.

\foundationfigure[H]{12_matrix_derivations}{A finite pointwise difference has a Leibniz defect. Commutation inside a full matrix algebra obeys the Leibniz rule exactly, with its output allowed to leave the diagonal subalgebra.}

\subsection{Differentiated corner paths and coarse reconstruction}

Let $(P_a)$ be a finite sharp atlas. Writing $X_{ba}=P_bXP_a$ and $B_{ba}=P_bBP_a$, insertion of $I=\sum_cP_c$ gives
\begin{equation}
 P_b\delta_B(X)P_a
 =i\sum_c\left(B_{bc}X_{ca}-X_{bc}B_{ca}\right).
 \label{eq:foundation-corner-path}
\end{equation}
Each term has a genuine intermediate packet $c$. One ordering applies $X$ then $B$, while the other applies $B$ then $X$. Replacing a matrix product by an entrywise product would destroy this path composition and the cancellation behind the Leibniz rule.

Summing the differentiated corners reconstructs $\delta_BX$. For a coarse partition with $Q_\alpha=\sum_{a\in C_\alpha}P_a$,
\[
 Q_\beta\delta_B(X)Q_\alpha
 =\sum_{\substack{b\in C_\beta\\a\in C_\alpha}}P_b\delta_B(X)P_a.
\]
This is exact aggregation of the already differentiated operator. It does not claim that discarding all internal matrix structure produces a new pointwise algebra with a nonzero exact derivation. The retained corners are the structure that makes the finite differential calculus work.

\section{Positive effects and sharp dilation}
\label{sec:foundation-effects}

A sharp packet atlas assigns mutually orthogonal subspaces to its labels. Many useful descriptions overlap. A detector may respond partly to several channels, and a frame may analyze the same component more than once. The correct replacement is a positive partition of the identity. Its weights are expectation values, and its channel vectors live in a larger space where orthogonality can be restored.

Throughout this chapter, inner products are conjugate linear in the first variable. A bounded state generator is denoted by $K$, with $K^*=-K$. When a Hamiltonian is present, $K=-iH$. The receiving label is written first in $J_{ba}$.

\begin{definition}[Finite effect atlas]
Let $\HH$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a finite label set. An effect atlas is a family of bounded operators satisfying
\[
 F_a=F_a^*\geq0,\qquad \sum_{a\in A}F_a=I.
\]
Its weight in a state $\psi$ is $p_a=\inner{\psi}{F_a\psi}$. The partition identity implies $0\leq F_a\leq I$, so $p_a\geq0$ and $\sum_a p_a=\norm\psi^2$.
\end{definition}

For a sharp atlas, $F_a=P_a$ and $p_a=\norm{P_a\psi}^2$. In general, $p_a$ is not $\norm{F_a\psi}^2$. The latter quantity is $\inner{\psi}{F_a^2\psi}$ and therefore loses precisely the positive defect $F_a-F_a^2$.

\begin{example}[Overlapping two-channel weights]
On $\C^2$, take
\[
 F_+=\begin{pmatrix}4/5&0\\0&1/5\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 F_-=\begin{pmatrix}1/5&0\\0&4/5\end{pmatrix},\qquad \psi=\binom10.
\]
The true weights are $4/5$ and $1/5$. Squared effect-vector norms would instead give $16/25$ and $1/25$, whose sum is $17/25$. The state still satisfies $F_+\psi+F_-\psi=\psi$, but its two summands are not orthogonal. Reconstruction and an orthogonal decomposition are different assertions.
\end{example}

\subsection{Continuity without orthogonality}

Suppose that a differentiable state curve satisfies $\dot\psi=K\psi$. Define
\begin{equation}
 J^{F}_{ba}=\operatorname{Re}\inner{F_b\psi}{KF_a\psi}
             -\operatorname{Re}\inner{F_a\psi}{KF_b\psi}.
 \label{eq:foundation-effect-current}
\end{equation}
This current is antisymmetric directly from its definition. Skew-adjointness also gives
\[
 J^F_{ba}=2\operatorname{Re}\inner{F_b\psi}{KF_a\psi}.
\]
The same bilinear expression occurs for sharp packets, but its interpretation now concerns expectation weights.

\begin{proposition}[Effect continuity]
Under these hypotheses,
\[
 \dot p_b=\sum_a J^F_{ba},\qquad \sum_b\dot p_b=0.
\]
If $F_b=F_b(t)$ is differentiable in operator norm, the first identity becomes
\[
 \dot p_b=s_b+\sum_a J^F_{ba},\qquad
 s_b=\inner{\psi}{\dot F_b\psi},\qquad \sum_b s_b=0.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Self-adjointness of $F_b$ and differentiation give
\[
 \dot p_b=2\operatorname{Re}\inner{F_b\psi}{K\psi}
\]
for a fixed effect. Summing the two terms of \eqref{eq:foundation-effect-current} over $a$ and using $\sum_aF_a=I$ gives
\[
 \sum_aJ^F_{ba}=\operatorname{Re}\inner{F_b\psi}{K\psi}
       -\operatorname{Re}\inner{\psi}{KF_b\psi}.
\]
The second real part is the negative of the first. The moving case adds the product-rule term $s_b$. Its total is zero because $\sum_b\dot F_b=0$. Antisymmetry cancels the finite double sum of currents.
\end{proof}

If a map $r:A\to B$ groups the labels, the coarse effect is $G_\beta=\sum_{r(a)=\beta}F_a$. Bilinearity proves
\[
 p^{\rm c}_\beta=\sum_{r(a)=\beta}p_a,\qquad
 J^{\rm c}_{\beta\alpha}
 =\sum_{\substack{r(b)=\beta\\r(a)=\alpha}}J^F_{ba}.
\]
No orthogonality is needed for this finite aggregation law. A divergence-free antisymmetric array may also be added to $J^F$ without changing its row sums. Thus the balance law determines the change in weight, while the generator-induced formula selects a particular representative of the current.

\subsection{Analysis, synthesis, and the range projection}

Choose Hilbert spaces $\KK_a$ and bounded maps $V_a:\HH\to\KK_a$ such that
\[
 \sum_aV_a^*V_a=I.
\]
The combined analysis map $V:\HH\to\KK=\bigoplus_a\KK_a$ is $V\psi=(V_a\psi)_a$. Its adjoint is synthesis, $V^*(y_a)_a=\sum_aV_a^*y_a$. Consequently
\[
 V^*V=I,\qquad R=VV^*,\qquad R^*=R^2=R.
\]
Here $R$ projects onto the closed range of the isometry $V$. The range need not fill $\KK$. If $\Pi_a$ is the coordinate projector, the compressed effect is
\[
 F_a=V^*\Pi_aV=V_a^*V_a,\qquad
 p_a=\norm{V_a\psi}^2=\norm{\Pi_aV\psi}^2.
\]
Every finite effect atlas admits this construction by taking $\KK_a=\HH$ and $V_a=F_a^{1/2}$. Positivity supplies the bounded positive square root. No choice of a measurement outcome or post-measurement state is being made by this algebraic dilation.

For $X\in\mathcal B(\HH)$, its channel block is $X_{ba}^{V}=V_bXV_a^*$. Inserting the partition on both sides proves
\begin{equation}
 X=\sum_{a,b}V_b^*X_{ba}^{V}V_a.
 \label{eq:foundation-channel-reconstruction}
\end{equation}
The lifted operator $\widetilde X=VXV^*$ is multiplicative on lifted operators, since $V^*V=I$. Its identity is $R$, not $I_{\KK}$. Conversely, compressing arbitrary ambient operators need not preserve multiplication:
\begin{equation}
 V^*ABV-(V^*AV)(V^*BV)=V^*A(I-R)BV.
 \label{eq:foundation-compression-defect}
\end{equation}
This is the exact missing-range term. Setting $A=B=\Pi_a$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \inner{\psi}{(F_a-F_a^2)\psi}
 =\norm{(I-R)\Pi_aV\psi}^2.
 \label{eq:foundation-unsharpness}
\end{equation}
Thus the failure of an effect to be sharp measures how much its coordinate projection leaves the embedded physical range. This identity also proves $F_a-F_a^2\geq0$ directly.

The dynamics respects the same construction. Put $\widetilde K=VKV^*$. It is skew-adjoint, and $\frac{d}{dt}V\psi=\widetilde K V\psi$. Moving adjoints across the inner product shows
\[
 2\operatorname{Re}\inner{\Pi_bV\psi}{\widetilde K\Pi_aV\psi}
 =2\operatorname{Re}\inner{F_b\psi}{KF_a\psi}=J^F_{ba}.
\]
The positive-effect current is therefore exactly the sharp current of this lifted flow evaluated on the embedded state. It is not obtained by treating arbitrary compression as an algebra homomorphism.

\section{Countable packets and the domain of a generator}
\label{sec:foundation-domains}

An infinite resolution introduces two separate limits. Packet vectors must reconstruct the state, and applying an unbounded operator to the partial reconstruction requires additional control. Writing an infinite sum of matrix blocks conceals this distinction unless the domain is stated first.

Let $(P_a)_{a\in A}$ be a countable orthogonal family of bounded projections with strong sum $I$. For finite $F\subset A$, write $S_F=\sum_{a\in F}P_a$. Strong completeness means $S_Fx\to x$ for each fixed $x\in\HH$, over the directed set of finite subsets. Orthogonality gives
\[
 \norm{S_Fx}^2=\sum_{a\in F}\norm{P_ax}^2,\qquad
 \sum_a\norm{P_ax}^2=\norm x^2.
\]
These are Hilbert-space statements. They contain no unbounded operator.

Now let $H:D(H)\subset\HH\to\HH$ be a densely defined symmetric operator. To write $HP_a\psi$ for every domain state, require
\begin{equation}
 P_aD(H)\subset D(H).
 \label{eq:foundation-domain-preserve}
\end{equation}
Define $\norm x_H^2=\norm x^2+\norm{Hx}^2$. A domain-compatible atlas is graph compatible when
\begin{equation}
 S_Fx\longrightarrow x\quad\text{in the graph norm for every }x\in D(H).
 \label{eq:foundation-graph-compatible}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, both $S_Fx\to x$ and $HS_Fx\to Hx$ hold in $\HH$. The second convergence does not follow from the first for an unbounded $H$.

\begin{example}[A small state can have a large generator image]
On $\ell^2(\N_{\geq1})$, let $He_n=ne_n$ on its maximal domain. The finitely supported vectors $x_N=e_N/N$ satisfy $\norm{x_N}=1/N\to0$, while $\norm{Hx_N}=1$. This gives a direct reason to track the generator tail in addition to the state tail. It does not contradict closedness, because $Hx_N=e_N$ has no norm limit.
\end{example}

\subsection{A maximal diagonal domain}

Let $(\lambda_n)$ be any real sequence and define
\[
 D(H_\lambda)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:
       \sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad
 (H_\lambda c)_n=\lambda_nc_n.
\]
The operator is dense because it contains every finitely supported sequence. It is symmetric by the reality of the multipliers. Its domain is maximal for this coordinate action.

\begin{proposition}[Self-adjointness of the diagonal realization]
The operator $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint. Its coordinate cutoffs converge in graph norm on $D(H_\lambda)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $y\in D(H_\lambda^*)$ and $H_\lambda^*y=z$, testing the adjoint identity against $e_n$ gives $z_n=\lambda_ny_n$. Since $z\in\ell^2$, the sequence $y$ belongs to $D(H_\lambda)$. Symmetry gives the opposite inclusion of domains, and the actions agree there. For $S_Nc=\sum_{n\leq N}c_ne_n$,
\[
 \norm{c-S_Nc}_{H_\lambda}^2
 =\sum_{n>N}(1+\lambda_n^2)|c_n|^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
\end{proof}

For positive $\lambda_n$, the quadratic-form domain instead uses $\sum_n\lambda_n|c_n|^2<\infty$. This is the domain of $H_\lambda^{1/2}$, not generally the domain of $H_\lambda$. With $\lambda_n=n$ and $c_n=n^{-s}$, the three thresholds are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c}
 \text{membership}&\text{condition}\\ \hline
 \ell^2&s>1/2\\
 D(H_\lambda^{1/2})&s>1\\
 D(H_\lambda)&s>3/2.
 \end{array}
\]
Each equality case diverges harmonically. Thus a state with finite mean positive energy can still lack the Hilbert-space derivative required by the Schr\"odinger equation. The harmonic oscillator example in Volume I has $\lambda_n=n+1/2$ for $n\geq0$ and the same asymptotic thresholds after replacing $n$ by $n+1$ in the coefficients.

\foundationfigure[H]{10_weighted_domains}{For $He_n=ne_n$, $n\geq1$, coefficients $a_n=n^{-s}$ encounter three different thresholds: state norm, quadratic-form domain, and operator domain. The finite partial-sum curves illustrate the analytic $p$-series criteria.}

\subsection{Countable continuity and the stronger scalar-row argument}

Suppose a supplied curve $\psi(t)\in D(H)$ is differentiable as a curve in $\HH$ and satisfies $\dot\psi=-iH\psi$. For a domain-preserving atlas, put
\[
 p_b=\norm{P_b\psi}^2,\qquad
 J_{ba}=2\operatorname{Im}\inner{P_b\psi}{HP_a\psi}.
\]
Symmetry gives $J_{ba}=-J_{ab}$. Differentiating the bounded projected norm gives
\[
 \dot p_b=2\operatorname{Im}\inner{P_b\psi}{H\psi}.
\]
Graph compatibility permits direct insertion of $HS_F\psi\to H\psi$. The formal development also proves a stronger statement for one receiving packet: symmetry moves $H$ onto that packet, so only the strong state sum is needed. Indeed,
\[
 \inner{P_b\psi}{HP_a\psi}=\inner{HP_b\psi}{P_a\psi},
\]
and the sum over $a$ converges to $\inner{HP_b\psi}{\psi}=\inner{P_b\psi}{H\psi}$. In fact the row is absolutely summable, since
\begin{align*}
 \sum_a\left|\inner{HP_b\psi}{P_a\psi}\right|
 &=\sum_a\left|\inner{P_aHP_b\psi}{P_a\psi}\right|\\
 &\leq\left(\sum_a\norm{P_aHP_b\psi}^2\right)^{1/2}
       \left(\sum_a\norm{P_a\psi}^2\right)^{1/2}
 =\norm{HP_b\psi}\norm\psi.
\end{align*}
Consequently $\dot p_b=\sum_aJ_{ba}$ without assuming graph compatibility. The two tail estimates describe the distinct arguments:
\begin{align}
 \left|\sum_{a\in F}J_{ba}-\dot p_b\right|
 &\leq2\norm{P_b\psi}\norm{HS_F\psi-H\psi},\label{eq:foundation-graph-row}\\
 \left|\sum_{a\in F}J_{ba}-\dot p_b\right|
 &\leq2\norm{HP_b\psi}\norm{S_F\psi-\psi}.\label{eq:foundation-strong-row}
\end{align}
The first bound uses graph-action control. The second uses symmetry and a fixed receiving packet. Neither states that the entire double array $(J_{ba})$ is absolutely summable.

\subsection{Infinite coarse cells}

For a partition $A=\bigsqcup_{\alpha}C_\alpha$, the strong sum $Q_\alpha=\sum_{a\in C_\alpha}P_a$ is a bounded orthogonal projection. Its weight is always
\[
 \norm{Q_\alpha\psi}^2=\sum_{a\in C_\alpha}\norm{P_a\psi}^2.
\]
To define a coarse current with $HQ_\alpha\psi$, additionally require $Q_\alpha D(H)\subset D(H)$. Fine domain preservation alone does not state this infinite-cell property.

Under this coarse-domain hypothesis, symmetry and the strong cell sums justify both iterated sums separately:
\begin{align*}
 J^{\rm c}_{\beta\alpha}
 &=2\operatorname{Im}\inner{Q_\beta\psi}{HQ_\alpha\psi}\\
 &=\sum_{b\in C_\beta}\left(\sum_{a\in C_\alpha}J_{ba}\right)
 =\sum_{a\in C_\alpha}\left(\sum_{b\in C_\beta}J_{ba}\right).
\end{align*}
For example, first summing $a$ moves $H$ onto $P_b\psi$, then the outer sum pairs $\sum_bP_b\psi$ with the fixed vector $HQ_\alpha\psi$. The reverse order has its own symmetric argument. Flattening these expressions to a single unordered sum on $C_\beta\times C_\alpha$ requires joint summability. Equality of two justified iterated sums does not supply that hypothesis.

For a simple warning, the antisymmetric scalar array with $a_{2n,2n+1}=1/n$, $a_{2n+1,2n}=-1/n$ for $n\geq1$, and all other entries zero has finite support in each row but infinite total absolute sum. This array is only a summation example, not an asserted physical realization of the current. It shows why rowwise convergence alone cannot authorize arbitrary rearrangement.

The coarse balance is obtained by differentiating $\norm{Q_\beta\psi(t)}^2$, using the bounded coarse projector. There is no need to interchange an infinite sum of derivatives. Likewise, the total packet norm is identified with $\norm{\psi(t)}^2$ by Parseval before its conservation is established. The order of these arguments keeps the domain and summation obligations visible.



\section{Constructing evolution and controlling truncation}
\label{sec:foundation-spectral-evolution}

A continuity theorem that assumes a differentiable solution does not construct one. For the real diagonal model, the construction is explicit and the precise differentiability domain can be proved. This supplies a complete small model in which the preceding distinctions can be inspected directly.

For real $(\lambda_n)$ define
\begin{equation}
 (U(t)c)_n=e^{-it\lambda_n}c_n,\qquad c\in\ell^2.
 \label{eq:foundation-spectral-flow}
\end{equation}
The modulus of every multiplier is one. Hence $U(t)$ is a unitary operator, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, and $U(-t)=U(t)^*$. For each fixed state it is strongly continuous. To prove the latter claim, split $c$ into a finite head and a small $\ell^2$ tail. The finite head is continuous coordinatewise, while the norm of the difference on the tail is at most twice its initial norm.

\begin{proposition}[The exact differentiability domain]
The orbit $t\mapsto U(t)c$ is differentiable in $\ell^2$ at one, equivalently every, time precisely when $c\in D(H_\lambda)$. On that domain,
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}U(t)c=-iH_\lambda U(t)c,
 \qquad H_\lambda U(t)c=U(t)H_\lambda c.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $c\in D(H_\lambda)$, each coordinate difference quotient tends to $-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n$. The elementary bound $|e^{-iu}-1|\leq|u|$ bounds the quotient magnitude by $|\lambda_nc_n|$. The squared difference from its limit is bounded by $4\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2$, a summable sequence. Dominated convergence therefore gives convergence in $\ell^2$.

Conversely, if an $\ell^2$ derivative $d$ exists, bounded coordinate evaluation gives
\[
 d_n=-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n.
\]
Since $d\in\ell^2$, one has $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Commutation and domain preservation follow from the same coordinate formula.
\end{proof}

The constructed orbit is the unique global domain-valued solution with a given domain initial state. If two supplied solutions have the same initial value, their difference $w$ satisfies $\dot w=-iH_\lambda w$. Symmetry gives
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\norm w^2
 =2\operatorname{Re}\inner{w}{-iH_\lambda w}=0.
\]
The initial zero norm remains zero. This uniqueness proof extends to supplied solutions of a symmetric operator, but the proof of existence above uses the explicit real diagonal construction.

For domain states, the orbit also satisfies the quantitative bound
\[
 \norm{U(t)c-U(s)c}\leq|t-s|\norm{H_\lambda c}.
\]
The constant belongs to the state. It is not an operator-norm bound for the unbounded generator. Spectral coordinate populations remain constant and their interpacket currents vanish. A different domain-preserving atlas can mix spectral coordinates and carry nonzero currents under the same evolution.

\subsection{Uniformity in time for a fixed state}

Coordinate cutoffs commute with $U(t)$. Thus for every $c\in\ell^2$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{U(t)c-S_NU(t)c}=\norm{c-S_Nc}.
 \label{eq:foundation-time-tail}
\end{equation}
The right side tends to zero independently of $t\in\R$. This gives uniform convergence over all times for each fixed initial state. For $c\in D(H_\lambda)$, differentiating the finite cutoff orbit and the full orbit gives a second exact identity:
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\frac{d}{dt}U(t)c-
       \frac{d}{dt}S_NU(t)c}
 =\norm{H_\lambda c-S_NH_\lambda c}.
 \label{eq:foundation-velocity-tail}
\end{equation}
This tail also tends to zero uniformly in time. State convergence alone does not imply this velocity convergence.

\begin{example}[Strong convergence with no differentiable limiting orbit]
For $\lambda_n=n$, take $c_n=C/n$ with $C=(\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-2})^{-1/2}$. This is a normalized $\ell^2$ state outside $D(H_\lambda)$. Every finite cutoff orbit is differentiable, and \eqref{eq:foundation-time-tail} gives uniform convergence to the full orbit. Yet the full orbit is nowhere differentiable in $\ell^2$, by the preceding proposition. In fact the norm of the cutoff velocity is $C\sqrt N$, which diverges.
\end{example}

For the faster normalized tail $c_n=C/n^2$, both errors are controlled:
\[
 \norm{c-S_Nc}^2=C^2\sum_{n>N}n^{-4},\qquad
 \norm{H_\lambda c-S_NH_\lambda c}^2=C^2\sum_{n>N}n^{-2}.
\]
The state tail is $O(N^{-3/2})$ in norm, while the velocity tail is $O(N^{-1/2})$. A small state error can therefore coexist with a much larger derivative error even inside the true domain.



\section{Which topology does reconstruction use?}
\label{sec:foundation-reconstruction-topologies}

Let $S_N$ be orthogonal projections tending strongly to $I$. Their ranks need not be finite. For a bounded operator $X$, the reconstructed corner sum is $S_NXS_N$. Its natural convergence can be stronger when $X$ belongs to a smaller operator class.

\begin{theorem}[Three reconstruction statements]
Under these hypotheses:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $X$ is bounded, $S_NXS_N\to X$ strongly.
\item If $X$ is compact, $\norm{S_NXS_N-X}\to0$ in operator norm.
\item If $X$ is Hilbert--Schmidt, $\norm{S_NXS_N-X}_2\to0$ in Hilbert--Schmidt norm.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the identity
\[
 S_NXS_N-X=S_NX(S_N-I)+(S_N-I)X.
\]
Since $\norm{S_N}\leq1$, application to a fixed $x$ bounds the error by
\[
 \norm X\norm{(S_N-I)x}+\norm{(S_N-I)Xx},
\]
which tends to zero.

For compact $X$, choose finite-rank $Y$ with $\norm{X-Y}<\varepsilon$. Strong convergence is uniform on each fixed finite-dimensional subspace, and self-adjointness of $S_N$ controls the right error by the corresponding left error for $Y^*$. Thus $\norm{S_NYS_N-Y}\to0$. The difference between the two reconstruction errors is at most $2\varepsilon$, proving the claim.

For the last assertion, fix an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ and define
\[
 \norm X_2^2=\sum_j\norm{Xe_j}^2<\infty.
\]
Each column $(S_N-I)Xe_j$ tends to zero, and its squared norm is bounded by $4\norm{Xe_j}^2$. Dominated convergence gives $\norm{(S_N-I)X}_2\to0$. The right error follows by taking adjoints, using $S_N^*=S_N$ and $\norm{X^*}_2=\norm X_2$. The ideal inequality $\norm{AY}_2\leq\norm A\norm Y_2$ and the displayed decomposition finish the proof.
\end{proof}

The Hilbert--Schmidt norm is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, and it bounds the operator norm. It measures the total square size of all matrix columns. In a coordinate packet basis, it also measures the square sum of all matrix entries. Retaining a larger square of entries removes a correspondingly smaller summable tail. Operator norm instead measures the largest action on a unit vector, allowing the testing vector to depend on the cutoff.

\begin{example}[The identity never has a small omitted tail in operator norm]
On an infinite-dimensional coordinate space, let $S_N$ retain the first $N$ coordinates. For $X=I$,
\[
 \norm{S_NIS_N-I}=\norm{S_N-I}=1.
\]
A unit vector $e_{N+1}$ witnesses the lower bound. Nevertheless, $S_Nx\to x$ for every fixed $x\in\ell^2$. This is the difference between pointwise control over states and uniform control over the full unit ball.
\end{example}

\subsection{Zero padding and the correct asymptotic tail}

For a diagonal bounded multiplier $f(H_\lambda)$, zero padding gives the exact formula
\[
 \norm{f(H_\lambda)-S_Nf(H_\lambda)S_N}
 =\sup_{n>N}|f(\lambda_n)|.
\]
For the unitary multiplier $f(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}$, this norm is one at every finite cutoff. Equation \eqref{eq:foundation-time-tail} remains valid. Uniformity in time for a fixed state and failure of operator-norm convergence are therefore compatible.

For $\lambda_n=n$, a resolvent at $i\eta$, $\eta\ne0$, has zero-padded error
\[
 \sup_{n>N}\frac1{\sqrt{n^2+\eta^2}}
 =\frac1{\sqrt{(N+1)^2+\eta^2}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The heat multiplier $e^{-tn}$ has error $e^{-t(N+1)}$ for fixed $t>0$. These tails decay because the operators are compact. At $t=0$ the heat operator is the identity, so the same norm-convergence assertion is false.

Two other bounded multipliers approach one along this positive spectrum:
\[
 b(n)=\frac{n}{\sqrt{1+n^2}},\qquad
 q(n)=\frac{n-i}{n+i}.
\]
Their correct anchored cutoff is
\[
 A_N(f)=S_Nf(H_\lambda)S_N+(I-S_N).
\]
The errors are then
\[
 \norm{b(H_\lambda)-A_N(b)}
 =\sup_{n>N}\left|\frac{n}{\sqrt{1+n^2}}-1\right|\longrightarrow0,
\]
and
\[
 \norm{q(H_\lambda)-A_N(q)}
 =\sup_{n>N}\frac2{\sqrt{n^2+1}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The identity tail is an analytic choice justified by these asymptotic multipliers. It is not a universal prescription for every two-sided or non-diagonal spectrum.

On a graph-compatible atlas, an unbounded generator has another reconstruction statement:
\[
 S_NHS_N\psi-H\psi
 =S_N(HS_N\psi-H\psi)+(S_N-I)H\psi\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad\psi\in D(H).
\]
This is convergence of the displayed output vectors in the ambient Hilbert norm. It neither takes an operator norm of $H$ nor asserts graph-norm convergence of those output vectors, which would require additional domain and second-action information.

\foundationfigure[H]{09_cutoff_topology}{Zero-padded unitary cutoffs converge on a fixed state but retain operator-norm error one. For the same spectrum $n\geq1$, the resolvent multiplier has a tail that decays in operator norm.}

\subsection{A bounded certificate for a nonreducing packet}

A packet need not commute with an unbounded Hamiltonian. Suppose now that $H$ is self-adjoint, $P$ is a bounded orthogonal projection preserving $D(H)$, and $[H,P]$ on $D(H)$ extends to a bounded operator $B$. For nonreal $z$, let $R_z=(H-z)^{-1}$. It maps $\HH$ into $D(H)$, so all products used below have their stated meaning. Multiplying the commutator identity on the domain by the resolvents gives
\[
 [R_z,P]=-R_zBR_z.
\]
Indeed, for $x\in\HH$, apply $H-z$ to $PR_zx$ to obtain $Px+BR_zx$, then apply $R_z$. Hence
\[
 \norm{[R_z,P]}\leq\norm{R_z}^2\norm B,
 \qquad
 \norm{[R_{i\eta},P]}\leq\frac{\norm B}{\eta^2}
 \quad(\eta\ne0).
\]
The estimate converts a domain-sensitive commutator into a bounded one. In the generic formal certificate, the inverse and its domain properties are supplied explicitly. The diagonal modules also construct concrete inverses. Neither statement licenses a formal inverse for an unspecified operator.

\section{The finite differential obstruction and matrix corners}
\label{sec:foundation-corner-derivations}

Finite arrays support many useful difference operators. What they cannot support is a nonzero linear derivation of the full pointwise algebra $\C^N$ with its ordinary product. This obstruction explains why a finite operator calculus must declare which algebra carries its differentiation rule.

\begin{theorem}[No nonzero derivation of the finite pointwise algebra]
Let $D:\C^N\to\C^N$ be complex linear and satisfy
\[
 D(fg)=D(f)g+fD(g)
\]
for every pair of vectors, where multiplication is coordinatewise. Then $D=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the coordinate idempotent $e_a$, the identity $e_a^2=e_a$ gives $D(e_a)=2e_aD(e_a)$. At a coordinate $b\ne a$, the right side is zero. At $b=a$, the equality reads $(D(e_a))_a=2(D(e_a))_a$, again forcing zero. Thus $D(e_a)=0$ for every basis vector, and linearity gives $D=0$.
\end{proof}

The theorem concerns the semisimple pointwise algebra $\C^N$. It does not assert that every finite-dimensional commutative complex algebra has only the zero derivation. For example, on $\C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, the map $D(a+b\varepsilon)=b\varepsilon$ is a nonzero derivation. The nilpotent element changes the algebraic hypothesis.

\begin{example}[The precise defect of a forward difference]
On a cyclic grid, let $D_hf_j=(f_{j+1}-f_j)/h$, with $h\ne0$. Expanding the product gives
\[
 D_h(fg)_j-(D_hf)_jg_j-f_j(D_hg)_j
 =h(D_hf)_j(D_hg)_j.
\]
Thus the ordinary Leibniz identity fails unless the displayed product vanishes. A small defect on sufficiently regular sampled functions is compatible with the no-go theorem, because that theorem concerns an exact identity for every vector at fixed finite resolution.
\end{example}

\subsection{Exact differentiation in the full matrix algebra}

Move now to $M_N(\C)$. To avoid confusing a Hermitian observable with the skew-adjoint state generator $K$, denote a Hermitian matrix by $B=B^*$ and define
\[
 \delta_BX=i[B,X]=i(BX-XB).
\]
Then direct multiplication proves
\begin{align}
 \delta_B(XY)&=(\delta_BX)Y+X\delta_BY,\label{eq:foundation-matrix-leibniz}\\
 (\delta_BX)^*&=\delta_B(X^*),\label{eq:foundation-matrix-star}\\
 \operatorname{Tr}((\delta_BX)Y)&=-\operatorname{Tr}(X\delta_BY).
 \label{eq:foundation-matrix-ibp}
\end{align}
For the first identity, the middle terms $-iXBY$ and $iXBY$ cancel. For the second, taking the adjoint reverses the product order and conjugates $i$, with $B^*=B$ restoring the stated sign. For the third, cyclicity moves the leading $B$ in $\operatorname{Tr}(BXY)$ to the end. The trace pairing is bilinear here. Combining \eqref{eq:foundation-matrix-star} and \eqref{eq:foundation-matrix-ibp} also gives the Hilbert--Schmidt identity
\[
 \inner{\delta_BX}{Y}_{\rm HS}=-\inner{X}{\delta_BY}_{\rm HS},
 \qquad\inner{X}{Y}_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(X^*Y).
\]

These identities preserve multiplication order. They do not turn $\delta_B$ into a derivation from diagonal matrices to diagonal matrices. Usually it leaves that commutative subalgebra.

\begin{example}[A nonzero derivative leaves the pointwise subalgebra]
For
\[
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 X=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
one obtains
\[
 \delta_BX=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}\ne0.
\]
The output is off diagonal. This is exactly how the matrix algebra permits a nonzero derivation without violating the pointwise theorem.
\end{example}

For Hermitian generators $B_i,B_j$, put $\mathcal F_{ij}=i[B_i,B_j]$. This curvature matrix is Hermitian, and the Jacobi identity gives
\begin{equation}
 [\delta_{B_i},\delta_{B_j}]X
 =-[[B_i,B_j],X]
 =i[\mathcal F_{ij},X]=\delta_{\mathcal F_{ij}}X.
 \label{eq:foundation-corner-curvature}
\end{equation}
Commuting generators produce commuting derivations. A nonzero curvature matrix need not act nontrivially on every observable: its action on a particular $X$ vanishes precisely when that $X$ commutes with it. This matrix identity provides an algebraic curvature mechanism. A physical geometric interpretation requires the additional structures developed in the gauge and gravity papers.

\section{Refinement cancellation and the cost of extrapolation}
\label{f:extrapolation}
Coarsening a packet atlas combines exact components of one description. A different use of refinement compares approximations made at several scales. The distinction matters. An algebraic cancellation of leading error terms requires an expansion in a common vector space, and a useful numerical result also requires control of the remaining error and of the sample perturbations.

Let $E$ be a real normed vector space and let $f(h)\in E$ be defined for $0<|h|<\delta$. Fix a refinement ratio $b>1$. If $f(h)$ represents operators on different Hilbert spaces, comparison maps must first place them in a common space where the following additions are meaningful. The formulas alone do not construct those maps.

The denominators below are positive. Each level is a finite linear combination of the original samples at successively refined scales.

\begin{definition}[The actual refinement tower]
Set $T_0f(h)=f(h)$ and, for $m\geq0$, define
\[
 T_{m+1}f(h)=\frac{b^{m+1}T_mf(h/b)-T_mf(h)}{b^{m+1}-1}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Exact response of a monomial]
For $r\in\N$ and $v\in E$,
\[
 T_m(h^rv)=c_{m,r}h^rv,\qquad
 c_{m,r}=\prod_{k=1}^{m}\frac{b^{k-r}-1}{b^k-1}.
\]
The empty product equals one. In particular, $c_{m,0}=1$, and $c_{m,r}=0$ for $1\leq r\leq m$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
At level zero the assertion is the definition. If it holds at level $m$, the next recursion multiplies the coefficient by
\[
 \frac{b^{m+1}b^{-r}-1}{b^{m+1}-1}.
\]
This appends the next factor to the product. For $r=0$, each factor equals one. For $1\leq r\leq m$, the factor at $k=r$ vanishes.
\end{proof}

Suppose that a finite expansion is available,
\[
 f(h)=F+\sum_{r=1}^{m}h^rv_r+R(h).
\]
Linearity and the proposition give the exact identity
\[
 T_mf(h)-F=T_mR(h).
\]
Only a finite sum has been used. No convergence of an infinite formal series is needed. The size of the right-hand side remains an analytic question.

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}[A quantified remainder and perturbation bound]
Let $p$ be a nonnegative integer and suppose
\[
 \norm{R(h)}\leq C|h|^p,\qquad
 \norm{g(h)-f(h)}\leq\varepsilon
 \quad(0<|h|<\delta),
\]
where $C,\varepsilon\geq0$. Define
\[
 A_{m,p}=\prod_{k=1}^{m}\frac{b^{k-p}+1}{b^k-1}.
\]
Then, throughout the same punctured interval,
\[
 \norm{T_mg(h)-F}\leq A_{m,p}C|h|^p+A_{m,0}\varepsilon.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The interval is stable under $h\mapsto h/b$. The triangle inequality applied to one tower step gives
\[
 \norm{T_{m+1}R(h)}\leq
 \frac{b^{m+1}\norm{T_mR(h/b)}+\norm{T_mR(h)}}{b^{m+1}-1}.
\]
Starting with the stated remainder bound and proceeding by induction multiplies its constant at step $m+1$ by $(b^{m+1-p}+1)/(b^{m+1}-1)$. Hence $\norm{T_mR(h)}\leq A_{m,p}C|h|^p$. Apply the same argument with $p=0$ to $g-f$. Linearity and the triangle inequality separate the two contributions.
\end{proof}

When $p=m+1$, this proves the expected order improvement under an explicit remainder hypothesis. It also retains the effect of noisy samples. Each factor in $A_{m,0}$ exceeds one, so extrapolation can amplify a uniform sample error even while cancelling several deterministic powers of $h$.

\subsection{A complete three-level example}
For $b=2$, direct substitution gives
\begin{align*}
 T_1f(h)&=2f(h/2)-f(h),\\
 T_2f(h)&=\frac{8f(h/4)-6f(h/2)+f(h)}{3},\\
 T_3f(h)&=\frac{64f(h/8)-56f(h/4)+14f(h/2)-f(h)}{21}.
\end{align*}
Take the exact scalar polynomial $f(h)=1+2h-3h^2+4h^3$. The responses are
\[
 T_1f(h)=1+\frac32h^2-3h^3,\qquad
 T_2f(h)=1+\frac12h^3,\qquad T_3f(h)=1.
\]
These are polynomial identities for every real $h$. If each of the three samples used by $T_2$ has absolute error at most $\varepsilon$, its output error is at most
\[
 \frac{8+6+1}{3}\varepsilon=5\varepsilon.
\]
This bound is attained by errors with signs matching the three weights. Thus exact removal of the first two powers does not imply a contraction on arbitrary perturbations. For the displayed polynomial, the perturbed second-level approximation has the explicit total bound $|h|^3/2+5\varepsilon$.

The calculation supplies a practical reading rule for later refinement claims. An exact coefficient identity, an asymptotic remainder estimate, and a stability bound are separate pieces of evidence. A physical approximation uses all three, together with the comparison maps that make its values commensurable.

\section*{Arithmetic resolution and quantum refinement}
The preceding constructions compare geometric and spectral resolutions. Arithmetic refinement provides another concrete family: finite unit registers, Haar packets, hierarchical Hamiltonians, and polyphase channels. The question remains the same. Which maps preserve the state, which preserve the dynamics, and what additional structure appears when hidden components are eliminated?

Normalized Haar averages identify coarse states inside a fine Hilbert space. Compatibility of the Hamiltonian, rather than normalization alone, determines whether that subspace carries the same evolution. Schur reduction and its time-domain memory equation describe the effect of components that cannot simply be discarded.

Infinite depth introduces a separate analytic problem. The hierarchical model specifies a common Hilbert space, a maximal operator domain, and the topology of approximation. Spectral decimation and hypergeometric companion functions provide exact coordinates within their declared domains. None of these identities alone identifies arithmetic depth with a physical observable.

The following account of covariant fiber dynamics supplies a candidate physical coupling and examines its energy and production constraints. That transition separates a mathematical refinement structure from a proposed model of matter.

\part{Completion and continuum evolution}
\section{The complete coefficient Hilbert space}
Let
\[
\KK=\ell^2(\Z^3;\C^4)
=\left\{a=(a_n):\sum_{n\in\Z^3}\norm{a_n}^2<\infty\right\}.
\]
Its inner product is $\inner{a}{b}=\sum_n\inner{a_n}{b_n}$. Absolute convergence follows from the scalar Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. The norm therefore measures the total squared amplitude across all Fourier packets. A finite family of amplitudes embeds by assigning zero to every absent mode.

For a finite set $S\subset\Z^3$, define the truncation $P_Sa$ by retaining $a_n$ when $n\in S$ and assigning zero otherwise. Then
\[
\norm{a-P_Sa}^2=\sum_{n\notin S}\norm{a_n}^2.
\]
The sum on the right can be made arbitrarily small because the full nonnegative series converges. Thus finite packets are dense in $\KK$. The statement concerns the norm of the omitted amplitudes and does not depend on a particular ordering of the integer lattice.

\begin{theorem}[Completion of a modewise isometry]
Suppose that for every mode $n$, $V_n:\C^4\to\C^4$ is a complex linear isometry. The coordinate rule $(Va)_n=V_na_n$ defines a complex linear isometry on $\KK$. If each $V_n$ has an inverse isometry $W_n$, the induced $V$ and $W$ are inverse maps on $\KK$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each $n$, $\norm{V_na_n}^2=\norm{a_n}^2$. Summability of the latter terms gives membership of $Va$ in $\KK$, and summing the equalities gives $\norm{Va}=\norm{a}$. Linearity holds coordinatewise. The two inverse identities hold on each coordinate and therefore on the coefficient fields themselves.
\end{proof}


Apply this construction to
\[
V_n(t)=e^{-itH_n},\qquad V_{h,n}(t)=e^{-itH_{h,n}}.
\]
The finite-dimensional norm preservation already proved supplies its hypothesis. Define
\[
(U(t)a)_n=V_n(t)a_n,\qquad (U_h(t)a)_n=V_{h,n}(t)a_n.
\]
Both maps are everywhere-defined unitary maps on $\KK$. Their inverses are obtained at time $-t$. The modewise time-group laws imply
\[
U(s+t)=U(s)U(t),\qquad U_h(s+t)=U_h(s)U_h(t).
\]
This construction uses the bounded unitary map on each mode. It does not apply an unbounded Hamiltonian to an arbitrary coefficient field. In particular, the evolution is defined for more initial states than the Hamiltonian action constructed below.

\subsection{The invariant finite packets}
Both families commute with every finite truncation:
\[
U(t)P_S=P_SU(t),\qquad U_h(t)P_S=P_SU_h(t).
\]
The equality follows directly from the diagonal mode action. It says that the full evolution restricts to the finite-packet evolution already constructed. It also says that the missing tail evolves without feeding new amplitude into the retained mode set in this free model.

This property would have to be reconsidered in a model whose coefficients couple different Fourier modes. The completion argument for a diagonal multiplier makes essential use of the simple resolved action, even though the general packet language also describes nondiagonal transfers.

\section{Removing the Fourier cutoff}
A finite-packet consistency theorem alone says nothing about an arbitrary field with infinitely many nonzero coefficients. The missing estimate must control the error introduced by truncating that field. Exact unitarity gives a bound whose tail terms do not grow with time.

\begin{lemma}[Two tails and a finite core]
Let $V$ and $W$ be linear isometries on a normed space. For any $a$ and any approximation $b$,
\[
\norm{Va-Wa}\le 2\norm{a-b}+\norm{Vb-Wb}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write the residual as $V(a-b)+(Vb-Wb)+W(b-a)$. The triangle inequality bounds its norm by the sum of the three norms. Each outer term has norm $\norm{a-b}$ because its operator is an isometry.
\end{proof}

Take $V=U_h(t)$, $W=U(t)$, and $b=P_Sa$. For a fixed finite $S$, Block 45 gives a compact-time estimate of the form
\[
\norm{U_h(t)P_Sa-U(t)P_Sa}\le K_{S,a,T}h^2
\]
for all $|t|\le T$ and sufficiently small positive $h$. The constant is allowed to depend on the support, the amplitudes, and the time window. Combining the estimates gives
\[
\norm{U_h(t)a-U(t)a}\le
2\norm{a-P_Sa}+K_{S,a,T}h^2.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Compact-time strong convergence]
For every $a\in\KK$, every $T\ge0$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that
\[
0<h<\delta,\quad |t|\le T
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\norm{U_h(t)a-U(t)a}<\varepsilon.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose a finite $S$ such that $\norm{a-P_Sa}<\varepsilon/4$. The finite-packet theorem gives a sufficiently small positive $\delta$ for which the core residual is less than $\varepsilon/2$ throughout the time interval. The two-tail inequality then makes the full residual less than $\varepsilon$. The choice of $S$ precedes the choice of $h$ and works for every time in the same interval.
\end{proof}


The quantifiers are important. One initial field and one compact time interval are fixed before the mesh scale is chosen. The theorem does not assert convergence in operator norm on the entire unit ball. It also does not assign a universal $O(h^2)$ rate to every $a\in\KK$. For arbitrary square-summable data, a small Fourier tail may require a large cutoff, and the finite-core constant may grow with that cutoff.

\section{Fourier synthesis on the physical torus}
The scalar Fourier characters $e_n(x)=e^{2\pi i n\cdot x}$ are normalized relative to Haar measure of total mass one. For a four-spinor field, apply the scalar Fourier coefficient map to each of its four coordinates. The resulting map is
\[
\F:\HH\longrightarrow\KK,
\qquad \HH=L^2(\T^3;\C^4).
\]
Block 47 proves the four-spinor Parseval identity and surjectivity of synthesis, producing a complex linear isometric equivalence. In ordinary notation,
\[
\norm{\F f}_{\KK}=\norm{f}_{\HH},\qquad
\F^{-1}\F f=f,\qquad \F\F^{-1}a=a.
\]
The inverse is understood as convergence in $L^2$. A general field need not have a pointwise-convergent Fourier series, and no such convergence is required here.

For a finite-support coefficient field, the inverse is the familiar finite sum
\[
\F^{-1}a=\sum_n e_na_n.
\]
The complete-space equivalence extends that reconstruction while retaining its exact norm. Its surjectivity is the step that rules out having built only a proper closed subspace of the physical field space.

\begin{definition}[Physical propagators]
Define
\[
\mathcal U(t)=\F^{-1}U(t)\F,
\qquad
\mathcal U_h(t)=\F^{-1}U_h(t)\F.
\]
\end{definition}
Both preserve the physical $L^2$ norm and inner product. Their group laws follow by inserting $\F\F^{-1}=I$ between consecutive factors. Their residual satisfies the exact equality
\[
\norm{\mathcal U_h(t)f-\mathcal U(t)f}_{\HH}
=\norm{U_h(t)\F f-U(t)\F f}_{\KK}.
\]
The compact-time convergence theorem therefore transfers to every $f\in\HH$ without an additional constant.


\atlasfigure{10_fourier_transport}{Fourier analysis and synthesis change the representation while preserving the Hilbert norm. The operator in each representation is related by conjugation.}

The physical torus in this theorem is a fixed flat compact space. The word physical identifies the function-space realization of the fields, rather than establishing empirical adequacy or deriving a spacetime geometry. Periodicity is an explicit boundary condition. The next part constructs the Hamiltonian on exactly this space and retains that same boundary condition.

\part{The unbounded Hamiltonian}
\section{A domain defined by the operator output}
The continuum mode energy grows with $|n|$. A square-summable sequence $a_n$ need not remain square summable after multiplication by $H_n$. This is why the full Hamiltonian is represented as a partial linear map with a specified domain.

Define
\[
\Dom(\widehat H_m)
=\left\{a\in\KK:\sum_n\norm{H_na_n}^2<\infty\right\},
\qquad
(\widehat H_ma)_n=H_na_n.
\]
The domain is maximal for this coefficient action: it contains precisely those coefficient fields for which the stated output belongs to the ambient Hilbert space. It is a vector subspace. For example, $\norm{x+y}^2\le2\norm{x}^2+2\norm{y}^2$ and linearity of each $H_n$ prove closure under addition. Scalar multiplication preserves summability as well.

Every finite-support field lies in this domain, since the output again has finite support. Density of finite-support fields therefore proves density of $\Dom(\widehat H_m)$ in $\KK$. Density matters because it gives uniqueness of an adjoint value when such a value exists.

The source represents this object with Mathlib's \path{LinearPMap}. The domain is a submodule and is carried by the operator itself. It is not replaced with a total function that assigns an arbitrary value to every vector outside the domain.


\section{The adjoint domain and self-adjointness}
Modewise Hermiticity gives symmetry on the maximal domain. If $a,b$ belong to that domain, the two series in
\[
\inner{\widehat H_ma}{b}
=\sum_n\inner{H_na_n}{b_n}
=\sum_n\inner{a_n}{H_nb_n}
=\inner{a}{\widehat H_mb}
\]
converge absolutely by Cauchy--Schwarz. This establishes the inclusion $\widehat H_m\subseteq\widehat H_m^*$, including the corresponding domain inclusion.

Equality requires the converse. A merely symmetric operator can have a strictly larger adjoint domain. Here the coordinate structure makes it possible to determine that domain directly.

\begin{theorem}[Self-adjoint maximal multiplier]
The densely defined operator $\widehat H_m$ equals its Hilbert adjoint.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $b\in\Dom(\widehat H_m^*)$ and write $c=\widehat H_m^*b$. By the adjoint relation,
\[
\inner{\widehat H_ma}{b}=\inner{a}{c}
\qquad(a\in\Dom(\widehat H_m)).
\]
Fix a mode $n$ and choose $a$ with the single nonzero coefficient $a_n=v$, where $v\in\C^4$ is arbitrary. Such a field belongs to the maximal domain. The adjoint identity becomes
\[

\section*{Resolution, dynamics, and reconstruction}
A physical description often begins by separating a state into spatial cells, frequency bands, spin channels, tensor factors, or spectral sectors. Such a separation is useful only when the components can be reconstructed, their interactions can be described, and different resolutions can be compared. Those requirements lead to the calculus developed here.

An orthogonal projector selects a packet. Placing an operator between two projectors gives a transfer block. A skew-adjoint generator determines an antisymmetric current between packet weights. Grouping the labels produces a coarser description in which internal currents cancel. These statements can be understood in a small matrix example before any infinite-dimensional analysis is needed.

The same questions become more demanding when frames move, states become mixed, or the system exchanges information with an environment. Countable resolutions introduce convergence. Unbounded operators introduce domains. Each extension retains part of the finite algebra and adds a hypothesis that must remain visible where it is used.

The free Dirac construction that follows gives these ideas a concrete analytic realization. Fourier modes resolve a spinor field, finite matrices govern its components, and completion leads to a self-adjoint Hamiltonian. Gauge transport, constrained gravity, and arithmetic refinement then test which parts of the same language survive in different settings.

\begin{readerroadmap}[title={The organizing question}]
Which quantities can be reconstructed exactly, which balances survive a change of resolution, and which additional hypotheses are required for an infinite or unbounded system?
\end{readerroadmap}

The mathematical arguments use ordinary complex linear algebra, operator theory, and Hilbert-space analysis. Formal source correspondences and verification records are collected in the technical appendices. Numerical illustrations explain specified examples rather than replacing universal proofs.

\[
e_n(x)=e^{2\pi i n\cdot x}=e^{i p(n)\cdot x}.
\]

Components of a spinor are numbered \(0,1,2,3\), in the exact order of
the source representation. For \(v,w\in\mathbb C^4\),

\[
\langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{r=0}^{3}\overline{v_r}w_r,
\qquad

\]

The inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear
in its second. The adjoint is therefore the conjugate transpose. Unless
indicated otherwise, a spinor norm is this Euclidean norm and an
operator norm is its induced operator norm. The field pairing is

\[
\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}

\[

\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},
\]

where

\[
\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Proposition PH01 (Hermitian Clifford relations).} The four
displayed matrices are Hermitian involutions. Distinct spatial
generators anticommute, and each spatial generator anticommutes with
\(\beta\):

\[
\alpha_j^*=\alpha_j,\quad \beta^*=\beta,\quad
\alpha_j^2=\beta^2=I_4,
\]

\[
\alpha_j\alpha_k+\alpha_k\alpha_j=0\quad(j\ne k),
\qquad
\alpha_j\beta+\beta\alpha_j=0.
\]

\emph{Proof.} The real diagonal entries of \(\beta\) are
\(1,1,-1,-1\), so its adjoint and square have the stated forms. Each
\(\sigma_j\) is Hermitian and squares to \(I_2\), by direct
multiplication. Their products are

\[
\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z,\qquad
\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x,\qquad
\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y,
\]

with reversed products equal to their negatives. For example,

\[
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix}=i\sigma_z.
\]

The other two follow by the same two-by-two multiplication; reversal
follows by taking adjoints. The block form gives

\[
\alpha_j^*=
\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j^*\\\sigma_j^*&0\end{pmatrix}
=\alpha_j,\qquad
\alpha_j\alpha_k=
\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_j\sigma_k&0\\0&\sigma_j\sigma_k\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Thus \(\alpha_j^2=I_4\) and the spatial anticommutators vanish. Finally,

\[
\alpha_j\beta=
\begin{pmatrix}0&-\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\beta\alpha_j=
\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\-\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},
\]

whose sum is zero. Every identity is an identity of the exact source
matrices. \(\square\)

\hypertarget{continuum-and-centered-mode-hamiltonians}{%
\section{Continuum and centered mode
Hamiltonians}\label{continuum-and-centered-mode-hamiltonians}}

For \(p\in\mathbb R^3\), define

\[
H(m,p)=m\beta+p_x\alpha_x+p_y\alpha_y+p_z\alpha_z.
\]

Its coordinates are

\[
H(m,p)=
\begin{pmatrix}
m&0&p_z&p_x-ip_y\\
0&m&p_x+ip_y&-p_z\\
p_z&p_x-ip_y&-m&0\\
p_x+ip_y&-p_z&0&-m
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

On mode \(n\), the continuum Hamiltonian is \(H_n=H(m,p(n))\). It is the
symbol of the differential expression

\[
-i\sum_{j=x,y,z}\alpha_j\partial_j+m\beta
\]

on the finite packet space: \(\partial_je_n=ip_j(n)e_n\), so applying
the expression to \(e_na_n\) gives \(e_nH_na_n\). For real spacing
\(h\), set

\[
q_j(h,p)=
\begin{cases}
\sin(hp_j)/h,&h\ne0,\\
p_j,&h=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Write \(q_h(n)=q(h,p(n))\) and \(H_{h,n}=H(m,q_h(n))\). The function
\(q_j\) is even in \(h\), and its value at zero is justified by
\(\sin z/z\to1\). For \(h\ne0\), a centered translation difference on a
periodic smooth function is

\[
(D_{h,j}f)(x)=\frac{f(x+he_j)-f(x-he_j)}{2h}.
\]

Here \(e_j\) is the j-th spatial unit vector, distinct from the Fourier
characters \(e_n\) and spinor vectors. Its action on a plane wave is
exactly

\[
D_{h,j}e_n
=e_n\frac{e^{ihp_j(n)}-e^{-ihp_j(n)}}{2h}
=i\frac{\sin(hp_j(n))}{h}e_n.
\]

The centered differential expression \(-i\sum_j\alpha_jD_{h,j}+m\beta\)
therefore has symbol \(H_{h,n}\). Its signs follow from \(-i\cdot i=1\).
At \(h=0\), the symbol equals \(H_n\) by definition. These formulas take
place on the continuum torus and use no sampled spatial data.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Proposition PH02 (Hermiticity and the mass shell).} For every
real \(m\) and \(p\in\mathbb R^3\),

\[
H(m,p)^*=H(m,p),\qquad
H(m,p)^2=(m^2+|p|^2)I_4.
\]

In particular, \(H_n,H_{h,n}\) are Hermitian for all real \(m,h\), and

\[
H_n^2=E_n^2I_4,\quad E_n=\sqrt{m^2+|p(n)|^2},
\]

\[
H_{h,n}^2=E_{h,n}^2I_4,\quad
E_{h,n}=\sqrt{m^2+|q_h(n)|^2}.
\]

\emph{Proof.} Adjoint is additive, and a real multiple of a Hermitian
matrix is Hermitian. PH01 therefore proves the first identity. Expanding
the square gives the square terms \(m^2\beta^2+\sum_jp_j^2\alpha_j^2\),
the terms \(mp_j(\beta\alpha_j+\alpha_j\beta)\), and the terms
\(p_jp_k(\alpha_j\alpha_k+\alpha_k\alpha_j)\) for \(j<k\). The
anticommutators vanish and all four squares are \(I_4\), giving
\((m^2+\sum_jp_j^2)I_4\). Substitution proves both mode statements.
\(\square\)

Hermiticity here is a statement about matrices acting on all of
\(\mathbb C^4\). Every linear map on this finite space is bounded and
everywhere defined. This is not a construction of the adjoint or domain
of an unbounded differential operator on the full field space.

\hypertarget{spectral-projectors-and-exact-mode-evolution}{%
\section{Spectral projectors and exact mode
evolution}\label{spectral-projectors-and-exact-mode-evolution}}

Let \(H=H(m,p)\) and \(E=\sqrt{m^2+|p|^2}\). Define the exact propagator

\[
U_H(t)=e^{-itH}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-itH)^k}{k!}.
\]

The series converges absolutely in operator norm, being dominated by
\(\sum_k(|t|\|H\|)^k/k!\). This is exact continuous-time evolution, with
no time step or series truncation.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Proposition PH03 (spectral splitting and closed propagator).} If
\(E>0\), define

\[
P_+=\frac12\left(I_4+\frac HE\right),\qquad
P_-=\frac12\left(I_4-\frac HE\right).
\]

Then \(P_\pm^*=P_\pm\), \(P_\pm^2=P_\pm\), \(P_+P_-=P_-P_+=0\),
\(P_++P_-=I_4\), and \(HP_\pm=\pm EP_\pm\). Both projectors have rank
two, and

\[
U_H(t)=e^{-itE}P_++e^{itE}P_-
=\cos(tE)I_4-i\frac{\sin(tE)}{E}H.
\]

If \(E=0\), then \(H=0\) and \(U_H(t)=I_4\). Equivalently, the closed
expression is valid with the continuous convention \(\sin(tE)/E=t\) at
\(E=0\).

\emph{Proof.} For \(E>0\), the Hermitian matrix \(K=H/E\) satisfies
\(K^2=I_4\). Thus

\[
P_\pm^2=\tfrac14(I_4\pm2K+K^2)=\tfrac12(I_4\pm K)=P_\pm,
\]

and \(P_+P_-=\tfrac14(I_4-K^2)=0\); the reversed product is the same.
Their adjoints equal themselves and their sum is \(I_4\). Also
\(K(I_4\pm K)=K\pm I_4=\pm(I_4\pm K)\), proving \(HP_\pm=\pm EP_\pm\).
Each displayed Clifford matrix has trace zero. Hence
\(\operatorname{tr}H=0\) and \(\operatorname{tr}P_\pm=2\). An idempotent
splits the space into its range and kernel, acting as identity and zero
respectively. Its trace is therefore its rank, proving rank two.

The identity \(I_4=P_++P_-\) and the two eigenvalue identities give, by
induction, \(H^k=E^kP_++(-E)^kP_-\) for every \(k\ge0\). Substitute into
the absolutely convergent series to obtain the spectral expression.
Expanding its projectors gives the cosine and sine expression.

When \(E=0\), the sum \(m^2+|p|^2\) of nonnegative squares is zero.
Therefore \(m=0,p=0\), and \(H=0\). Its exponential is \(I_4\). The
quotient \(\sin(tE)/E\) tends to \(t\) at zero; multiplying its filled
value by \(H=0\) gives the same identity. No division by zero is used.
\(\square\)

The proof applies unchanged to \(H_{h,n}\), with energy \(E_{h,n}\). A
positive-energy continuum mode can have \(E_{h,n}=0\) at a nonzero
spacing when \(m=0\) and all centered components vanish. That mode uses
the zero-energy branch. Positivity of the continuum energy does not
license division by the centered energy at every spacing.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Proposition PH04 (group law, unitarity, and stability).} For
real \(s,t\),

\[
U_H(0)=I_4,\qquad U_H(s+t)=U_H(s)U_H(t),
\]

\[
U_H(-t)=U_H(t)^{-1}=U_H(t)^*,
\qquad U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=U_H(t)U_H(t)^*=I_4.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\langle U_H(t)v,U_H(t)w\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad
\|U_H(t)v\|_2=\|v\|_2
\]

for all spinors. These statements hold for both mode Hamiltonians at
every real \(m,h,t\).

\emph{Proof.} When \(E>0\), the spectral form and orthogonality of
\(P_\pm\) give

\[
U_H(s)U_H(t)
=e^{-i(s+t)E}P_++e^{i(s+t)E}P_-=U_H(s+t).
\]

At zero time the sum is \(I_4\). Hermiticity of the projectors and
reality of \(tE\) give \(U_H(t)^*=e^{itE}P_++e^{-itE}P_-=U_H(-t)\).
Setting \(s=-t\) proves the inverse identities. When \(E=0\), every
assertion follows from \(U_H(t)=I_4\).

For any matrix \(A\), expansion and interchange of two finite sums gives
\(\langle Av,w\rangle=\langle v,A^*w\rangle\). Thus

\[
\langle U_H(t)v,U_H(t)w\rangle
=\langle v,U_H(t)^*U_H(t)w\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle.
\]

Take \(w=v\) and then nonnegative square roots to obtain norm
preservation. PH02 supplies the mode cases. \(\square\)

The Block 44 proof uses the equivalent bounded-operator argument:
\(-itH\) is skew-adjoint, and its exponential is unitary. Our spectral
proof supplies additional explicit projectors and formulas.

\hypertarget{fourier-orthogonality-and-packet-conservation}{%
\section{Fourier orthogonality and packet
conservation}\label{fourier-orthogonality-and-packet-conservation}}

Let \(J_n:\mathbb C^4\to L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^4)\) be
\(J_nv=e_nv\).

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Proposition PH05 (mode isometry and finite Parseval identity).}
For modes \(n,k\) and spinors \(v,w\),

\[
\langle J_nv,J_kw\rangle_{L^2}
=\begin{cases}\langle v,w\rangle,&n=k,\\0,&n\ne k.\end{cases}
\]

In particular, \(J_n\) is a linear isometry and

\[
\left\|\sum_{n\in S}J_na_n\right\|_{L^2}^2
=\sum_{n\in S}\|a_n\|_2^2.
\]

\emph{Proof.} The constant spinors factor out of the scalar integral:

\[
\langle J_nv,J_kw\rangle_{L^2}
=\langle v,w\rangle\int_{\mathbb T^3}e^{2\pi i(k-n)\cdot x}\,dx.
\]

The integral is the product of three one-dimensional integrals. For
integer \(r\), the integral of \(e^{2\pi irx}\) over \([0,1)\) is \(1\)
when \(r=0\); for \(r\ne0\), it is \((e^{2\pi ir}-1)/(2\pi ir)=0\). The
product is therefore \(1\) exactly when \(n=k\). Linearity is immediate,
and setting \(k=n,w=v\) proves isometry. Expansion of the squared norm
of the finite sum gives a double sum of pairings. The off-diagonal
pairings vanish and the diagonal pairings are \(\|a_n\|_2^2\).
\(\square\)

Define the evolved packets

\[
f(t,x)=\sum_{n\in S}e_n(x)U_{H_n}(t)a_n,\qquad
f_h(t,x)=\sum_{n\in S}e_n(x)U_{H_{h,n}}(t)a_n.
\]

Both remain in \(\mathcal F_S\). Their operators \(U_S(t),U_{h,S}(t)\)
have the finite block diagonal coefficient actions with blocks
\(U_{H_n}(t),U_{H_{h,n}}(t)\).

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Theorem PH06 (exact finite-packet norm conservation).} For every
real \(m,h,t\), finite \(S\), and coefficient family \(a\),

\[
\|f(t)\|_{L^2}^2=\|f_h(t)\|_{L^2}^2
=\sum_{n\in S}\|a_n\|_2^2=\|f_a\|_{L^2}^2.
\]

Both packet evolutions preserve the \(L^2\) inner product between two
packets in \(\mathcal F_S\), and each forms a one-parameter unitary
group there.

\emph{Proof.} Apply PH05 to the evolved coefficients and PH04 on each
mode:

\[
\|f_h(t)\|_{L^2}^2
=\sum_{n\in S}\|U_{H_{h,n}}(t)a_n\|_2^2
=\sum_{n\in S}\|a_n\|_2^2.
\]

The continuum argument is identical. For coefficient families \(a,b\),
the same two propositions give

\[
\langle f_{h,a}(t),f_{h,b}(t)\rangle_{L^2}
=\sum_{n\in S}
\langle U_{H_{h,n}}(t)a_n,U_{H_{h,n}}(t)b_n\rangle
=\sum_{n\in S}\langle a_n,b_n\rangle.
\]

Composition of coefficient blocks proves the packet group law, and
inverse time proves surjectivity. This establishes unitarity on
\(\mathcal F_S\) using only finite sums. \(\square\)

The quantity conserved is squared Hilbert norm, or total probability for
a normalized state. The parameter \(m\), the positive shell value
\(E_n\), and Hamiltonian expectation are different quantities. Calling
squared norm a packet mass does not identify it with the rest mass or
physical Hamiltonian energy.

\hypertarget{generator-consistency-and-dispersion-error}{%
\section{Generator consistency and dispersion
error}\label{generator-consistency-and-dispersion-error}}

The mode Hamiltonian difference contains no mass term:

\[
\Delta_{h,n}:=H_{h,n}-H_n
=\sum_{j=x,y,z}\delta_j(h,n)\alpha_j,
\qquad
\delta_j(h,n)=q_j(h,p(n))-p_j(n).
\]

Define

\[
C(n)=\frac16\left(\sum_{j=x,y,z}|p_j(n)|^6\right)^{1/2}.
\]

This constant depends on the fixed mode and increases cubically with
momentum scale. That dependence is essential in a fixed-cutoff result.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}
\textbf{Proposition PH07 (quadratic generator consistency).} For every
real \(h\) and fixed mode \(n\),

\[
\|\Delta_{h,n}\|=|\delta(h,n)|\le h^2C(n).
\]

For every fixed finite packet,

\[
\left\|\sum_{n\in S}e_n\Delta_{h,n}a_n\right\|_{L^2}^2
=\sum_{n\in S}|\delta(h,n)|^2\|a_n\|_2^2,
\]

and

\[
\left\|\sum_{n\in S}e_n\Delta_{h,n}a_n\right\|_{L^2}
\le h^2\left(\sum_{n\in S}C(n)^2\|a_n\|_2^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]

\emph{Proof.} First prove the scalar estimate without a sign
restriction on \(h\). The fundamental theorem of calculus gives
\(|\sin u|\le|u|\), since \(\sin u=\int_0^u\cos v\,dv\) and
\(|\cos v|\le1\). Therefore

\[
|1-\cos u|=2\sin^2(u/2)\le u^2/2.
\]

For \(z\ge0\), integrate this bound in
\(\sin z-z=\int_0^z(\cos u-1)\,du\) to obtain \(|\sin z-z|\le z^3/6\).
Oddness of the residual proves \(|\sin z-z|\le|z|^3/6\) for negative
\(z\). For \(h\ne0\), substitute \(z=hp_j(n)\) and divide by \(|h|\):

\[
|\delta_j(h,n)|\le \frac{h^2|p_j(n)|^3}{6}.
\]

For \(h=0\), the residual is zero by definition and the bound still
holds. Squaring and adding proves \(|\delta(h,n)|\le h^2C(n)\).

The Hermitian matrix \(\Delta_{h,n}\) satisfies
\(\Delta_{h,n}^2=|\delta(h,n)|^2I_4\) by PH01. Hence

\[
\|\Delta_{h,n}v\|_2^2
=\langle v,\Delta_{h,n}^*\Delta_{h,n}v\rangle
=|\delta(h,n)|^2\|v\|_2^2.
\]

Its induced operator norm is exactly \(|\delta(h,n)|\): the upper bound
holds on every vector and equality holds on every unit vector. Apply
PH05 to the residual coefficients for the packet equality, substitute
the scalar bounds, and take nonnegative square roots. \(\square\)

The checked generator results state corresponding \(O(h^2)\) estimates
as \(h\to0^+\). The explicit constant and all-real inequality above are
traditional deductions. Precisely, \(r(h)=O(h^2)\) means that some
\(M,\varepsilon>0\) satisfy \(\|r(h)\|\le Mh^2\) for
\(0<h<\varepsilon\). Fixed support and amplitudes permit finite
summation of such bounds; no estimate uniform over all integer modes
follows.

The reverse triangle inequality in \(\mathbb R^4\), applied to
\((m,q_h(n))\) and \((m,p(n))\), gives

\[
|E_{h,n}-E_n|\le|q_h(n)-p(n)|\le h^2C(n).
\]

Moreover, \(|\sin(hp_j)/h|\le|p_j|\) for \(h\ne0\), and the filled value
is equal at zero. Thus \(0\le E_{h,n}\le E_n\). For a fixed mode,
Taylor's formula gives

\[
q_j(h,p(n))=p_j(n)-\frac{h^2p_j(n)^3}{6}+O(h^4),
\]

\[
E_{h,n}^2=E_n^2-\frac{h^2}{3}\sum_jp_j(n)^4+O(h^4).
\]

For clarity, Taylor's theorem through degree four has zero even
coefficients for sine, and its fifth-derivative remainder is at most
\(|hp_j|^5/120\). Division by \(|h|\) gives \(O(h^4)\); squaring the
three expansions and summing preserves that order for a fixed mode. If
\(E_n>0\), the square root is smooth near \(E_n^2\), so

\[
E_{h,n}=E_n-\frac{h^2}{6E_n}\sum_jp_j(n)^4+O(h^4).
\]

If \(E_n=0\), then \(m=0,n=0\) and \(E_{h,n}=0\) exactly for every
\(h\). The expansion containing \(1/E_n\) is not used.

For fixed time, the phase error on either energy branch obeys

\[
|e^{\pm itE_{h,n}}-e^{\pm itE_n}|
\le |t|\,|E_{h,n}-E_n|,
\]

by integrating the derivative of \(s\mapsto e^{\pm its}\) between the
two real energies. Phase comparison alone does not compare full spinor
evolution: the eigenspaces also depend on the kinetic vector. The
operator argument below controls both effects.
